#3193. ‘Inter Alia’ Starring Rosamund Pike Sells Out; ‘Hamilton’ With Christopher Jackson Tops $3M – Broadway Box Office

Inter Alia, the previewing production of Suzie Miller’s new play starring Rosamund Pike, seems about to repeat its London success here on Broadway, with the first seven-performance week selling out and grossing $993,103.

The play (opening at the Music Box Theatre on December 1) was one of the stronger performers on Broadway for the week ending November 22, along with other sell-outs A Few Good Men, Hamilton, Much Ado About Nothing, Other Desert Cities and, in its final week, The Imaginary Invalid starring Bill Irwin (grossing $599,290).

Top earner was, far and away, Hamilton, with Christopher Jackson back in the role of George Washington (through January 3), sending box office soaring to $3,039,502. Closest runner-up was Other Desert Cities at $2,562,632. Next, in order, were Much Ado About Nothing ($2,073,288), The Lion King ($1,936,616), and Harry Potter and the Cursed Child ($1,699,842). Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Steven Hack Dies: Actor On 'American Horror Story', 'Ratched', 'Marvel's Agent Carter', 'General Hospital'; Original Cast Member Of Broadway's 'Cats' Was 68 News West End Hit 'The Comedy About Spies' Will Transfer To Broadway This Spring

Other Desert Cities, with Julia Louis-Dreyfus leading a cast that includes Ed Harris, Allison Janney, Joe Keery and Lily Rabe, was, as usual, the priciest Broadway option, with an average ticket price of a whopping $328.88. Hamilton was the runner-up at $284.20. No other show broke the $200 mark, with the average ticket for all 38 productions going for $128.75.

Another recent arrival of the fall season, the acclaimed Here There Are Blueberries, had an excellent week at the Barrymore, grossing $1,035,188 and filling 99% of seats. Much Ado About Nothing, starring Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell, continued doing gangbusters, grossing $2,073,288 for its opening week, even with press tickets and opening night comps.

The Fantasticks, at the Hayes in a production by the nonprofit Second Stage, grossed $375,151, filling 95% of the seats.

Galileo had a fairly rough week at the Shubert, with star Raúl Esparza missing four performances due to a concussion suffered during a rehearsal (he returned to the show Friday, November 20). In previews, the musical took in $699,975 for six performances, down about $10,000 from the previous week when there were only five performances. Still, 92% of seats were occupied, with an average ticket price of $92.71; opening night is December 6.

Attendance at Downstate, the critically acclaimed play at the Booth, was at 94% of capacity, for a gross of $377,378, and Wanted, at 86% at the James Earl Jones, grossed $661,143.

A few specialty, holiday-season productions pulled so-so crowds last week, with the magic-illusion show Now You See Me Live selling about 77% of seats at the Hirschfeld for a gross of $648,118, while Blue Man Group’s A New Holiday Surprise opened at the Lunt-Fontanne on November 17, filling 60% of seats for the week at a modest average ticket price of $44.36 and an equally slim $317,376 gross. It’s A Wonderful Life: A Live Radio Play, in previews at the Broadhurst (it opened last night following a November 18 gala performance) sold about 76% of available seats for a $457,581 gross.

Chicago grossed $1,182,400 for the week, donating net proceeds from the 30th anniversary Monday performance to the Entertainment Community Fund. And Buena Vista Social Club took in $917,221, filling 96% of seats at the Schoenfeld and announcing that former New York Yankees player-turned-musician Bernie Williams will be extending his limited engagement in the show through the end of the musical’s run on January 17, 2027.

In all, the 38 Broadway productions grossed a total $40,374,391 for the week ending November 22, about the same as the previous week and even with last year at this time. Attendance was 313,587, down 2% from the previous week but up 8% year-to-year.

In the 26th week of the 2026-27 season, Broadway has grossed $843,441,665 season-to-date, down about 7% from last year at this time, with total attendance of 6,853,368 down 2% year-to-year.

All figures courtesy of The Broadway League. For more box office information visit the League’s web.

#3191. UGREEN’s excellent liquid cooled 25W MagSafe battery for iPhone is now 40% off

Recently, UGREEN introduced a new Qi2.2 25W 10000mAh MagSafe battery bank for iPhone. There have been plenty of these, but this one has an interesting new twist: liquid cooling. For Black Friday, it’s on sale for 40% off, making it more affordable than ever.

On the back of the battery, there’s a window that showcases the liquid within the battery bank moving throughout it. This should help keep it a little bit cooler than most MagSafe battery banks.

UGREEN says that it’ll be around 18 degrees cooler than usual, and while that’s probably true – it’s worth nothing that it still isn’t a cold battery bank, it’s just cooler than usual. It’ll still feel warm in your hand.

On the bottom of the battery bank, UGREEN integrates a USB-C cable for charging your phone or any other USB-C device that can’t (or you prefer not to) charge wirelessly. I found it a bit handy at times, since of course wireless charging is never as energy efficient as wired charging.

I will admit, the battery bank is a little bit thick, and the lack of a kickstand is somewhat bothersome at this price point, especially when so many others offer one. That said, if heat is a concern of yours with MagSafe battery banks, this one will definitely solve that for you.

On the side, it offers a small display for showing battery percentage and charging speed.

One last thing of note: if you’re buying an iPhone Duo, this will stick out from the bottom of the phone. This is true for most MagSafe accessories on iPhone Duo, though.

The UGREEN MagFlow battery bank comes in at $149, which is quite pricey for a MagSafe battery of any kind. For Black Friday, it’s on sale for just $90.23 on Amazon for Prime members, making it much more palatable if you’re looking for a MagSafe battery bank that doesn’t get as hot as the competition.

#3189. 10 Shows Like 'Yellowjackets' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end. Whether or not it sticks the landing, it's been one helluva ride, and we'll soon have room in the streaming schedule for other other shows about young people having a pretty rough go of it while just trying to survive.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, not just a show about girlfights. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami. The island was formerly home to a prestigious high school, and a bunch of students have snuck back for an ill-timed party on the last day of class. A bad idea, clearly, after the storm hits. Kraam (Papangkorn Lerkchaleampote), one of the few students who actually lives on the island, is trapped there along with a couple dozen classmates. Kraam knows the island, but Anan (Chutavuth Pattarakampol) assumes leadership while other students either take on necessary roles or fall in line. As the miniseries progresses, the new social order breaks down, even as the island's mysteries reveal themselves and things get weirder and more complex. Stream The Stranded on Netflix.

A handful of influencers get invited to a remote island, which is obviously a very good thing to agree to that will not lead to dramatic complications in any way. Behind the neon-lit party vibes, there's a cult at work and some ritualistic shenanigans with deadly consequences. Eden is more concerned with the survival horror than with some of the deeper themes and mysteries of Yellowjackets, but we're still playing with shifting power dynamics in this Spanish import. Stream Welcome to Eden on Netflix.

The premise of The Leftovers is brilliantly subdued: Around two percent of the world's population disappears without explanation, and it's enough to upend just about everything. Politics have adapted to the new normal, religions have collapsed and reformed, and families have had to make peace with the inexplicable loss of loved ones. The first season revolves around the Garvey family, led by Kevin (Justin Theroux), a sheriff whose wife (Amy Brenneman) left him to join a cult, while subsequent seasons broaden the scope to bring in other characters in other locations. It's more philosophical than Yellowjackets, and quieter, but the shows share an interest in the lingering effects of trauma, and in the stuff we get up to under threat and in the dark. Stream The Leftovers on HBO Max.

The 100 tells the story of the descendants of refugees of nuclear devastation who return to Earth from their habitat in space to encounter the remnants of humanity who have survived on Earth. Naturally, the first people sent to scope things out are the juvenile delinquents (better them than me), and they discover that three civilizations have risen up in the aftermath of the apocalypse, and they are all pretty scary (including one populated by cannibals, naturally). More sci-fi than horror, but the survivalist themes and mysteries here make it more than a decent match. The show builds an impressive mythology over the course of its run, leading to a conclusion that’s borderline metaphysical. Stream The 100 on Pluto TV or buy it from Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

A massive apocalyptic tidal wave strikes during the 10-year reunion of the graduating class of an all-girls high school. The event leaves them all trapped together (a nightmare in any event), and forced to survive while reliving old struggles and dramas. It's Yellowjackets-esque, absolutely, but also Australian and a comedy, which doesn't feel like as much of a stretch as you'd think given the over-the-top nature of that show. Stream Class of '07 on Prime Video.

A remote, charming town with some deep, dark secrets (the biggest of which, and one that it shares with Yellowjackets, is rather strongly hinted in the title), Gannibal stars Yuya Yagira as Daigo Agawa, a police officer from the big city who takes a job in the super cute (and, of course, remote) village of Kuge following some personal trouble. The perfectly charming Goto family runs the town, more or less, and welcomes Daigo and his family. It's all looking pretty great—until a mysterious man gives Daigo's daughter a severed finger as a gift, and his wife Yuki finds the words "Run Away" scrawled over a door in their new home. Just a couple of reasons why I'm more of a city person. Stream Gannibal on Disney+ and Hulu.

This latter-day plane crash narrative goes all-in on mystery and philosophy, virtually pioneering the timey-wimey reveal format that makes Yellowjackets so juicy. We kick off with flashbacks that peel back the layers of the various crash survivors before diving headfirst into warm-weather polar bears and mysterious underground bunkers and monsters made of smoke. Whether it's an uncommonly smart network show that rewards careful viewing or a load of nonsense is in the eye of the beholder—but it remains one of the most discussed and debated shows in TV history. Stream Lost on Disney+ and Hulu.

Kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense new forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

One of Apple’s most beloved products this year was undoubtedly the MacBook Neo. Unlike some of its other budget products, Apple seems interested in updating the MacBook Neo on an annual cycle, and we may get the next MacBook Neo around March.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is targeting the iOS/macOS 27.4 release cycle for the release of the new MacBook Neo, as well as the A19 budget iPad, iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and OLED iPad Air.

While he notes that this cycle runs between February and March, it doesn’t necessarily mean the products will launch on the earlier end of that spectrum. As expected, the next MacBook Neo will bump up from the A18 Pro chip with 8GB of RAM to the A19 Pro chip with 12GB of RAM.

Apple will also introduce new colors on the MacBook Neo “frequently,” though it’s unclear if we’ll see that with the next iteration. From the Power On newsletter:

The other thing I’ve heard is that Apple plans to refresh the MacBook Neo’s colors frequently. We’ll see if that trend starts with the first follow-up.

I’m certainly excited to see the next generation MacBook Neo, especially with 12GB of unified memory. While 8GB is certainly fine, heavy multitaskers will notice it, especially with unoptimized software.

The bigger question is: will the next MacBook Neo have a price increase? With additional RAM included, it feels inevitable.

Hopefully backlit keyboard if they increase price

Apple increased the price of MacBook Neo from $599 to $699 back in June, and in October the company also silently decreased the education discount by $50, meaning the education price has increased from $499 to $649 since launch.

#3187. Broadway Producers & Stagehands Union Reach Tentative Contract Deal, Avoiding Holiday Strike

The Broadway League and IATSE Local One of theater workers have reached a tentative deal to avoid a strike that could have disrupted the lucrative holiday season. The agreement is pending ratification by union members.

In a joint statement from the League and the union, the two sides announced “they have reached a tentative agreement, pending ratification by the bargaining unit. The respective parties will inform their members of the details of this agreement in the coming days.”

The union said details of the tentative agreement will be provided to Local One members ahead of the Local’s December membership meeting, when members will decide whether to ratify the agreement. That meeting is scheduled for December 20. Related Stories News 'Inter Alia' Starring Rosamund Pike Sells Out; 'Hamilton' With Christopher Jackson Tops $3M - Broadway Box Office News Steven Hack Dies: Actor On 'American Horror Story', 'Ratched', 'Marvel's Agent Carter', 'General Hospital'; Original Cast Member Of Broadway's 'Cats' Was 68

Local One represents thousands of theater workers who build, install, maintain and operate Broadway’s productions systems including staging and scenery, lighting, sound, video and special effects. Watch on Deadline

The union’s previous agreement with the League expired July 26, with negotiations underway since September. During that period, both sides agreed to narrow initial demands to focus on wage increases and benefits. Just recently Local One members authorized a strike if negotiations broke down.

Separate negotiations between the League, the trade organization representing producers and theater owners, and the Theatrical Wardrobe Union IATSE Local 764 are ongoing. The local has authorized a strike if a deal isn’t reached.

In its announcement about today’s deal, IATSE added, “Local 764 members have been bargaining with The Broadway League since June, and their previous agreement expired July 26. The League canceled bargaining sessions scheduled for November 18 and 19, and Local 764 has called on the League and Broadway producers to immediately set new dates and return to the table.

“Among the major unresolved issues are wages and a longstanding gender pay gap affecting Broadway wardrobe workers. Wardrobe work on Broadway has historically been performed predominantly by women and paid at significantly lower rates than stagehand classifications historically held predominantly by men. Although recent negotiations have narrowed that gap, Local 764 department heads today must work nearly 45 percent longer to earn pay comparable to workers in similar department-head roles.”

Local 764 members, according to the union, are seeking an agreement “that continues progress toward pay equity and does not widen that longstanding disparity.

iOS 27 includes a really clever new feature that aims to solve the awkward middle ground between cellular and Wi-Fi connectivity. Here’s how it works and how you can turn it on.

In a support document, Apple explains that Connectivity Assist uses cellular data to improve your connection when Wi-Fi is slow or unusable. Apple uses examples like your backyard or driveway, as well as “coffee shops, airports, sports venues, and everywhere in between.”

Essentially, the feature detects when your Wi-Fi connection is weak or unusable and intelligently uses cellular data to keep you connected.

One practical example I’ve noticed is when I walk out of my house and get in my car. Oftentimes, my iPhone will cling to my house’s weak Wi-Fi connection, making it hard to start playing Apple Music and queue up directions in Apple Maps.

Connectivity Assist solves that problem. My phone can now intelligently use cellular data to help that transition away from Wi-Fi. It’s one of many really nice quality-of-life improvements in iOS 27.

Another thing to be aware of is that you might use more cellular data with Connectivity Assist turned on. You can monitor your data usage via your carrier’s app or website, as well as in the Settings app on iPhone.

Cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

At its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a big payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

The true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3180. Five recent tech outages were not due to AI; the next round will be

Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.

That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future …

Earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other. A widespread Microsoft 365 outage occurred when two unrelated issues coincided. The next day saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centers. A few days later, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Many Apple services went offline later the same week, with retail stores also affected. Finally, United Airlines had its own widespread IT outage that grounded a significant number of flights.

Each had their own unrelated causes, with the White House stating that rumors of an AI-facilitated systemic attack by a hostile state were false.

However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that we should expect future tech outages as a result of attacks facilitated by AI-discovered vulnerabilities. CNBC reports him issuing the warning on CNN’s State of the Union.

The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.

You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot.

We already saw an example of this last month when a vulnerability discovered in PHP saw a significant number of websites being taken offline.

Microsoft President Brad Smith says it isn’t just a question of bad actors exploiting vulnerabilities discovered by AI, but companies rushing to patch these may inadvertently cause systems to fail, as Newsweek reports.

What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems.

Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you’re trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can’t take as much time to test what you’re changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong.

Major IT failures look set to be a routine event in the coming weeks and months.

#3177. As Apple works on AI agent features, banks are already blocking them

One of the most dramatic shifts in the AI landscape is the emergence of intelligent agents that can use iPhone and Mac apps in order to carry out tasks on our behalf.

We can already use third-party chatbots in this way, and we know Apple is working hard to turn Siri AI into an agent. However, before the company even gets the chance, banks are already blocking them, and this may be just the start …

The science fiction promise of AI has always been to be able to tell a computer what we want done and have the task carried out for us automatically. That’s starting to turn into a reality with the emergence of AI agents.

We’ve already seen Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Muse gain agent capabilities, and Apple is expected to bring these to Siri AI at some point next year.

Earlier this month, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said that the company ultimately wants to go in this direction and may add these abilities next year. CEO John Ternus has reportedly been pushing Craig Federighi for faster software development, with specific mention of “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” which seems likely to mean agentic capabilities.

Last week also saw a since-deleted Apple job listing detailing plans for autonomous AI agents.

We’ve already seen some of the ways in which this can go wrong, and we recently outlined three significant risks. Wired reports that banks are now responding to these by either blocking AI agents or warning customers that using them can be dangerous.

JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

Wells Fargo even goes as far as using capitals in its latest terms, stating that it will not be responsible for the consequences.

Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK

We can likely expect similar pushback in sectors like online shopping as companies fear high returns costs and other consequences from mistakes by AI agents.

Personally, I don’t give any AI agents access to any of my banking or other financial services, considering the risks to be too high. I don’t see my position changing any time soon.

What’s your take? Would you trust an AI agent with access to your bank accounts? If not, would Apple launching agentic capabilities for Siri AI change your view? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3176. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Creating Glenn Close’s Over-the-Top Looks by Leaning Into Drusilla’s ‘Narcissist’ Nature

Being a member of Capitol society in Panem is an honor not to be taken lightly, at least if you’re Drusilla Sickle, played by screen legend Glenn Close in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”

In the book, Drusilla is the cruel and vain escort for Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) and the rest of the District 12 tributes in the 50th Hunger Games, where she uses over-the-top fashion to broadcast her social status. Close worked closely with costume designer Bina Daigeler and hair, makeup and prosthetics designer Natalie MacGowan Spencer to ensure the character translated properly from Suzanne Collins’ best-selling prequel novel to the screen. Related Stories Tony Awards Will Remain on CBS Through 2032 Under New Five-Year Deal 'NCIS: New York' Sells Across 135 Markets Globally (EXCLUSIVE)

One challenge Daigeler faced was meeting Close’s request that each outfit felt connected, creating a through line that explained why Drusilla changes from one look to the next. Despite the drastic differences between each outfit, Daigeler established continuity through the character’s accessories, most notably a collection of gold medals and military-inspired epaulets that created a sense of authority.

“She wears all these medals, because somehow she thinks she is the top general of the capital,” Daigeler tells Variety.

And, not dissimilar to red-bottomed Louboutin shoes, Daigeler gave Drusilla dramatically long black nails that were painted red underneath to show her abundant wealth.

The character’s Capitol allegiance also went beyond her wardrobe, with Spencer overseeing her hair and makeup. While creating the looks, Spencer relied heavily on Collins’ source material to remain faithful to the author’s vision. Collins describes Drusilla as having implanted tabs that pull the skin on her face back, which Spencer wanted to honor. But because there wasn’t enough time each morning for an extensive prosthetics process, Spencer turned to Hollywood tape to tightly pull Close’s skin back, creating a distorted appearance. She later added tabs on the sides of Close’s face to complete the illusion, along with fake teeth that heightened Drusilla’s “scary” and “eerie” appearance.

“[Glenn] really wanted to pull it so taut that it changed all of her facial features, which it really did,” Spencer tells Variety.

Daigeler and Spencer’s shared mission: to create visuals that resonate with the franchise’s devoted fans — who “know their stuff inside out,” Spencer quips. “They’re so passionate.” When the book was released and casting announcements began rolling out, Spencer would regularly check social media to see what fans envisioned for the adaptation and what details they hoped to see on screen.

Below, Spencer and Daigeler break down the process of creating each of Drusilla’s costumes, hair and makeup, as well as the inspiration behind each look.

Drusilla makes her grand entrance at the District 12 reaping, wheeled into the frame wearing a bold yellow ensemble. The outfit is a stark contrast to the muted colors worn throughout Panem’s poorest district — the exact irony Spencer and Daigeler hoped to portray by making that the character’s brightest look in the film.

“It shouldn’t have any practicality. That is why she was driven in,” Daigeler says of the tightly-cinched yellow coat dress. “It was supposed to be very stiff.”

To complement the dress’ high collar, Spencer styled Close with an orange bob that also paid homage to the film’s ‘70s aesthetic. At Close’s request, the look was completed with a raven headpiece — which, to be clear, was not an intentional nod to Lenore Dove’s name poem.

“For me, that sort of represents the children of the district — something that’s taxidermied and dead on their head,” Spencer says about the headpiece. “And [Drusilla’s] so proud of that statement.”

Black medals and military-inspired shoulder plates further accentuated the ensemble, reinforcing Drusilla’s self-appointed authority. “She looked like a yellow general,” Daigeler adds.

When representing District 12 at the Capitol’s chariot parade, Drusilla’s color palette dims to an all-black look that publicly links her to the district’s coal-mining industry. To elevate the outfit and solidify her Capitol status, Daigeler experimented with different textures to create the illusion of leather-like skin while also keeping her gold medals and fringed military epaulets.

“We wanted to give it strength,” Daigeler says of the outfit, which, she notes, also signals that things are getting more serious in the film’s storyline. “We wanted it to be a little bit aggressive and very demanding. And very Capitol.”

Close initially wanted to style the look with an extravagant, fluffy hat, but she and Spencer ultimately settled on a simpler black wig with pointed horns so as not to distract from Drusilla’s face. The shorter bangs draw more attention to the exaggerated eye makeup and the face-slimming tabs.

Drusilla settles on a softer green dress for the tributes’ interviews with Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin), which once again challenged Daigeler to maintain the character’s threads between outfit changes.

“Where’s the strength? Where’s the craziness?” she asked herself when accessorizing Drusilla’s third look, a crepey, olive-hued gown with a high neck and massive, billowy sleeves.

This time, Daigeler forwent Drusilla’s medallions and instead made a statement by adding red gloves, tights and boots, paired with spiky necklaces.

Spencer leaned further into the softer ensemble by adding a wave to Drusilla’s hair, washed with a light shade of pink. “I really like fabrics and the colors and how the hair and makeup is going to be one big look altogether,” Spencer notes.

Drusilla’s final appearance comes after Haymitch is declared the victor of the 50th Hunger Games — or, at least in Drusilla’s mind, after she is declared the victor. Complete with a purple sash, the look was designed to make it seem as though Drusilla herself had won the games.

This was the only outfit not described in Collins’ novel, giving Daigeler the creative freedom to execute her own vision. Knowing Drusilla would appear on the colorful stage, she wanted to put her in a bold red ensemble that would ensure she stood out.

Without a predetermined silhouette in mind, Daigeler drew inspiration from designers Alexander McQueen, Talyano and Balenciaga, as well as Renaissance-era shapes.

“I went to a beautiful fabric store in London, and I just found all these beautiful, different textured red fabrics,” Daigeler says. “I didn’t have it clear what would be the silhouette of the dress, but I knew that it should be an evening gown and somehow huge and over the top.”

Spencer completed the transformation by leaning into the showgirl-inspired makeup, settling on a bright red lip and feathered hair.

“[Drusilla’s] like a performer. When you really do think about it, she’s a narcissist. ‘This is me. I’m bold. I’m dominant,'” Spencer says. “We had all the showgirls — all of those big colors and the feathers and everything else, so it’s almost like a carnival of entertainers coming together on the stage. The set design, the colors, all the background people in the crowd are so, so important. What you’re portraying is a performance. It’s entertainment, and that’s who they are.”

#3174. The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

We’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

And focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

Digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:

When time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

Sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

SpiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

Mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

Flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

#3172. Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, stock up 30%

Nvidia has announced that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately. The company’s share price jumped more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also making significant gains.

It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so …

Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month. The New York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the company’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days. Things got even worse when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

That led to Huang being fired resigning on November 12.

Despite putting the company at enormous risk and initially lying to its board of directors, there were calls in some quarters for Huang to be reinstated. He responded by saying that he would be “honored” to return if asked to do so.

The board of directors, however, said that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones said: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”

That changed today, with the company making the announcement in a press release.

Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The company’s stock price jumped by more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also up per Yahoo Finance.

Nvidia shares soared more than 30% Monday morning […] The S&P 500 (^GSPC) rose 4.5% following seven straight days of declines. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) jumped more than 1,200 points to recover by 2.5% following its worst week since the COVID-related sell-off in 2020. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) rallied 7%.

#3170. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

Early 2027 is going to be a surprisingly important period for the iPhone, and it's all thanks to the iPhone 18. Rather than release the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 in the fall, both phones have are reportedly launching early next year — with rumors claiming they'll arrive alongside iPhone 18e in the spring.

Now that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo are out in the world, the rumors are starting to reveal more about the three upcoming iPhones. The latest leaks suggest that we may even see some design changes, especially in the look and feel of the rear cameras.

First look at the iPhone 18 Air and iPhone 18 dummy units. The biggest change is the iPhone 18 Air, which now features two rear cameras instead of one, while the standard iPhone 18 retains a design similar to the iPhone 17. https://t.co/MdOVuwPlm3November 20, 2026

According to dummy units leaked by Sonny Dickson, the iPhone 18 will look more or less the same as the iPhone 17, complete with the two vertical camera lenses on the back. The iPhone Air 2 will apparently be similar to the original iPhone Air, albeit with an additional camera lens.

That's right, the iPhone Air 2 could fix one of its biggest issues and take some visual inspiration from the iPhone Duo in the process. However, the camera bar on the dummy units does stretch across the entire width of the phone, whereas the iPhone Duo only covers around three quarters of a single side.

It's likely that this is an ultrawide camera, which should mean the Air 2's camera capabilities will be closer to that of the iPhone 18 rather than the (presumably) single-camera iPhone 18e. That's even more likely when you remember that telephoto lenses take up a lot of space, and considering the slimline nature of the iPhone Air, that space is already at a premium.

Of course, we do need to be wary of all sorts of leaks and claims online, especially since Dickson recently posted alleged Galaxy S27 Ultra dummy units that contradict every rumor we've heard so far. So take these designs with a grain of salt.

While the iPhone 18 may not be getting any changes (if Dickson's dummy units are to be believed), the same may not be true for the iPhone 18e. Engadget claims to have seen CAD files of the phone, and apparently it could be coming with a square-shaped camera bump.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The site also claims that other CAD images showcase the iPhone Air 2 with a second rear camera, and an iPhone 18 that is mostly unchanged from the iPhone 17.

Engadget doesn't provide any of the CAD images, or even renders of what the redesigned camera bump might look like. However, Engadget says it looks like the square module on the back of the iPad Pro M5, which gives us some idea of what this alleged redesign could look like — assuming the claims are actually true.

Personally, I'm a little bit skeptical, on account of the fact that we don't actually see the CAD images that are referenced in the initial report. Likewise, I'm not so sure Apple would redesign the iPhone 18e's camera bump considering the E-series cameras have so far been solo camera lenses with a pinhead-sized microphone and LED flash. A boxed-in bump seems like an odd design choice.

Plus, that redesign wouldn't really work if the iPhone 18 does stick with the same design as before. I'd be more inclined to believe reports that the iPhone 18 would get a square camera bump, but we don't know if such a thing will happen. Dickson's dummy unit, and Engadget's own reporting, suggest not.

We'll find out for sure next year, and current rumors suggest that these three phones will arrive in February or March.

A reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to the most comparable GAAP measure is available on our earnings materials on the company's Investor Relations website. Following our prepared remarks, we will conduct a question-and-answer session with our team. As previously communicated in our press release on our management transition, we will not be providing 2027 guidance today. With that, I'm pleased to turn the call over to Axel beginning on Slide 4.

Axel Meier: Thank you, Chris, and welcome to everyone joining us on this call. I would like to start by reiterating that the recent management changes have proven experience in financial management, operational transformation, manufacturing and customer delivery as Fluence works to strengthen production systems and processes, improve execution and reinforce financial discipline. The management changes also reflect the continued strong support from our controlling shareholders, Siemens and AES, and their confidence in Fluence's potential and significant market opportunity. In terms of my own background, I have more than 3 decades of experience at Siemens, including senior leadership positions in communications, industry and infrastructure. Most recently, I served as the CFO of Siemens Smart Infrastructure.

In that role, I helped to shape the business into a strong and reliable performer, delivering 23 consecutive quarters of year-over-year profit margin expansion and disciplined cash conversion, while at the same time, significantly growing the business. I was one of the first members of the Fluence Board of Directors in 2020, and thus, I have a long history with the company and a deep understanding of its business. I continue to believe that Fluence is well positioned to succeed in this rapidly growing energy storage market.

As we noted in our recent press release, the Board is keenly focused on strengthening Fluence's ability to capitalize on its competitive capabilities, including our differentiated products and our record $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ] backlog as of the end of fiscal '26. Our transformation strategy is designed to deliver on commitments to customers and suppliers, improve financial and operational execution, prioritize profitable growth and strengthen cash generation. Bernerd will add more color today on what we mean by each of these objectives, but we are not yet in a position to provide details. However, we do expect to provide 2027 financial guidance on our first quarter call in February. Turning to Slide 5.

I'll review the highlights of our fourth quarter and full year results. We had order intake of $3.5 billion in quarter 4 2026, approximately 150% higher than our previous best of $1.4 billion just set last quarter. We ended the quarter with a backlog of $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ], representing 39% growth over the third quarter and 68% growth over the $5.3 billion at our last fiscal year's end. Total liquidity at quarter end was approximately $855 million, in line with our liquidity at the end of the third quarter.

These were key achievements in fiscal year 2026, but our overall performance did not result in the profitability required to create value for our shareholders, nor did we deliver on the commitments that we have made to our customers and suppliers. This new management team has committed to the transformation of our business expected to convert our backlog into profitable growth as measured by EBITDA. Now to Slide 6 for an update on market demand trends. We're continuing to see rapid growth in the energy storage market across our key customer segments. Increasing electrification and competitive pricing for storage relative to new generation and a growing number of applications for battery storage are driving this growth.

Developers view storage as a way to enhance project economics. Utilities see storage as a means of shaving peak demand and reinforcing voltage across the grid. Data centers see storage as a critical path to improving the quality and speed to power. Fluence is well positioned with respect to all of these customer segments, and we have been receiving interest from each of them as reflected in our strong order intake. Turning to Slide 7. As I noted earlier, quarter 4 2026 order intake was a record of $3.5 billion, accounting for more than half of the full year '26 of total $6.2 billion.

Following our revised guidance call in mid-September, we booked approximately 70% of our fourth quarter orders, reconfirming customer confidence in Fluence's capabilities. Our fourth quarter total also included $586 million of orders that were awarded by a hyperscaler as we discussed on our third quarter earnings call. We are seeing ongoing momentum in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 and expect it to continue in future quarters, driven by demand across power developers, utilities and data centers. We do have a healthy mix of both new and repeat customers and orders continue to be concentrated in our core markets, U.S., Europe and Australia. Please turn to Slide 8 as I discuss the growth of our backlog.

As I noted earlier, the strong order intake during the fourth quarter resulted in the growth of our backlog to $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ] at September 30. Approximately 1/3 of our backlog is expected to convert to revenues in each of the next 3 fiscal years. Our backlog continues to reflect the accelerated growth we are harnessing in the U.S., which accounted for approximately 70% of our total backlog, up from 58% in fiscal year 2025. From a customer segmentation standpoint, developers and power producers are the largest segment, followed by utilities and data centers, which account for 10% of our backlog today and represents our fastest-growing customer segment.

Turning to Slide 9 and the competitive advantages of our Smartstack products. From a product standpoint, Smartstack represents over half of our backlog, and we expect that percentage will grow further as we deliver the remainder of our older product lines. This represents a rapid adoption rate when considering that Smartstack was launched relatively recently. Although we have shared these points in the past, I think it's worth reiterating why we believe that our Smartstack product is gaining traction with customers so quickly: higher energy density, which reduces the size of the required area of footprint; modular design, which allows Smartstack units to be deployed in 5 parts, including our Smart Skid with 4 battery modules.

This enables customers to deploy Smartstack with a forklift instead of a crane; available with domestic content, allowing our customers to capture U.S. tax credit. Fluence's products have a strong track record of availability as validated by DNV with 99% fleet performance availability for large energy storage projects; fire safety testing and cybersecurity features, both of which are designed to give our customers confidence in our product; integrated hardware and operating system, which provides an improved ability to smooth load and carry out other functions. Smartstack is a result of the internal product development by Fluence, coupled with the strength of our suppliers.

Now I'd like to turn the call over to Ricardo Roizen, who will review our fiscal 2026 results in more detail and provide an update on liquidity, beginning on Slide 11.

Ricardo Roizen Gottlieb: Thank you, Axel. First, I'd like to share with you a bit of my background and experience that I'm bringing to Fluence at this critical time. I have worked at AES for 18 years, most recently serving as CFO of AES Andes. My experience gives me not only a familiarity with the energy generation industry, but also a deep understanding of the perspective of a long-term strategic shareholder and the importance of delivering sustainable value for all our shareholders. AES Andes has also been a customer of Fluence, so I am already familiar with the company and our products. Much of my background has centered on financial discipline, cash and working capital management, capital allocation and operational execution.

These areas are particularly relevant to Fluence as we focus on strengthening execution, improving margins and cash generation and positioning the company for sustainable profitable growth. Turning now to our fiscal 2026 results on Slide 12. Revenue for the fiscal fourth quarter was $744 million and for the full year, we generated revenues of $2.3 billion, with both periods coming in below our forecast, primarily driven by delays in project delivery due to production shortfalls at our contracted manufacturing facility in Houston. A key driver impacting our full year results was approximately $90 million of penalties associated with delayed deliveries. Adjusted EBITDA for the fourth quarter was negative $112 million and for the full year was negative $203 million.

These results were also impacted by $85 million, primarily due to cost overruns associated with equipment and manufacturing costs related to the delivery of new products, in addition to $25 million of increased sales and marketing expenses and R&D expense. While this performance is disappointing, our transformation strategy is structured to address this impact, as Bernerd will discuss shortly. Please turn to Slide 13 for an overview of our liquidity profile. We ended the year with total liquidity of $855 million, which includes $379 million in cash. This is consistent with our position at the end of the third quarter. During the fourth quarter, we built our inventory position to $970 million, more than double the year ago.

75% of this inventory is equipment and materials awaiting assembly into our finished products, some of which has already been delivered to customers from our Houston facility. The remaining inventory is finished product as of September 30. These materials are expected to fulfill customer delivery commitments that will then convert to revenue and cash in fiscal year 2027. Our intent is to recycle this working capital into new projects in our backlog, supporting our expectation for no external capital needs during fiscal year 2027. Our revolver is one of the credit facilities included in our total liquidity profile.

We are proactively working with our banks to address the EBITDA covenant in our revolving credit facility through an amendment and extension, which was also granted last year. At the same time, the issues we experienced at our new manufacturing facilities are being resolved and operational performance is improving. With that, I will turn the call over to Bernerd to cover our transformation strategy, beginning on Slide 15.

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Thank you, Ricardo. In my prior position at AES, I was involved with the creation of Fluence, then the customer of Fluence. More recently, I was named to Fluence's Board. And on September 16, I became the company's Chief Operating Officer. I have spent my career driving transformation, performance and expansion across multiple businesses at AES, including as the Chief Executive Officer of their Clean Energy business. I would like to share with you the opportunity I see with Fluence and why I was motivated to take this role. As Axel discussed, battery storage has entered a period of accelerating growth. In my view, once-in-a-generation opportunity driven by falling prices and increasing applications.

Fluence is a leading participant in this industry with very competitive terms as reflected by our order intake and backlog. The challenge in front of us is to deliver on this backlog with execution that drives profitability. During my career, I have successfully faced and resolved execution issues similar to those that Fluence has been experiencing. And I am confident that these are solvable. These fixes must be made with urgency and discipline so we can reach our goals. Turning to Slide 16. Over the next 5 slides, I will outline our transformation strategy. We have 4 main pillars: delivering on our commitments to customers and suppliers, improving financial and operational execution, prioritizing profitable growth and strengthening cash generation.

I will address each of these in turn, beginning on Slide 17. First, delivering on our commitments to customers and suppliers. To realize the value of our $9 billion (sic) [ $8.9 billion ] backlog, our supply chain must supports the delivery of projects on time and on budget. To that end, we have been expanding manufacturing capacity at home and abroad. Production at our Houston facility, which was running approximately 3 units per day in early September, is now producing at 10 units per day over the past few weeks. Also, since the September call, we have welcomed customers at the Houston facility, so they can verify the progress we have made.

Across our suppliers, we now have production capacity of 25 gigawatt hours to serve our international and U.S. markets with a wide range of domestic content configurations, which supports our ability to deliver our 2027 and 2028 backlog. We expect further improvement in our facilities as well, which will position us to grow our backlog for 2028 and beyond. As we carry projects from 2026 to 2027, we are looking at the timing of expected production against our delivery commitments. In some cases, we will revisit timelines with customers who may have flexibility in order to mitigate potential penalties. In other cases, we will be discussing where contract pricing reflects the value of customization adjustments requested by the customers.

Second, improving financial and operational execution. We are working on putting systems and processes in place to enhance commercial, operational and financial discipline. For example, we are implementing a more robust pricing model with strong internal controls to help ensure a systematic approach to inputs and assumptions and our expected margins above this cost. We are also strengthening our integrated planning process across materials, production and delivery. This will help mitigate the potential for cost overruns such as those we experienced in the fiscal year 2026. Third, prioritizing profitable growth.

There are a few components to prioritizing customer segments and markets in order to most effectively allocate our resources: improving pricing discipline, particularly for customization adjustments, strengthening project execution to achieve gross margin and profit targets on a project-by-project basis, and reviewing and rightsizing our cost structure. Additionally, given the size of our backlog, over time, we expect to achieve economies of scale in cost of goods sold. The fourth pillar is to strengthen cash generation and avoid accessing capital markets. We will protect liquidity by looking at cash commitments and expenditures and recycling working capital into new projects. Longer term, we will generate positive cash flow by improving profitability.

With that, I will now turn the call back over to Axel for closing remarks on Slide 21.

Axel Meier: Thank you, Bernerd. In summary, we are focused on implementing our transformation strategy to deliver on commitments to customers and suppliers, improve financial and operational execution, prioritize profitable growth and strengthen cash generation. These fixes are being made with urgency and discipline so we can restore the confidence of our shareholders, lenders, customers, suppliers and employees. We look forward to sharing updates on our progress.
