Can you comment on expectations for margin recovery in fiscal '27? Do you anticipate any additional kind of project-related costs, onetime items, liquidated damages extending into fiscal '27? And then just wondering, like is the 10% to 15% adjusted gross margin range still the right level we should be thinking about longer term here?

Axel Meier: Justin, it's Axel. Let me frame it this way. So if I look into last fiscal year, in particular in quarter 4, I'd say there's three elements which yielded into the loss we were realizing. The one is we had this challenge on the ramp-up in our Houston facility, which prevented us from basically executing on the revenue with the lost margin associated with this, first comment. The second comment is if you don't deliver, you run the risk of liquidated damages. A big part of liquidated damages we saw in the last fiscal year were contributing based on this fact.

And the third one is cost overruns, where we, to some degree, underestimated new products, which we launched in the market. Now having said this, number one and number two are being addressed as we talk when it comes to safeguarding the capacity in our manufacturing environment. On the cost side, we are driving transformation. We are tightening the activities within the company, optimizing cost position there in order to realize the margin quality we also have booked. And then lastly, on your question, is 10% to 15% the right frame? Yes, it is. But I think the issue is more -- it's not the short term. It's something which we are basically aiming for.

And I know everyone is anxious when we are laying out the guidance and how the years after will look like. So we reconfirm we will come back to you for fiscal '27 after the quarter 1 call or in the quarter 1 call. And we also have agreed in the management team that in the second half of the fiscal year, we go in depth with you with the capital markets and give you a view on the outer years.

Operator: Our next question comes from Davis Sunderland with Baird.

Davis Sunderland: Most of my questions on backlog have been covered. Maybe just one other thing to pick on there. Is there any color you can give as to the percentage of backlog or maybe the amount of backlog that is specifically domestic content tied to that Houston facility? And then I have one follow-up.

Chris Shelton: Davis, Chris Shelton. So domestic content from the Houston facility is the question. Could you just restate it maybe?

Davis Sunderland: Yes. Just trying to get a sense for how much of the backlog is planned capacity or was planned capacity to come out of that facility?

Chris Shelton: Got it. Yes. So we haven't broken down -- broken our capacity build by facility yet. I think what we've said -- what we're experiencing is particularly in the U.S., but also globally, we've got customers that are interested in either domestic content or imported solutions. So that's -- we can serve the U.S. market from -- Bernerd would have something to add on the capacity we're seeing.

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: Yes. I think when we look at the capacity, there are two things here. If we look at our backlog, our backlog has moved from being more in the 50-50 U.S. and international. Actually, when you look at 2024, probably was actually 60% international, 40% U.S. and has been in the 50-50, and now it's actually switching to be more weighted to the U.S. market than the international market. I need, for top of my mind in this moment, I think we are in the 60% in 2027 and growing in 2028 when we look at the market. If you look at the capacity, we have a wide range of our supply chain.

So when you look at the product Gridstack Pro 2000 and Gridstack Pro 5000, those are deliveries from the United States, and mostly those are products for domestic content and for the U.S. market. When you look at the Smartstack, that is really what is heavy in our backlog that you are looking, is that modularity. We can go in threshold that go as low -- we can do 0. That is the easy path to go. But we can go in any threshold that go up to 25% all the way to 100%, depending on what is the request, the customer needs in order that they can hit the ITC.

So more than the specific number of our supply chain to satisfy the U.S. market, what I will say is the flexibility of our supply chain in the way that has been structured our product, the Smartstack, in order to serve a wide range of domestic content all the way through 100%. So if you look at all of that, we sum it up probably 60% for 2027 at this point and growing due to that flexibility. Again, the acceptance of the product has been great in the market. And again, one more time, our focus is on execution.

As we open up a slot, we're going to have more capacity to bring in, and that will be more order intake and further expansion we can discuss when we enter more in date in 2027.

Davis Sunderland: That's super helpful. Maybe just one other, and it's a good segue from your last comment. Just in thinking about the order intake and the conversations you guys are having with customers, has there been anyone coming to the table who maybe previously wanted domestic content, but due to just tightness in the market or timing or whatever the reason may be, is now opting for internationally produced cells or internationally produced capacity just to get it as soon as possible? Or is there still, I guess, the preference for domestic content? And I'll leave it there.

Bernerd Raymond Da Santos Avila: No, thank you. I only will say I confirm the comment. Yes, there are customers that are looking at any range of what is called domestic content or what we call U.S. market nondomestic.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ameet Ishwar Thakkar with BMO Capital Markets.

Ameet Ishwar Thakkar: Maybe just one quick one. I think Ricardo was pretty clear that your plan doesn't involve any external capital at this point. But just is that contingent on kind of amending the revolver? I think your leverage test ratio goes to 3.5x in the beginning of 2027. Just any color there, I'd appreciate it. And if you could give us any color on kind of what drove kind of the incremental $174 million of additional nonrefundable deposits for '27 as well.

Ricardo Roizen Gottlieb: Sure. So if we step back, I would say, today, we have a strong liquidity position similar to the previous quarter. Total with all the facilities, we have $855 million. In addition to that, we have built up inventory to $970 million. So what I can tell you today is that as production improves, as Bernerd mentioned, we will be converting that inventory in cash. And we will show the improvement in the liquidity as we move forward. So we are in a solid position today. In terms of the revolver, the revolver is important. The revolver today is not drawn. It's only used for letter of credit.

And what we are doing today is that we are talking with our banks, which are relationship banks, to anticipate any potential issue to amend and extend that facility with time not to have any problem.

Operator: That concludes today's question-and-answer session. I'd like to turn the call back to Chris Shelton for closing remarks.

Chris Shelton: Thanks, everyone, for the time this morning. And please don't hesitate to reach out to me for any follow-up questions you have. I know we had a couple on the call or any others that are top of mind as you go through our disclosures. Thank you, and have a good day.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3166. The Best Early Black Friday 2026 Gaming Deals on Laptops, Consoles, Handhelds, and Accessories

Getting your gaming gear fix during the holiday shopping season is an annual tradition, but it’s more crucial this year than ever. The RAM shortage has driven up all electronics prices, right when the biggest game of all time arrives after a 13-year wait. So any discount you can score can have a big impact on your wallet. Before the main event starts, you can get started with some early Black Friday gaming deals here.

Game consoles are obviously more expensive than they used to be, even when they came out years ago. But bundle deals are still some of the best way to shave some cash off the sticker price. We’ve also got some deals on accessories, which aren’t always hit quite as hard by the component shortage, so there’s more room for savings.

Well, let’s get the bad news out of the way up front: There probably won’t be that many deals on console hardware. Certain retailers might offer discounts on bundles, but given the price increases over the last year, and the already-high demand, your best bet for those is likely checking individual retailers close to you.

Nintendo’s the only major outlier, with a discounted Switch 2 with Mario Kart World bundle for $500, or $50 off the normal retail price. That deal will be live now through Dec. 5. You can also pick up a Switch 2 bundle with Switch Sports Resort for $530. If you’re still interested in VR, you can also pick up a Meta Quest 3S bundle for $298 ($52 off) through Saturday.

PC gaming is just as susceptible to the component shortage as consoles, but since there’s a wider range of models, it’s a bit easier to find deals on individual units.

#3165. RayNeo Black Friday deals: AR smart glasses that turn your Mac and iPhone into a 307-inch screen

Still waiting for tech like the Vision Pro, but in normal everyday glasses and sunglasses? The industry leader in AR glasses shipments has something to say.

The best Apple accessories share a distinct DNA: immaculate industrial design, lightweight ergonomics, tactile physical precision, and friction-free performance that feels native from minute one. Launched globally this fall, the RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo iO pair premium materials and bleeding-edge optics with the one thing Mac and iPhone owners actually want from a display accessory — plug it in, and it works.

RayNeo isn’t a small player making a big claim here. The company took the No. 1 spot in global AR smart glasses shipments across the first half of 2026, with 24.8% market share according to IDC and 23.9% according to Counterpoint Research.

Its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is live now through November 30, with the flagship GT Max at $335 (down from $429), the lighter GT at $249 (down from $329), and the camera-free iO smart glasses at $389 (down from $499). Everything is available on RayNeo.com and Amazon US.

Watching a movie on your iPhone is convenient, but craning your neck for a comfortable view is hardly cinematic. Having a premium AR display in sunglasses form, without packing a bulky mixed-reality headset or computing puck, opens up entirely new possibilities.

The RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo GT connect to your device over a single USB-C cable. Instead of clunky goggles, the GT Series puts a massive virtual display — 59 degrees of field of view on GT Max, to be exact — into a sleek, understated sunglasses design that blends into coffee shops and airport lounges at just 68 to 78 grams. That single USB-C connection carries uncompressed video and powers the glasses directly: no secondary battery packs to carry, no charging anxiety, and zero wireless lag.

One thing to check before you buy: the glasses need a device that outputs video over USB-C (DisplayPort Alt Mode). That covers the iPhone 15, 16 and 17 series, Macs from 2015 onward with USB-C, iPad from the 10th generation on, and USB-C handhelds like the Steam Deck. The iPhone 16e, 17e and iPhone Air have USB-C ports but don’t output video over them, so they aren’t supported. Consoles and older Lightning devices need RayNeo’s HDMI adapter.

Both GT Max and GT use dual 1080p Micro-OLED panels, delivering a Full HD image to each eye with ultra-smooth 120Hz refresh rates in 2D mode. GT Max adds 38 pixels per degree, 98% DCI-P3 cinematic color coverage, and TÜV Rheinland triple eye-comfort certification. Each model offers three selectable virtual screen sizes, depending on how immersed you want to be:

GT Max’s wider field of view provides a more expansive picture, while GT offers a featherweight design. For travel, the appeal is simple: an immaculate 307-inch personal theater that slips right into your daily bag alongside your Apple gear.

The GT Series also functions as an instant, private external display for a USB-C Mac. That makes the glasses invaluable far beyond streaming media, especially when you need an expansive, shoulder-surfer-proof dual-monitor workspace on a flight, train, or co-working desk.

Both GT and GT Max include three native 3DoF hardware display modes, meaning you can position your virtual screen around your head:

Because the tracking runs on dedicated silicon inside the glasses, none of it taxes the Mac or iPhone you’re plugged into. The glasses draw minimal power directly from the connected device and include a four-speaker spatial acoustic array co-tuned by Bang & Olufsen, with a directional Whisper Mode that cuts sound leakage on a plane or in an office.

GT Max also comes in three sizes based on inter-pupillary distance (IPD) — small for under 64mm, medium for 64–67mm, large for over 67mm — ensuring a tailored, comfortable fit.

If an everyday display frame came out of Cupertino today, it would look like RayNeo iO. Rather than heavy visors, iO pairs with your iPhone through the RayNeo app to project glanceable, contextual intelligence into genuine everyday eyewear.

iO uses a high-efficiency binocular MicroLED optical engine to float high-contrast green text into your sightline, presenting a virtual image equivalent to a 33-inch screen viewed from two meters away. With peak eye-level brightness rated at 1,300 nits, reading notes and prompts stays crystal clear even under direct midday sun without occluding your real-world surroundings. The waveguide is 97% transparent and the optical engine is hidden inside the frame, so from the outside these read as ordinary glasses — most people never clock them as smart eyewear at all.

For presentations and pitches, the built-in teleprompter scrolls your notes in sync with your natural speaking cadence, so you keep your eyes locked on your audience instead of looking down at your phone. During face-to-face meetings or international travel, the glasses deliver live subtitles and two-way translation right on the lenses, with support for 55 languages and 109 accents at roughly one second of latency.

Beyond live translation and teleprompting, RayNeo iO acts as a constantly evolving heads-up companion. RayNeo pushes frequent over-the-air (OTA) software updates, continually expanding what the glasses can do throughout your day.

Just now coming to iO is heads-up turn-by-turn navigation, which projects glanceable directional arrows, street names, and real-time transit alerts directly into your line of sight. Whether you’re walking through a new city or cycling down busy streets, you can navigate without holding your iPhone in front of you or looking down at your wrist. Alongside navigation, regular software updates continue to introduce new lifestyle tools, customizable notification filters, and contextual dashboard widgets that keep the hardware feeling fresh.

There’s more coming in December, too: RayNeo is opening the iO SDK to the public, so third-party apps — and community-built ones from people with no development background — start landing on the platform shortly after the holidays.

A four-microphone array with a bone-conduction sensor captures clear audio for automated meeting minutes and AI summaries that extract key action items. RayNeo V1 and Google Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite are built in and free out of the box — no subscription required for everyday voice response, contextual reasoning, and ambient assistance. On the temple, an intuitive Smart Crown lets you scroll notifications and highlight key moments with familiar, physical micro-precision.

The titanium frames weigh just 33 grams and are rated IP54 for dust and water resistance, with a battery good for up to two days of typical use, 6.2 hours of continuous live translation, and a 25-minute charge to 80%.

iO supports Bluetooth 5.4 and carries Apple’s MFi (Made for iPhone) certification. It also has no speakers by design — which sounds like an omission until you realize what it buys you. RayNeo’s ultra-slim titanium temple arms sit flush against your ears and leave them completely free, so your AirPods stay in with Spatial Audio, Transparency Mode, and Active Noise Cancellation untouched for music and calls, while iO handles your heads-up visual intelligence.

RayNeo’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals run November 19 through November 30 on RayNeo.com and Amazon US, in two phases: the main Black Friday sale through November 26, then Black Friday Weekend and Cyber Monday from November 27 to November 30.

RayNeo GT Max is $335, down from $429 (22% off), delivering an expansive 307-inch view with the widest field of view in the lineup. RayNeo GT is $249, down from $329 (24% off), for a lighter take on the same idea. Every GT series purchase includes a complimentary RayNeo Lens Shade.

RayNeo iO is $389, down from $499 (22% off), and the bundle with the portable eyewear charging case is $428, down from $549. Two extras make the iO deal considerably better than the sticker suggests:

Bundles carry the deepest percentage discounts of the event: GT with the Pocket TV Pro streaming hub is $369 (30% off, and the combination adds native Dolby Vision playback), and GT Max with Pocket TV Pro is $469 (25% off). RayNeo.com also stacks site-wide savings on top — $20 off orders over $299, $40 off over $400, and $90 off over $600.

Elsewhere in the lineup, the Air 4 Pro is $233 (from $299), the Air 3s is $210 (from $269), Pocket TV Pro is $155 (from $199), and the JoyDock Switch adapter is $69 (from $89). The Air models hold their promotional pricing through December 7. Also new as of November 19, though at full launch price rather than a discount: the $449 RayNeo GT Max Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Limited Edition, with a sandblasted digital camo finish and a custom in-lens tactical OSD.

Ready to take your iPhone and Mac beyond the screen? Explore RayNeo GT Max and GT for a massive, private view of movies and work, or choose RayNeo iO for glanceable insight, live captioning, and camera-free AI intelligence right in sight.

The best AV receivers tested for power, sound and connectivity — these amps deliver on movie night

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your soundbar just hasn't been making your movies sound as cinematic as they deserve, then perhaps it's time you entered the world of the home theater with one of the best AV receivers.

That's how you get the best surround experience possible, after all. If you're willing to invest in some speakers as well. One per channel, of course. We never said it would be cheap.

Our favorite amplifier at the moment is the Denon AVR-X4800H. It's an excellent performer with loads of great features, and doesn't cost as much as similar options. or if you need something that handle any format you throw at it, I'd recommend the Marantz Cinema 50.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

A sonic tour de force, the X4800H is a home theater amplifier with long-term appeal. The provision of a full board of 8K/4K 120Hz HDMI inputs, and coverage of all the significant home cinema sound formats, ensures that this Denon amp will partner any display or source you might acquire for a long time to come.

It's not the smallest box, but that's because it's fill with loads of amplification tech, supporting nine channels for massive surround sound or an Atmos system. The screen on the front makes it easy to read what mode its in, and then there's an easy setup mode when you plug it into your TV or projector. From there, you can setup all of the different settings and features to get the most out of your receiver.

The sound is powerful enough to make the experience feel almost physical. The soundstage is crisp and detailed, but there is a sense of power and precision as well; directional panning is totally convincing. While Denon rates on-board power at 9x 125W (into 8 Ohms) / 200W (into 6 Ohms), it sounds rather more muscular than that.

You'll get the most out of this amplifier while watching movies, especially those with detailed sound effects and soundtracks. But this also makes it a great companion for music, with your favorite tracks coming out of the two-channel stereo sounding light and agile, with immersive 3D audio mixes.

The Marantz Cinema 50 is one of the most future-proof home theater amps we've seen. The connectivity on offer is truly impressive with 8K and 4K 120Hz support, 6 HDMI inputs plus three outputs, and an impressive auto calibration system.

Format support is extensive with Dolby Atmos, DTS:X and Auro 3D capable, as well as Sony’s 360 Reality Audio. It’s also IMAX Enhanced certified, which is a great advantage if you like to stream movies on Disney+, after the company introduced IMAX audio mixes for select movies (including a lot of Marvel) in mid-2024.

If you’re looking for an AV amp that can deliver massive dynamics, with whip-crack fast transients and a fearsome bass extension, the Cinema 50 doesn’t disappoint. It’s a tremendously exciting listen and steers gunfire shootouts beautifully, with effortless panning, and even at high volume there's no hint of strain.

It does music well too. Marantz’s lauded HDAM amplification circuitry is warm and melodious. In 2-channel mode, we’d say the Cinema 50 is comparable to a high-quality mid-range stereo amp, and with strong format support is as future-proof as they come right now.

The Marantz Cinema 70S is a half-height lifestyle AV receiver perfect for smaller spaces and viewing rooms. The sonic signature has a warm sound that works with hi-res audio as well as movies and gamers.

You can run a 5.1.2 Atmos setup with a uniform 50W delivered across all 7 channels and it was peerless with movie soundtracks. In "Army of Thieves" (Dolby Atmos, Netflix), our reviewer really got the sense that they were travelling into the inner mechanism of the safe when Ludwig Dieter lays his hands on the lock, during the safecracking competition. The clicky travel of the dial is crisply delineated against the symphonic score, which rises all around.

Hooked up to a Fire TV stick listening to Dolby Atmos music mixes from Tidal, our reviewer was thrilled at just how seamlessly the 360 presentation was. Billy Porter’s "Break A Sweat" places the listener firmly in the middle of the dance floor, with horns in the surround, the vocal dead center and the main beat gyrating across the LCR.

In our 5.1.2 configuration, there were no sonic gaps or dips with any kind of content, just a totally immersive listening experience.

When testing models for inclusion in our best AV receivers page, we play a range of media, including movies, music and games, to evaluate overall sound quality performance.

We also test any companion software that may come with an AV receiver, and factor in how easy it is to set up and use each receiver with a reference speaker system. Other features we consider include the different kinds of connectivity options, all of which determine how well it will work with your home entertainment setup.

We also take into account power output, the number of supported audio channels and subwoofer outputs, and available processing software for decoding movie soundtracks as well as their ability to handle music sources — all factors that greatly affect how each speaker will sound in your living room.

An AV receiver is an amplifier that's designed for home cinema and movie watching. You plug it into your TV with an HDMI cable, and then it takes the audio signal, and processes it for separate speakers. You need to have speakers for an AV receiver to work — it's a kind of go-between device.

You could have as many speakers as you like, although there's a minimum of two. Everything from a normal stereo (two speakers) up to a much larger surround setup (7.1 and above). It needs to be plugged into the power as well. Remember to budget for speakers with an AV receiver.

This is a big question to ask yourself. Do you have the space for multiple speakers around the room? What kind of watching do you do? Can you budget for more than two speakers?

If the answer to any of those questions is no, then you don't need an AV receiver. I'd argue, in fact, that very few people need an AV receiver — you're much better off with the space-saving capabilities of one of the best soundbars, or the musical chops of a pair of HDMI-enabled powered speakers like the Kanto Ren.

But, if you love watching movies, you've got plenty of space, plenty of budget, and permission from your significant other, then an AV receiver might be just what you've been looking for.

Everyone's movie room is different. They're different shapes and have different furniture inside, which can affect the sound of your system. In order to make movies sound their best, no matter what's in your room, manufacturers have built room correction systems that listen to the sound and then compensate for the differences in decor and shape.

Some, like Denon and Yamaha, have made their own room correction systems built into companion apps. Many amplifiers come with microphones to aid the process, and its built into the setup of the device. It's well worth going through the stages, and it can make a big difference to bass extension and surround sound placement.

Yes, you can! And you most certainly should. Your AVR can be used as the central pillar of a home music system, especially as more and more devices can connect to whole-home music streaming devices. That means you can connect your turntable, CD player, or other devices.

For turntables, there are a couple of things to bear in mind. Some AVRs do not have a built-in phono pre-amp, and so you'll need either a separate device or a TT with a pre-amp built in. If your AVR has a built-in pre-amp, you'll need to make sure you connect your TT to the correct RCA plugs. They'll be labeled "phono."

They are good for gaming, though it depends on the types of games you like to play. For immersive RPGs filled with movie-like cutscenes and massive set pieces, you're in for a sonic treat. For fast-paced online shooters, you'll likely want to stick with your gaming headset.

Just make sure that your new AVR and your TV support HDMI 2.1 for the best audio and visual experience possible. That means that 4K120Hz will be supported, along with Variable refresh rates and other game-specific features can be supported.

If you want to get the most out of the home theater experience, then you should pick up some Atmos speakers for the full effect. Without them, you won't get the spatial audio channels that make the sound come from above you — it's well worth it if you can stump up the cash.

Buying something as complex and multi-talented as an AV receiver can be overwhelming to a casual consumer, so if you’re serious about transforming your sound output into something more theater-like, start educating yourself on the necessities by familiarizing yourself with the things to consider.

Something to know right out of the gate is that most seven-channel AV receivers support a speaker configuration of 5.1.2, which is the standard 5.1 surround layout with two additional height/up-firing speakers. Models that feature nine channels of amplification can be used for either 5.1 with four Dolby height speakers (5.1.4) or 7.1 surround with two height channels (7.1.2). Speaker models such as those in the new Klipsch Reference series could make a great partnership for a home cinema setup, and has several upward-firing height speakers to meet Dolby Amos requirements.

Finding the best AV receiver isn’t just about HDMI inputs. Sure we like plenty of inputs, but the number of outputs is important too, particularly if you plan on running both a flatscreen and a projector in the same room.

If you're considering an AV receiver as a connectivity hub for a music system as well as movies, then be sure to check out our guide to the best turntables for any budget. Many of the receivers available today come with a built-in moving-magnet phono stage to enable vinyl playback from any of the record decks we've tested.

Do you need 8K or High Frame Rate HDMIs? If your AV receiver is unlikely to have a games console connected then the answer is no. In which case there are some great deals to be had on AVRs with regular HDMI 2.0 inputs.

Dolby Atmos compatibility is a given (and by default that means you’ll get DTS:X too), but how many channels do you need? Given the option, 9 channels always trump 7, because it opens up more speaker options such as 5.1.4 or 7.1.2, for example.

Don’t have a full Dolby Atmos home theater loudspeaker setup? Look for a model that offers height virtualization technology, so you can enjoy an immersive audio experience even when you don’t have a full set of physical speakers.

Power isn’t just about roof-raising volume, and even if you’re not lucky enough to have a dedicated movie room, a model with big amplification makes sense. A high power output means an AVR can deliver dynamic transients, and pressure load a space without clipping or strain.

One of the most confusing things about any kind of home cinema system is the surround sound channel numbers you'll often spot on the box. What do they mean, and what do they tell you about the receiver that you're about to buy?

Those numbers denote the channels that are available to use with the receiver. It's broken up into three different sections. The first number is the surround channels. The middle is for subwoofers. The final number is the height channels, for Dolby Atmos and DTS:X.

Say, for example, that you've got a receiver that's got a 7.1.4 surround sound setup. That means you've got seven surround channels that you could use for a centre, left and right stereo, two side surrounds, and then a pair of rear surrounds. You've then got a single subwoofer channel.

Finally, you've got four height channels that you can place around the room in predetermined Atmos spots. You can use Atmos testing videos to make sure all your speakers are in the right place.

#3162. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

#3161. Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the company’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services …

Apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The company has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the company hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I said at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the company’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

After its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the company set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple said it was 95% of the way there.

The company also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and New Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

Potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

Back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said that the AI boom was “challenging” to the company’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are currently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

At the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

More challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the company’s most recent environmental progress report, it said that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

We’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report said the company had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

However, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

What happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the company moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the company’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

Do you think Apple will succeed? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3160. AirPods Pro 3 were worth the upgrade for one standout feature

AirPods Pro 3 (now only $149, down from $249) offer many advantages over AirPods Pro 2, but after a year of use, the improvements to Active Noise Cancellation alone have proven worth the upgrade.

I’ve been using AirPods Pro 3 for over a year, and they had a lot to live up to because I already loved AirPods Pro 2 so much. Initially I found the new ear tips less comfortable, but thankfully that issue went away after a little extra time.

Some highlights of AirPods Pro 3 include the longer battery life, with 8 hours per charge compared to 6 on the previous model. The charging case’s new Ultra Wideband chip also makes it easier to find when it’s lost. Some users will appreciate the heart rate sensor, but I wear an Apple Watch all the time so it doesn’t benefit me much.

These new features are nice to have, but Active Noise Cancellation is where AirPods Pro 3 become a major upgrade. Apple says it’s “the world’s best in-ear Active Noise Cancellation.” Here’s how the new ANC compares to previous models:

I spend nearly my entire workday with AirPods Pro 3 in my ears. Whether I’m working from home with young kids around or at a busy coffee shop, I rely on ANC to block out background noise and help me focus.

One reason I’ve been especially impressed with the ANC upgrades is that I didn’t have any real complaints about ANC on AirPods Pro 2. But Apple managed to deliver improvements in AirPods Pro 3 I had no idea I needed, and when I’ve tried going back to AirPods Pro 2 I couldn’t believe how much noise was let in.

If Active Noise Cancellation is important to you, I highly recommend AirPods Pro 3.

#3159. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.00, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $20 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $49.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails for $69.99 for a physical copy on Switch 2, but Nintendo is selling it for $49 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $48.97 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

With the amount of shipping labels I need printed and documents that need copying for my household, a printer has become a quiet essential for my home. That's why I wanted a simple, do-it-all machine, and I refer to our experts, Nikita Achanta and Eric Butterfield, for all the in-depth recommendations they have to offer.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When it comes down to it, the Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II is quite simply the only printer you'll ever need. Yes, it can print, scan, copy and fax, but it does it all with a hassle-free setup experience and rapid speeds across the board. When a printer actually gives easy step-by-step instructions on how to fix a paper jam, you know it's a good one.

In our tests, it delivered a five-page text print job in just 11.31 seconds (26.5 pages per minute) and scanned in color in 6.22 seconds, and that's faster than its inkjet competitors.

And this 250-capacity printer (plus an extra 150 prints in the middle section) has quick start-up, too, as our reviewer, Nikita, found it effortless to get up and running, with warm-up times as quick as 14 seconds from off.

It isn't just speed, as print quality is consistently sharp and detailed, both in color and black and white, and everyday jobs came out looking just as sharp as they did on our screens. Where the MF753Cdw II pulls ahead of inkjet competitors like the more budget-friendly Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is in raw speed and features.

You get much faster printing and a true all-in-one experience (there's no faxing on the G3290), but running costs are higher if you print in volume. Against the business-class Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850, the MF753Cdw II still keeps up on print speed and quality but can’t match those rock-bottom ink costs.

That’s the main compromise here: the per-page price is higher than what you’ll find with most ink tank printers (around 5.1 cents per color page and 2.7 cents per mono print). But not by that much, and that shouldn't put you off grabbing this workhorse.

If you want a dependable, fuss-free machine for everyday tasks — letters, homework, invoices, you name it — the MF753Cdw II is the best fit for most households.

Unless you need faxing in your life, this is the all-in-one printer to grab if you're after a reliable machine for excellent prints. The Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW stands out largely thanks to its exceptionally low ink costs: just 0.3 cents per black page and 0.94 cents per color page based on our lab testing. That's value you can't ignore.

In daily use, the T780DW keeps pace with demanding routines. It prints standard text documents at 12.4 pages per minute (ppm) and handles double-sided text at 6.7 ppm. These speeds put it among the fastest inkjets we've tested for both single and duplex jobs, making it reliable for everything from schoolwork to business invoices.

Print and scan quality are equally reassuring. In our hands-on tests, text and graphics came out crisp and accurate, while color scans preserved detail and clarity.

The main compromise is its 20-sheet automatic document feeder. While fine for light multi-page copying and scanning, if you've got a large batch of documents, it will take some time to do. That, and there's no USB thumb drive port, and don't expect to make double-sided copies or scans via the automatic document feeder (ADF).

In any case, for those who want low running costs and easy printing, the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW will fit in nicely with your home or office.

Whether you're a photographer or just need highly detailed, colorful prints, the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is the all-in-one printer for you. Sure, it may come with fewer additional features, but it excels where it matters: print quality and affordability.

It's a modest printer; it has just one paper tray and no document feeder, and it's not the speediest option. But for home use, it's an excellent choice. Expect this to deliver reliable, high-quality prints with the versatility to do documents, photos and double-sided print jobs. Speaking of which, those graphic prints and glossy photos will come out with plenty of detail and natural, accurate colors.

While the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 prints at pretty average speeds, it actually excels at double-sided documents. In our testing, it printed single-sided pages at an average of 9.2 pages per minute, but double-sided text documents cranked up to 7.2 pages per minute, the fastest duplex print speed we've recorded of any recent ink tank printers.

And thanks to its easy setup process, robust wireless support (this thing can print via Wi-Fi or a smartphone app) and low ink costs (we estimate color prints cost roughly 0.9 cents per page, significantly lower than the 1.9 cents per page category average), I recommend the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 for anyone seeking an affordable, reliable ink all-in-one printer, especially for photo printing.

If your at-home office needs fast, reliable color printing day in and day out, the Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850 is just the printer you'll want. In our tests, it handled a six-page mixed color document in just 1 minute and 8 seconds (5.3 pages per minute), nearly doubling the category average, so you won’t be waiting on big print jobs during busy stretches.Where the ET-5850 really stands out for speedy work prints is its speed with graphics-heavy jobs. Letter-size glossy photos print in 2 minutes and 21 seconds, far outpacing typical inkjets. The three separate paper input trays mean you can keep letter, legal, and specialty papers ready to go, which helps minimize interruptions if multiple people are printing different document types.

Moreover, you're getting an impressively low ink costs with a device capable of handling more than 3,000 pages per month. During our testing, we found an extremely low per-page cost of 0.4 cents for text pages, and 1.6 cents per color page. The printer can scan, copy and fax, uses dual 250-page paper cassettes and has a 50-sheet automatic document feeder.

Setup was mostly straightforward, but we did run into some hiccups. Connecting to our network required manually entering a router password (WPS isn’t supported), and the touchscreen flagged network issues before resolving. Once added, using the printer with a Mac was simple, but it’s worth noting you might spend extra time on initial setup and troubleshooting.If you’re after an all-in-one that keeps pace with high-volume, graphics-rich business tasks and want flexible paper handling, the ET-5850 is a great fit.

Alright, this one's a little different from any other all-in-one printer, as the Inkwon Tag is a one-of-a-kind portable color inkjet printer. Instead of printing, scanning or copying documents, this pocketable printer delivers all the fun stuff — instant photo prints for scrapbooks, heat transfers for creating custom T-shirts, temporary tattoos and even stickers.

This 4-in-1 portable printer is as tiny as it is light, coming in at 4.1 x 3.8 x 1.7 inches and weighing just 8.2 ounces. Our reviewer, Nikita, has no problems carrying this around in a pocket, as it's actually smaller than the best big phones around today.

Despite its size, you'll find it boasts surprisingly good print quality, no matter the image. It uses a CMY three-dye-based ink system (no dedicated black ink, though) with a resolution of 600 dpi, making it excellent for small prints of friends and loved ones, designs of your choosing or even screenshots from games. And it's all extremely easy to use, right from setting it up to the very user-friendly app for editing and printing photos.

It isn't perfect, as it can only handle one sheet of paper at a time, and don't expect it to create any borderless prints. It's also quite a pricey portable printer, coming in at $299, but its ink costs and paper refills are much more value-friendly when compared to its competition, especially from Canon or Instax (plus, those brands don't offer 4-in-1 portable printer options with sticker or heat transfer capabilities).

To have a mini, portable printer by your side to instantly create stickers to personalize whatever you want, temporary tattoos for parties, heat transfers for customized T-shirts and Polaroid-like photos, all at low running ink costs? As far as portable all-in-one printers go, the Inkwon Tag is a winner.

If you're looking for a compact, capable printer purely for stickers and photo prints, then the StickerPix Print + Cut is exactly what you're after. It comes in an adorable design, is fast at printing stickers and offers loads of templates to customize what you want to print. There are only 18 sheets of sticker/photo paper out of the box, so you'll need to invest in more, and the Inkwon Tag offers a bit more "all-in-one" versatility, but the Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut is well worth grabbing for all things stickers! Read our full Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut review

(★★★★☆)The Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW bucked the trend of printers gouging you on ink costs by coming with roughly a year's worth of ink (depending on how much you print) pre-loaded in the extra-large ink cartridges, so you get a great price-per-page right out of the gate. On top of that, the Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW offers solid printing, scanning and copying. But this model is trickier to find these days, and more of the current Brother printers of its kind do just the job for less these days. Read our full Brother INKvestment MFC-J995DW review

(★★★★☆½)The Brother MFC-L2750DW XL is the best multifunction laser printer we've reviewed in years for everything but color prints. Every print is sharp and clean, and it's packed with features including a quick ADF, fast duplex printing and copying, fax capability, and a second paper tray. But this is one pricey machine!Read our full Brother MFC-L2750DW XL review

(★★★★☆)Looking for another photo printer option? The Canon Pixma TR8620 is a fantastic shout that offers plenty of office features, from scanning and faxing to a 20-page ADF, a duplexer for two-sided printing, and two paper trays for keeping two types of paper at the ready. But that extra ink cartridge does bump up the cost of ink. Read our full Canon Pixma TR8620 review

To help you find the best all-in-one printer, we put each model through an extensive range of printer tests, including timed prints of text, mixed text and graphics and color photos. The resulting prints are carefully examined for errors and issues, and compared with samples from other printers to determine the print quality.

We time every test print to see how quickly the machine handles document printing, and closely examine the finished product to determine how well different printing tasks are handled.

We also test the scanning and copying functions of the printer, timing how quickly it captures a page and comparing the results to the original images to determine how well it captures color and detail.

To measure the cost of owning and operating a printer, we look at the current street price of ink refills and the estimated number of pages that each cartridge can produce, and calculate the cost of printing a single page.

Not sure which all-in-one printer to buy? Obviously, you want a printer that performs well, so all of our reviews and rankings discuss a printer's output quality and speed, but there's more to an all-in-one printer than just how quickly it can crank out documents.

Some companies even offer subscription services that save you money while sending you ink just in time to replace that empty cartridge. Learn more in our article HP Instant Ink vs. Canon vs. Epson: Are ink subscriptions worth it?

Ink-tank printers, a type of Inkjet, usually offer the lowest running costs because their refill bottles deliver far more pages than conventional cartridges.

In our guide, the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW is the best-value option for home or light-office use, while the Epson EcoTank Pro ET-5850 pairs very low per-page costs with the capacity and features needed for heavier business printing.

You should compare current cost-per-page figures with your expected print volume, not just the printer’s upfront price.

Choose an inkjet if you print color graphics or photos, want a lower upfront price or value the low ongoing costs of an ink-tank model. Choose a laser all-in-one if your priority is fast, sharp text documents and a responsive office workflow.

The Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II is our top pick, as it's a fast laser workhorse, whereas the Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290 is the stronger fit for photo printing.

An automatic document feeder (ADF) is worthwhile if you regularly scan, copy or fax multi-page documents, as it feeds the sheets for you instead of requiring one page at a time on the scanner glass.

It matters less for occasional household printing or photo-focused use. Also check its capacity and whether it supports double-sided scanning: an ADF does not automatically mean both sides can be scanned in one pass.

Some can, but not every all-in-one printer with an ADF supports automatic double-sided scanning or copying. Do not confuse duplex printing with duplex scanning: a printer may print on both sides of a sheet while still requiring you to turn over originals when scanning or copying.

Check the model’s specifications before buying; the Brother INKvestment MFC-T780DW has an ADF but does not support duplex scanning or copying through it.

Many current all-in-one printers support wireless mobile printing through a manufacturer app, Apple AirPrint or another built-in service. The Canon MegaTank Pixma G3290, for example, supports Wi-Fi and printing through a smartphone app.

Before buying, confirm that the printer works with your phone or tablet, operating system, preferred app and network setup. Some features may require the device and printer to be on the same Wi-Fi network.

#3157. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

#3156. iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the new GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

As a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

GymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

AirPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods users a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

In testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t update as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk showed 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

Does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

What is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

If I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.
