#3138. Vipshop (VIPS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Loyal members now drive most online spending as discretionary demand softens.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:38PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Vipshop (VIPS +3.33%) reported third-quarter results that management described as being in line with internal expectations despite a challenging macro retail environment. The company observed a moderation in total customer counts but reported growth in its core SVIP segment, which now accounts for a majority of online spending. Management emphasized a focus on revenue quality and margin health over low-margin volume, supported by disciplined cost control and optimized merchandising. The company also introduced stand-alone segment disclosure for the Shan Shan Outlets business, highlighting its outperformance relative to the broader retail sector. Significant capital returns to shareholders were confirmed through a combination of share repurchases and the declaration of a special cash dividend.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, good day, everyone, and welcome to Vipshop Holdings Limited's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, I would like to turn the call to Ms. Jessie Zheng, Vipshop's Head of Investor Relations. Please proceed.

Jessie Zheng: Thank you, operator. Hello, everyone, and thank you for joining Vipshop's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. With us today are Ya (Eric) Shen, our Co-Founder, Chairman and CEO; and Mark Wang, our CFO. For today's call, Eric's prepared remarks will be delivered via AI synthesized voice modeled on his own, while he will join us live to conduct the Q&A session. Before management begins, I would like to remind you that the discussion today will contain forward-looking statements made under the safe harbor provisions of the U.S. Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ materially from our current expectations.

Potential risks and uncertainties include, but are not limited to, those outlined in the safe harbor statements in our earnings release and public filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which also applies to this call to the extent any forward-looking statements may be made. Please note that certain financial measures used on this call, such as non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP net income attributable to Vipshop's shareholders and non-GAAP net income per ADS are not presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Please refer to our earnings release for details relating to the reconciliations of our non-GAAP measures to GAAP measures. With that, I would now like to turn the call over to Mr. Ya (Eric) Shen.

Ya (Eric) Shen: Good morning, and good evening, everyone. Welcome, and thank you for joining our third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. During the third quarter, we continued to navigate a complex retail environment. Soft discretionary consumer sentiment, coupled with holiday shifts and unseasonal conditions, created a challenging backdrop for our business. We delivered financial results that came in largely in line with our expectations. Total customer count saw a slight moderation amid a cautious consumer environment. However, our core SVIP segment demonstrated consistent resilience, growing by 9% year-over-year, contributing 55% of our online spending. This loyal base, over 80% of whom are family shoppers purchasing across multiple categories, has played a critical role in supporting overall ARPU and reinforcing our operational stability.

While our online business faces ongoing headwinds, this environment is reinforcing our discipline around merchandising and customer mix. We remain committed to high-quality growth underpinned by strong retention and healthy unit economics rather than pursuing low-margin volume that could dilute our long-term value proposition. During the third quarter, we continued to refine our merchandising approach to align with a more selective consumer by strategically prioritizing high-value core supply while remaining agile with on-trend inventory. We enhanced our market relevance and captured selective pockets of growth whenever our assortment hit the mark. For instance, we quickly adapted our product mix to resilient sportswear and outdoor essentials as well as new season fashion apparel rollout.

By increasingly pairing these assortments with seasonal and festive moments, we successfully captured targeted demand across summer outings, the back-to-school period and the fall transition. As brand partners continue to navigate excess inventory across channels and become increasingly willing to release quality stock, we are seeing attractive sourcing opportunities. Our position as a trusted off-price partner allows us to secure more desirable merchandise at compelling discounts. This enables us to deliver exceptional value to our customers. For instance, our recent flash sale events featuring multiple on-trend apparel and outdoor brands achieved strong sell-through rates among our high-value customers, highlighting the potential of our opportunistic buying practice. Our repositioning of the Made for Vipshop exclusive line is focused and steady.

We are rebuilding scale through a broader selection of higher-quality hero products codeveloped with or specifically allocated by our brand partners. This exclusive line is a key evolution of our merchandising model aimed at sharpening our long-term differentiation. We are continuing to refine product exclusivity, assortment relevance and pricing flexibility to reinforce the line's quality for value proposition. During the third quarter, we launched a branding refresh around "Dress The Best for 70% less," which performed as intended. The campaign effectively expanded our target audience pool, filtering for high-intent shoppers who recognize true off-price value. We will continue to invest selectively in acquiring customers with a higher chance of better conversion, retention and long-term contribution.

For our SVIP segment, our tailored tiered service model continues to drive robust engagement. We are elevating this framework to optimize lifetime value progression, including plans to roll out a brand-new membership tier system that rewards higher spending members with richer exclusive privileges across merchandise, pricing services and cross-industry partnerships. At the same time, we recognize that sustainable long-term health requires pairing customer quality with broader top-of-funnel expansion. We are leveraging this transitional period to sharpen our acquisition model, enhance retention and LTV economics and lay a solid foundation for a disciplined return to customer growth as macro conditions improve. In the third quarter, our technology strategy became more focused and execution-oriented.

We are deepening where we deploy AI, prioritizing areas where we possess proprietary data and deep operating expertise across merchandising, operation and customer experience. Initial benefits are already materializing. Customer engagement is strengthening through AI-enhanced personalization and customer service. Additionally, marketing efficiency has improved through AI-optimized campaign targeting and disciplined spend allocation. Advancing our vision to integrate customer and merchant data into smart operations, we are deploying AI agents across two hubs: first, to drive deeper insights into customer behavior; and second, to unlock merchandising insights by leveraging our unique brand relationships, specialized workflows and inventory dynamics. Together, these capabilities allow us to identify emerging opportunities faster and act with greater agility.

As these use cases evolve, they should structurally strengthen our platform foundation, laying the groundwork for incremental efficiency and margin gains over time. We will continue to evaluate application through the lens of disciplined investment and measurable business outcomes. Turning to Shan Outlets. The business delivered solid performance, achieving 12% sales growth year-over-year against a seasonally slower backdrop. During the quarter, we successfully opened a new outlet in Wuxi, further expanding our physical retail footprint. Across our portfolio, performance continues to benefit from strong asset occupancy, targeted brand and category optimization, particularly in outdoor sports and premium apparel as well as sustained momentum from local tourism, membership engagement and event-driven foot traffic.

As we celebrate our 18th anniversary and the milestone of surpassing 10 million SVIP membership, we remain focused on improving the quality and resilience of our business through a challenging demand environment. Our priorities are to strengthen the fundamentals that matter most: differentiated merchandise, customer loyalty, operating efficiency and disciplined capital allocation. We believe these efforts will help build a stronger platform that can support healthier, more sustainable growth over time. At this point, let me hand over the call to our CFO, Mark Wang, to go over our financial results. [Interpreted - AI agent]

Mark Wang: Thanks, Eric, and hello, everyone. In the third quarter, our revenue landed at the lower end of our guidance range due to cautious consumer spending. Our operational agility and focus on margin quality allowed us to protect our core operating profitability. Gross margin stood resilient at 22.9%, broadly flat year-over-year. Importantly, we achieved this by dynamically optimizing our merchandising mix and avoiding aggressive subsidies amid broader promotional pressure. Non-GAAP operating margin held firm at 7.6%, slightly up year-over-year as proactive cost containment initiatives more than offset our deliberate decision to maintain key investments in brand marketing and core technology.

As Eric indicated, we remain highly disciplined in our overall capital allocation, funding initiatives that preserve the economics and capabilities needed to generate profitable growth when demand normalizes. We will continue to return excess capital to shareholders. For 2026, total shareholder returns will have reached $938 million, comprising approximately $300 million in share buybacks, an annual dividend of $300 million paid earlier this year and an upcoming special dividend of roughly $338 million, fully delivering on our commitment to return no less than 75% of our 2025 non-GAAP net income to shareholders.

With the continuous expansion of Shan Outlets scale, we are pleased to introduce stand-alone segment disclosure for Shan Outlets this quarter to provide greater visibility into its underlying value within our broader omnichannel ecosystem. On a reported basis, net revenues from Shan reached nearly RMB 1 billion, up 1% year-over-year, with income from operations rising 36% to RMB 390 million. Reported results reflect the deconsolidation of two outlets following the issuance of the Vipshop commercial REIT this June. On a comparable basis, excluding those two outlets from the prior year period, net revenues from Shan grew in the low 20s year-over-year, underscoring the resilience and outperformance of our offline outlets amid a softer consumer environment.

Looking ahead, while macro headwinds persist, our focus remains on prioritizing revenue quality, driving operational efficiency and safeguarding margin health by managing the business with prudence through the cycle, while reinforcing our operational resilience and positioning the company for sustainable long-term value creation. Now moving to our detailed quarterly financial highlights. Before I get started, I would like to clarify that all financial numbers presented below are in renminbi, and all the percentage changes are year-over-year changes, unless otherwise noted. Total net revenues for the third quarter of 2026 were RMB 20.4 billion compared with RMB 21.4 billion in the prior year period. Gross profit was RMB 4.7 billion compared with RMB 4.9 billion in the prior year period.

Gross margin was 22.9% compared with 23.0% in the prior year period. Total operating expenses were RMB 3.8 billion compared with RMB 3.9 billion in the prior year period. As a percentage of total net revenues, total operating expenses were 18.8% compared with 18.5% in the prior year period. Fulfillment expenses were RMB 1.8 billion compared with RMB 1.9 billion in the prior year period. As a percentage of total net revenues, fulfillment expenses were 8.8% compared with 8.7% in the prior year period. Marketing expenses were RMB 735.5 million compared with RMB 670.2 million in the prior year period. As a percentage of total net revenues, marketing expenses were 3.6% compared with 3.1% in the prior year period.

Technology and content expenses were RMB 499.2 million compared with RMB 438.6 million in the prior year period. As a percentage of total net revenues, technology and content expenses were 2.4% compared with 2.1% in the prior year period. General and administrative expenses were RMB 806.9 million compared with RMB 984.6 million in the prior year period. As a percentage of total net revenues, general and administrative expenses decreased to 3.9% from 4.6% in the prior year period. Income from operations increased by 3.8% year-over-year to RMB 1.31 billion from RMB 1.26 billion in the prior year period. Operating margin increased to 6.4% from 5.9% in the prior year period.

Non-GAAP income from operations was RMB 1.5 billion compared with RMB 1.6 billion in the prior year period. Non-GAAP operating margin increased to 7.6% from 7.5% in the prior year period. Net income attributable to Vipshop's shareholders was RMB 1.1 billion compared with RMB 1.2 billion in the prior year period. Net margin attributable to Vipshop shareholders was 5.2% compared with 5.7% in the prior year period. Net income attributable to Vipshop's shareholders per diluted ADS was RMB 2.21 compared with RMB 2.42 in the prior year period. Non-GAAP net income attributable to Vipshop's shareholders was RMB 1.3 billion compared with RMB 1.5 billion in the prior year period.

Non-GAAP net margin attributable to Vipshop shareholders was 6.2% compared with 7.0% in the prior year period. Non-GAAP net income attributable to Vipshop's shareholders per diluted ADS was RMB 2.64 compared with RMB 2.98 in the prior year period. As of September 30, 2026, the company had cash and cash equivalents and restricted cash of RMB 23.0 billion and short-term investments of RMB 4.0 billion. Looking forward to the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect our total net revenues to be between RMB 29.2 billion and RMB 30.9 billion, representing a year-over-year decrease of approximately 10% to 5%. Please note that this forecast reflects our current and preliminary view of the market and operational conditions, which is subject to change.

With that, I would now like to open the call to Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We'll now take the first question. This is from Thomas Chong from Jefferies.

Thomas Chong: I have two questions. The first question is about the monthly revenue trend that we are seeing so far in Q4. Can management comment about how is October and month-to-date performance so far in November? Are we actually seeing we are hitting the low end or the high end of our revenue guidance? And my second question is about our 2027 outlook. Given the uncertainties about the macro environment and the soft consumer sentiment, can management share your thoughts about 2027 revenue and margin outlook, if there's any visibilities that can be shared at this point. [Foreign Language]

Jessie Zheng: So maybe first on the monthly revenue trend in Q4 to date. We've been into Q4 for almost 2 months. October was actually really bad in terms of sales performance. So that's why we are not so optimistic about the fourth quarter overall, and that's why we guided the revenue, the top line is going to decline by 5% to 10%. And with that in mind, it's still too early to evaluate whether we are going to hit the lower or higher end of the guidance range. Looking ahead to 2027, our focus is actually towards profitable growth execution, although we don't expect the consumption environment is going to change dramatically overnight.

From our own perspective, we continue to focus on what we can do in terms of our core competencies, especially we believe that the structural enhancements we have done in the past year in terms of merchandising, SVIP engagement, operational discipline and AI integration will give us a better foundation for us to achieve flattish to and even return to growth. On the margin side, we have always been very focused on margin safety and discipline, and we have a better control over margins.

We believe that even as macro headwinds persist into 2027, we are going to see a net profit margin largely comparable to what we have seen in the past several years, including the normalized non-GAAP net margin for 2026. Jessie Zheng: In terms of Shan's performance, the outlet business still delivered solid performance, achieving 12% sales year-over-year against a seasonally slower backdrop. And we currently have a total of 23 outlets, and we will continue to add 1 to 2 outlets every year because we believe that we still have a lot of cities underpenetrated by the outlet business, and we have proved that we have a great operational team that can make the success rate very high and it serves as a stabilizer to the group revenue and earnings in terms of increasing contribution. So from the group level, we will continue to provide strong support for Shan's future expansion.

Mark Wang: Okay -- [ I'm ] Mark -- and let me answer your second question. Regarding Shan segment financials, net revenues came in at nearly RMB 1 billion, up 1% year-over-year on a reported basis. And on an apple-to-apple basis, adjusting the prior year period to exclude the 2 deconsolidated outlets, that's Zhengzhou and Harbin, which we issued the commercial REITs in the second quarter, Shan revenue grew over 20% year-over-year. And operating income surpassed RMB 300 million, representing 36% year-over-year growth. Notably, this quarter, Shan accounts for a meaningful 5% of the group revenue and over 20% of the group operating income. On the new segment disclosure, there are several considerations.

The first is against a broadly soft retail environment, Shan business has continued to grow rapidly. Second, as Shan has continued to scale, we want to proactively provide investors with stand-alone visibility into Shan's performance, so investors can better understand and appreciate its intrinsic value. The enhanced segment disclosure will help investors better evaluate the intrinsic value of these high-quality assets.

#3137. MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker says it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also quickly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

Qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

#3136. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys

“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once.

The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.

Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.

But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.

McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”

It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”

Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver

LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis

Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”

How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”

Dina Genkina is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum focused on computing and hardware. She holds a PhD in atomic physics and lives in Brooklyn.

i saw some published test results of a 1950's airborne radar system using an optical computer to do a Fourier transform of the 2D radar return data for military target detection. Basically you have a cathode ray TV tube, and a lens in front of it, and at the focal point of the lens is a Fourier Transform of what showed up on the TV tube. it is Fundamental Fourier optics. Xerox used this in some of their photocopiers too. Really fast processing! Femtoseconds. Maybe its time had come to bring it back again!

I recall HP looking at this in the late 90s. Also, it is not just energy consumption possibility but the reduction of byproduct heat by using photons.

Will be interesting to watch and see if the energy costs of the analog-digital transformations drop enough to spread optical into more parts of the computing hardware. Meantime, I'd be interested in what our readers think of the idea of diversifying methods for different parts of computing.

There's a lot of money, talent and education invested in silicone. A technology has to be a lot better at the start and have a clear path to continuous improvement before real money is put into it. Inertia is a very powerful force.

who SAYS "digital computing" is the best way? it is just all we had to deal with in large scale. Digital computers have a LOT of baggage--such as having to digitize an entirely analog world into 1's and 0's. Analog computers were popular in the 1940's thru the '60's. Our brains are not digital computers, maybe there is a biological computer coming soon?

The Eight Sleep Pod 6 comes in two parts: a control tower and a cover... plus an app but no mattress. The cover is fitted with a series of water tubes (to heat and cool) and sensors (to track the temperature) which feed back to the control hub to keep your sleep climate even throughout the night.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up…

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. #3132. IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems

Standards and certifications foster socially responsible products

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems.

In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity.

Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens, who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030. And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.”

Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced.

This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website, a podcast series, and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact.

The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality, but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools.

The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous and intelligent systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators.

The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote.

IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd, which includes two certifications: one for individuals and one for products.

The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative

The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program, which can certify it and issue the certification mark.

IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program. This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements.

The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members.

The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle.

The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability.

Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues.

“The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.”

To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “Ethically Aligned Design: 10 Years of Impact” podcast series. It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks.

The episodes center around the vision for EAD, the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards.

The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices.

The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems.

The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog articles about the IEEE 7000 series and educational resources to continue to raise awareness and support of this groundbreaking work.

This article was updated on 18 November 2026.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3131. Crypto trading still forces users to choose between convenience and control

A candlestick chart on a dark screen shows prices sliding lower, mostly in red candles.

As security concerns persist across centralized exchanges, a new generation of trading platforms is attempting to make self-custody easier without recreating the complexity of decentralized finance.

For years, cryptocurrency trading has involved a trade-off. Centralized exchanges offer relatively straightforward interfaces, but users must generally trust those platforms to hold their assets. Decentralized alternatives allow traders to retain control of their funds, although navigating wallets, blockchain networks, gas fees and bridges can make the experience considerably more complicated.

That divide has become increasingly relevant as security breaches and operational failures continue to expose the risks of centralized custody.

The challenge for developers is no longer simply to build decentralized trading infrastructure. It is to make that infrastructure accessible enough for users who have become accustomed to the convenience of traditional exchanges.

London-based cryptocurrency trading platform Byrrgis is among the companies attempting to address that problem. Its public launch on November 24 introduces expanded cross-chain trading functionality, token analysis tools and a simplified wallet experience built around a non-custodial architecture.

On centralized cryptocurrency exchanges, users typically transfer assets into wallets controlled by the platform. While this arrangement simplifies trading, it also means customers depend on the exchange’s security practices, financial stability and withdrawal policies.

Non-custodial trading changes that relationship by allowing users to retain control of their private keys and authorize transactions directly from their wallets.

However, self-custody introduces its own challenges. Users become responsible for protecting their wallets, understanding transaction approvals and navigating potential vulnerabilities in smart contracts.

It also does not automatically eliminate exposure to third-party infrastructure, particularly when trading involves cross-chain protocols or external liquidity providers.

The question is whether developers can reduce those operational barriers without introducing new forms of dependency.

“Security and control over funds should not come at the expense of a simple trading experience,” said Siraaj Ahmed, CEO of Byrrgis. “With our full public launch, we’re bringing together cross-chain trading, token analysis and portfolio management in one place, while allowing users to maintain control of their assets instead of handing them over to a centralized exchange.”

One of the persistent usability problems in decentralized finance is fragmentation.

Trading assets across different networks can require separate wallets, native gas tokens and bridging transactions. Users may also need to understand which blockchain holds a particular asset before executing a trade.

Byrrgis is attempting to abstract some of that complexity through a trading interface supporting Solana, Ethereum, BNB Chain and, according to the company, Robinhood Chain.

Its cross-chain routing system is designed to let users initiate supported swaps with a single transaction signature rather than manually moving assets between networks.

A feature called Universal Gas is intended to remove the need to maintain separate native gas-token balances for supported transactions.

These approaches reflect a broader direction in blockchain development known as chain abstraction, where the underlying network infrastructure becomes less visible to the end user.

Yet simplifying the interface does not remove the technical risks of cross-chain execution. Routing systems, liquidity providers and smart contracts can still introduce points of failure, even when users retain custody of their wallets.

Another challenge facing cryptocurrency traders is the amount of information required to evaluate unfamiliar assets.

Market liquidity, trading momentum and on-chain risk indicators are often distributed across multiple analytics platforms, making comparisons difficult for less experienced users.

Byrrgis has incorporated a feature called Scout Score, which assigns supported tokens a rating between 0 and 100 based on a combination of on-chain risk, market momentum and tradability indicators.

The scores update as market conditions change, offering a consolidated assessment alongside the platform’s token discovery tools.

Such systems may make complex information easier to interpret, but they also raise questions about transparency and reliability.

A numerical score can simplify research, yet its usefulness depends on how indicators are weighted, how frequently data is updated and whether the methodology can identify emerging risks.

A high rating should not be interpreted as a guarantee of safety or future performance.

Beyond cross-chain trading and token analysis, Byrrgis has introduced card-based cryptocurrency purchases, a redesigned wallet onboarding process and changes intended to improve swap execution.

The platform also includes tools for tracking holdings across networks and managing multiple positions from a single interface.

These additions illustrate a wider challenge for decentralized trading applications: competing with the user experience of centralized platforms while preserving the characteristics that distinguish self-custody.

Coros has launched the Vertix 4 as its new flagship smartwatch, and it’s a major upgrade over the Coros Vertix 2S with an AMOLED display, a more attractive design that has a built-in flashlight, and satellite maps.

I’ve been testing the Vertix 4 for five days, which isn’t nearly enough time to get through its extensive battery life, but I have been able to get some first impressions of the watch by doing four runs with it, comparing it directly to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro.

You’ll find my early likes and dislikes for the Coros Vertix 4 below, along with its price and specs. For those wondering why Coros went from 2S to 4, skipping a Vertix 3, it’s to bring the Vertix 4 into line with its other watches: the Coros Apex 4 and Coros Pace 4 Pro.

The Coros Vertix 4 launched on 24 November 2026 and will be available to order from 27 November. It costs $799 in the U.S. and £669 in the U.K., a $100/£70 price rise on the Vertix 2S.

It does come in significantly cheaper than the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, though, which starts at $999. However, there are some rivals that come in cheaper than the Vertix 4, with the Suunto Vertical 2 titanium model, costing $699/£639, and older Garmin Fenix models appearing in sales — the Garmin Fenix 8 is $749 at Amazon right now, for example.

The Vertix has previously had a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display, and while that does have some advantages, most notably longer battery life, I much prefer the AMOLED display on the Vertix 4.

It’s a very big, bright screen and easier to read than the MIP display on the Vertix 2S in all conditions I find, even in bright sunlight.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The new satellite maps also look great on the display, and the battery life on the Vertix 4 is still very good.

While it would have been great for Coros to make the Vertix 4 available with both MIP and AMOLED options, as Garmin does with the Fenix, it’s perhaps not practical in production terms, and I do think AMOLED is the better option here, with the Apex 4 offering a MIP alternative in the Coros line-up.

Adventure watches are, by design, big and bold devices to strap to your wrist, but the Vertix 2S was a little too huge, and the Coros Vertix 4 is a much more enjoyable watch to wear all day.

It’s thinner and lighter than its predecessor while having a larger display, and doesn’t feel too bulky even on my slim wrist.

In the past, I think Coros watches could be accused of prioritizing substance over style, which is no bad thing, but it’s better to have both, and both of the brand’s 2026 launches — the Pace 4 Pro and now Vertix 4 — have been more attractive than past options.

Ever since Garmin added a built-in flashlight to the Fenix 7X, it’s been a feature that people have wanted in their smartwatch, and the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get it.

Coros has swerved from the usual flashlight setup used by other brands, though, sticking its light on the side of the Vertix 4, between the digital dial and back button, as opposed to on the top as Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit do.

This has its advantages — the flashlight naturally focuses the way your arm is pointing, and you can switch the orientation of the buttons on the watch if you wear it on your right wrist.

I’m still on the fence about whether I prefer this or having the flashlight on top of the watch, but ultimately it’s a big addition to the Vertix line in general, and a very handy feature to have.

Another interesting new feature on the Vertix 4 is satellite maps, which you can download to the watch and use instead of the standard maps. This is a feature I’m testing in beta, with it expected to launch in early 2027.

The satellite maps look great on the AMOLED display, and at times, it's a bit clearer to see what’s around you using them, especially in the forest.

It was pretty quick and easy to get my local area onto the watch through the Coros app, though the satellite map files are larger than the standard, so you will want to be choosy with the areas you download to the watch.

While the standard maps on the watch work fine, having the satellite option is useful at times, and it differentiates the Vertix 4 from other brands since these maps are free.

The Vertix 2S offers incredible battery life — it lasted me 22 days on a charge and even outperformed the Garmin Enduro 2 on this front.

Given the switch to an AMOLED display, the fear would be that the Vertix 4 fell short on this front in comparison, but the listed stats are still very impressive for the watch.

Coros suggests it will last up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on, and it offers 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on.

So far, the Vertix is on track to beat those estimates for me, although aided by the fact that I haven't used it for sleep tracking so far.

With the screen always on and running every day using the most accurate multi-band mode, it’s on track to last over 10 days.

All the Coros watches launched over the past couple of years have impressed me with their GPS accuracy, and that’s the case with the Vertix 4 so far as well.

I’ve been running with it and the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, with both set to their most accurate mode, and checking the GPS tracks afterwards. The Vertix 4 tracks have been spot on and in line with the Fenix 9 Pro on pace and distance stats throughout the runs too.

Unlike GPS accuracy, the heart rate accuracy of the Vertix 4 has been a bit iffy in my early testing when comparing the readings to a chest strap.

In the Vertix 4’s defence, I’ve been testing it in cold weather, when optical sensors on watches do tend to be less accurate, but I’ve still been a little underwhelmed by the results.

On my easy runs, it’s mostly been pretty close to a chest strap, but on a hard progression run, the Vertix 4’s readings were too high throughout. Based on my early tests, you’d definitely be wise to pair a chest strap to the Vertix 4, at least in cold conditions.

The Vertix 4 is noticeably slimmer and lighter than past versions, but it’s still quite a big watch, and Coros does not offer any size options, something that Garmin does with the Fenix 9.

There are the Apex 4 and Pace 4 Pro as smaller alternatives in the Coros line-up, but if you want the flagship model, you have to accept that it only comes in one size, and it’s a biggie.

It doesn’t take long when testing a Coros watch to realize that they really make sports watches, not smartwatches.

The Vertix 4 can store music, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch; it doesn’t pair with streaming services. It also doesn’t offer NFC payments, and you can’t customize the watch face as much as on rivals.

Personally, I don’t miss these smart features much, but they are a selling point not only true smartwatches like the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but also Garmin watches, which combine great sports tracking with useful smarts.

#3129. Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

Introducing Claude Ship (beta): Claude can review your pull requests, work on fixes, and approve the ones your team's policy allows.The goal is to help you ship code as fast as you can write it. pic.twitter.com/b9OBAhEBmr
