#3128. PennantPark (PFLT) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Core income covered the dividend while the second JV nears its target.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:41PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

PennantPark (PFLT +0.48%) reported core net investment income that supported its base dividend and allowed for the declaration of a supplemental distribution. Management stated that the company is prioritizing the expansion of its second senior secured loan joint venture toward a $1 billion target while maintaining a portfolio heavily weighted toward first lien floating rate debt. The company reported a significant concentration in the government services and defense sectors, citing durable federal funding priorities and resilient cash flow profiles as key investment drivers. Management indicated that the core middle market remains a source of attractive risk-adjusted opportunities despite uneven M&A activity and ongoing macroeconomic uncertainty.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the PennantPark Floating Rate Capital's Fourth Fiscal Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Today's conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] It is now my pleasure to turn the call over to Mr. Art Penn, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of PennantPark Floating Rate Capital. Mr. Penn, you may begin your conference.

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to PennantPark Floating Rate Capital's Fourth Fiscal Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. I'm joined today by Rick Allorto, our Chief Financial Officer. Rick, please start off by disclosing some general conference call information and include a discussion about forward-looking statements.

Richard (Rick) Allorto: Thank you, Art. I'd like to remind everyone that today's call is being recorded and is the property of PennantPark Floating Rate Capital. Any unauthorized broadcast of this call in any form is strictly prohibited. An audio replay of the call will be available on our website. I'd also like to call your attention to the customary safe harbor disclosure in our press release regarding forward-looking information. Our remarks today may also include forward-looking statements and projections. Please refer to our most recent SEC filings for important factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from these projections. We do not undertake to update our forward-looking statements unless required by law.

To obtain copies of our latest SEC filings, please visit our website at pennantpark.com or call us at (212) 905-1000. At this time, I'd like to turn the call back to our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Art Penn.

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Thanks, Rick. I'll begin with an overview of our fourth quarter results, including the continued expansion of our PSSL II joint venture. I'll then discuss the current market environment and how we believe PFLT is positioned going forward. Rick will follow up with a detailed review of our financial results, after which we will open up the call for questions. For the quarter ended September 30, core net investment income was $0.25 per share. This exceeded the current base dividend of $0.08 per share per month or $0.24 per share for the quarter. In accordance with our revised dividend policy, PFLT will pay an aggregate supplemental dividend of $0.005 a share over the next 3 months.

The supplemental dividend represents 50% of the excess of the net investment income above the base dividend. As of September 30, our NAV per share was $10.15, which is down approximately 1% from the prior quarter. Despite the ongoing macroeconomic and geopolitical environment, our portfolio remains conservatively positioned with a median debt-to-EBITDA of 4.5x, interest coverage of 2.2x and loan-to-value of 43%. Additionally, PIK, pay-in-kind income remained among the lowest in the industry and equaled just 1.3% of total interest income for the quarter. As of September 30, our portfolio totaled $2.4 billion. And during the quarter, we invested $222 million in both new and existing investments at a weighted average yield of 9.6%.

We invested $116 million into 5 new portfolio companies with a median debt-to-EBITDA of 4.8x, interest coverage of 2.2x and a loan-to-value of 36%. Our existing portfolio continues to drive capital deployment. During the quarter, we invested additional capital totaling $106 million into existing portfolio companies. 1.8% of the portfolio is on nonaccrual at cost and 0.7% at market value. Out of 159 companies, 7 are on nonaccrual. On an overall basis, the percentage of our portfolio on nonaccrual remains low, and we believe this reflects the consistency of our underwriting process and our disciplined approach to credit selection. Our 2 joint ventures remain an important component of our investment strategy.

As of September 30, the PSSL portfolio totaled $1.1 billion, and that joint venture continues to reinvest repayment proceeds into new investments. The PSSL portfolio is performing well and for the quarter ended September 30, generated an annualized cash yield on invested capital of 11.5%. As of September 30, the PSSL II portfolio totaled $386 million, and we remain focused on scaling that JV in a measured and disciplined manner. Since quarter end, PSSL II invested an additional $40 million, increasing the total portfolio to $426 million. The PSSL II portfolio has grown 33% since the June quarter, and we are pleased with its income generation.

Over time, we expect to grow the JV to more than $1 billion in assets, consistent with PSSL. Based on the current conditions, we expect this expansion to occur over the next 12 to 18 months while maintaining our disciplined underwriting standards. For the quarter ended September 30, PSSL II generated an annualized cash yield on invested capital of 11.8%. Turning to portfolio positioning. I'd like to highlight our government services and defense investments. Government services and defense remains one of our highest conviction sectors and has historically been among our best-performing investment areas. We remain highly constructive on the long-term outlook for government services and defense because the sector possesses several characteristics that align well with our investment philosophy.

Demand has historically been supported by durable federal funding priorities and long-term contracts that provide meaningful revenue visibility and stability. Many of these businesses exhibit resilient cash flow profiles, variable cost structures and are generally less sensitive to broader economic cycles than many commercial industries. In addition, the sector continues to benefit from active M&A markets and strong valuation support, thereby providing multiple avenues for value creation. One example of this is Aechelon Investco. Through our equity co-investment in Aechelon Investco, we have an ongoing equity investment in a fast-growing defense tech company, Shield AI.

Shield AI recently announced an acquisition and a capital raise at an indicative valuation for our investment of $7 million above the value on September 30 of $5.5 million. This increase equates to $0.07 per share. Within the government services and defense industry, our investments are focused on businesses supporting the Department of War and other mission-critical government agencies. We focus on companies addressing high-priority national security initiatives, including modernization of defense systems and digital infrastructure, cyber and electronic warfare capabilities, modeling and simulation, counter drone technologies and next-generation autonomous systems. We believe these priorities will remain central to U.S. defense spending for years to come, creating a favorable backdrop for continued investment opportunities.

As of September 30, government services and defense represents approximately 18% of PFLT's portfolio. And given our experience of sourcing capabilities and the attractive opportunity set, we intend to maintain or increase that exposure over time. Turning to software. Our exposure represents approximately 4.1% of the portfolio. These investments follow our core middle market strategy and consist of cash pay loans with financial covenants, moderate leverage and relatively short durations. The businesses provide mission-critical enterprise software to regulated industries, including defense, health care and financial services. Let me now turn to the broader market environment. M&A activity has increased over the past 6 to 9 months, although overall conditions remain uneven.

Private equity sponsors remain active, and we're seeing a growing pipeline of attractive opportunities across both new originations and add-on investments. We're optimistic that activity levels will remain elevated throughout the remainder of this year and into next year. We expect increased transaction activity to drive repayments across the portfolio, including opportunities to monetize equity co-investments and redeploy capital into income-generating investments. In the core middle market, the pricing for high-quality first lien term loans remains attractive, typically ranging from SOFR plus 500 to 550 basis points with leverage of approximately 4.5x EBITDA. Importantly, these structures continue to include meaningful covenant protections in contrast to the covenant-light structures prevalent in the upper middle market.

We believe the current environment favors lenders with established private equity sponsor relationships, consistent access to deal flow and disciplined underwriting. These are long-standing strengths of the PennantPark platform. We continue to believe that the core middle market offers attractive risk-adjusted opportunities. Companies in this segment generally have EBITDA of $10 million to $50 million and often operate below the practical threshold of the broadly syndicated loan and high-yield markets. As a result, lenders can typically conduct extensive diligence, negotiate meaningful financial covenants, structure transactions with appropriate leverage and equity cushions and maintain regular access to company financial information. Our credit quality since our inception over 15 years ago has been excellent.

PFLT has invested $9.5 billion in over 550 companies, and we've experienced only 27 nonaccruals. Since inception, PFLT's loss ratio on invested capital is only 13 basis points annually. As a provider of strategic capital, it fuels the growth of our portfolio companies, in many cases, we participate in the upside of the company by making an equity co-investment. Our returns on these equity co-investments have been excellent over time. Overall, for our platform from inception through September 30, we've invested over $635 million into equity co-investments and have generated an IRR of 25% and a multiple on invested capital of 2x. Looking ahead, our experienced team and broad origination platform position us well to generate attractive deal flow.

Our mission remains consistent, which is to deliver a stable and well-covered dividend while preserving capital. Everything we do is aligned to that objective. We continue to focus on investing in high-quality middle market companies that generate strong free cash flow. We capture that value through first lien secured loans, and we pay out those contractual cash flows in the form of dividends to our shareholders. With that overview, I'll turn it over to Rick for a more detailed review of our financial results.

Richard (Rick) Allorto: Thank you, Art. For the quarter ended September 30, GAAP and core net investment income was $0.25 per share. Investment income was comprised of $58 million in interest income, $5.9 million in dividend income and $0.8 million in other income. Our operating expenses for the quarter were as follows: interest and expenses on debt were $24.8 million, base management and performance-based incentive fees were $12.5 million. General and administrative expenses were $2.2 million and provision for taxes was less than $0.1 million. Net realized and unrealized change on investments, including provision for taxes, was a loss of $10.5 million for the quarter. As of September 30, NAV was $10.15 per share compared to $10.26 per share last quarter.

At quarter end, our debt-to-equity ratio was 1.5x, and our capital structure is diversified across multiple funding sources, including both secured and unsecured debt. As of September 30, our key portfolio statistics were as follows: the portfolio remains well diversified, comprising 159 companies across 32 industries. The weighted average yield on our debt investments was 10.2% and approximately 99% of the debt portfolio is floating rate. PIK income equaled only 1.3% of total interest income. The portfolio is comprised of 89% first lien senior secured debt, less than 1% in second lien and subordinated debt, 3% in equity of PSSL and PSSL II and 8% in equity co-investments. With that, I'll turn the call back to Art for closing remarks.

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Thanks, Rick. In conclusion, I'd like to thank our exceptional team for their continued dedication and our shareholders for their trust and partnership. We remain focused on delivering durable earnings, preserving capital and creating long-term value for all stakeholders. That concludes our remarks at this time. I'd like to open up the call to questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We'll go first to Robert Dodd with Raymond James.

Robert Dodd: Congrats on the quarter. On the question, I think you said you'd like to increase exposure to aerospace and defense because it's obviously a particular area you've got expertise. On that, I mean, is that going to necessitate monetization of equity first? Obviously, your leverage is kind of stable, but it's not low. It's not like you have a ton of available capital to increase allocation there. So I mean, what's the mechanism you think would work to generate that mix shift in terms of -- is it equity monetization? Is it shrinking other sectors that you're exposed to? Can you give us any color there?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes. So thanks, Robert. Appreciate the question. So we said we intend to maintain or increase. So we're at about 18% right now. So I think 18% to 20% is probably the relevant zone. I don't know that we'd want to get much more than 20% here.

And look, as deals pay off and they do, we'll look to reinvest back in the industry and maybe we'll add a touch to it if it's stuff where there's real tailwinds behind it like we found in Aechelon and Shield AI, kind of the -- we tend to invest in kind of the higher tech portion of defense and government services, whether it be cyber or drones or satellites and things of that nature. It's less kind of tanks and guns and things. So it's more in the services area. So we think there's a lot of tailwinds there.

We think given geopolitical issues and just given the shifting of defense dollars to more of these higher services, higher tech areas, we think makes some sense. But 18% to 20% is probably kind of where we cap out.

Robert Dodd: Got it. Got it. One more kind of -- your software is quite low, but obviously, Shield AI or Aechelon, that was an AI business where you did very well, if you -- which just shows you can do well in AI if you pick the right asset. So would you be willing to take up software exposure from where you are, if it's obviously the right maybe a defense adjustment software or software services business. I mean, how things get allocated to software or not is somewhat ephemeral sometimes. So is that something where you would be willing to go up higher?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Well, it's a great question. You're asking a great question, which is how do you define software, kind of AI, some people think it's software or it's a version of software. So AI is obviously a critical question we ask of every potential investment we make is what is AI going to mean for this particular industry? What's AI going to mean for this particular company? And we try best we can, and we have a lot of expertise internally. We have a lot of external expertise that we access to try to help us find areas where we have some -- let's put it this way.

If we feel like we have tailwinds behind the particular industry or the particular niche or the particular company that then we'll be more positive and supportive of making investment versus where we think there's wind in our face and we have a headwind, whether you define it as software or AI or technology, these are all different kind of potential shades of gray. But like some of our North Stars are in defense and government services, if the companies that we finance can provide excellent services at a lower cost to the government, that's usually a winner, assuming those services have a defensive moat around it. Same thing, by the way, for health care.

Health care does have a reimbursement question. So our North Star is can we find companies that have a defensive moat that generate a high-quality service for a lower cost so that whoever the payer is, whether it's the government or insurance companies, that company can be a winner. So I'm trying as best I can answer your question, Robert. It's sometimes hard to kind of select where software begins in AI, where software ends and AI begins, but kind of the rubric in the North Star is finding companies that have a moat that have some tailwind that is defensible and provide high-quality products and services at a lower-than-normal cost. Does that make sense?

Operator: We'll go next to Melissa Wedel with UBS, excuse me.

Melissa Wedel: Given the disclosure in the press release about some transferring of assets to PSSL II post quarter end. When we think about the fourth quarter in particular, it seems like there are a few moving parts. There's that transfer of, I think it was $40 million of assets and then also. How are you thinking about sort of the seasonality of deal flow in this December quarter? December can tend to be seasonally busy, but I think we've heard across the industry that this particular quarter, we might see a little less activity.

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes, it's a great question, and you're alluding to the fact that typically in our industry, Q4 is pretty heavy Q4 calendar quarter and Q1 calendar quarter is usually light just because in the deal business, if you're selling a company, you may want to get it sold by year-end. And so there tends to be a seasonal uptick in calendar Q4 and calendar Q1 tends to be lighter. That's the historical. But I think you're alluding to what we agree with, which is it's harder to see that particular phenomenon this year. We think calendar Q4 is moderate, and we think calendar Q1 will be moderate. Again, hard to say. The business is lumpy, can be lumpy.

But kind of it's hard to sit here and say there's a real conveyor belt or assembly line of -- and we can predict with any real accuracy what our originations are going to be in this environment. It's an interesting environment. And look, our North Star here is we just have to select excellent credit. And if we see good deals, we should do them. And if we don't see good deals, we should sit on our hands, and that's kind of the way we operate our business on a deal-by-deal basis.

But I'd say, in general, what you alluded to in your question, which is more moderate Q4 calendar and probably moderate Q1 calendar is probably how we see it at this point in time.

Melissa Wedel: Got it. And then the forward curve is pricing in a few more rate hikes through next year. And then when we think about what might be driving that, it really seems to be driven by expectations for stickier inflation. I'm curious how you're thinking about your portfolio broadly in terms of your borrowers being able to pass on costs and sort of protect EBITDA and service that debt. How do you think about the tension between higher inflation, higher borrowing costs and credit?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes. So it's a great question. We have -- the name of this particular company is floating rate capital. So -- and most of our industry is -- acts towards floating rates. So when rates go up, that certainly shifts value from the equity to the lenders. And on one hand, that's really nice. And on the other hand, your correct question is, can they afford to pay the higher rates. And as we've disclosed our credit stats, on average, we're kind of mid-4s leverage and kind of 2.2, 2.3x interest coverage. By and large, we think our portfolio is positioned to handle interest rate increases.

And by and large, the companies are generating enough margin and have enough of a moat to persist and do well. And of course, as always, there's always a handful of companies. We have something like 160 companies in this portfolio. We have companies or so around the platform. There's always going to be a handful of companies that, for whatever reason, idiosyncratic or not, are going to be falling short. That's just our business. That's the model. We model for it. There's always a handful of companies that -- whether it's their performance or whatever.

So we don't anticipate a default -- a significant default or nonaccrual increase as a result of rates going up another 50 basis points or so. That's what we think today. And we think on net on margin, it will be a positive for the economics of the company.

Operator: We'll go next to Chris Muller with Citizens Capital Markets.

Christopher Muller: So I guess looking at yields on new investments, they increased about 60 basis points from last quarter, but still about 90 basis points below a year ago. So I guess looking ahead, how do you guys think yields will trend in the context of higher base rates and possible spread compression?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Base rates, not that this is above our pay grade, Chris. The market is, I guess, suggesting 50 more basis points. It's about as good as a guess as anybody has at this point. In terms of spread, we kind of think we've stabilized here in the 500 to 550. Every so often, a particularly strong credit may get a 475. But kind of this 500, 550 is kind of we think the applicable zone. In the upper end of our market, if we say our market is 10 to 50 of EBITDA, in the upper end of that, call it, the 25 to 50 of EBITDA zone.

Because the big brands have receded from our space a bit, we've seen a bit more spread widening, not material, but it's a little bit more -- a little bit of widening in that 25 to 50 because when you think about it, the big brands when they're raising all that money would sometimes come down and compress spreads in our kind of core middle market world. They've kind of left the space due to all the reasons you know and the cash flows out of their systems in the private wealth channel. So that 25 to 50 space has really been a really nice space.

And as you look at our -- the deals we've been doing recently in our pipeline, we've been exercising that opportunity in that 25 to 50 of EBITDA because of the deal flow and because the spreads are widening a touch.

Christopher Muller: Got it. That's helpful. And then I guess looking at nonaccruals, it looks like they ticked up quarter-over-quarter. Just anything you can share on the new additions there?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes. Look, the only thing there that connects them, and we've talked about this in the last few calls, this is just the seasoning of the post-COVID vintage. So these were deals that were done in '21, '22, a, interest rates were really low then; and b, business models, the world was kind of had different business models. Like, for instance, one of the companies sell shoes on the Internet. Guess what? Shoes were being sold on the Internet very heavily post-COVID. They're still being sold on the Internet, but less so, more shoes as we revert to the mean and society shoes are getting bought in actual physical stores. So we have a car wash nonaccrual post-COVID.

People had a lot of disposable income to keep their cars squeaky, clean and they bought subscription to car wash companies. And today, that kind of mid-level, lower-level consumer is a little bit more squeezed in this K-shaped economy and car wash revenues have gone down across the industry. So I think these are kind of the examples kind of connecting the handful of nonaccruals we have, that's kind of the one theme. It's kind of that post-COVID 2021, 2022 vintage.

Operator: Our next question comes from Arren Saul Cyganovich with Truist Securities.

Arren Saul Cyganovich: Just kind of on that health of the portfolio trend, maybe you could talk about the growth rates you're seeing in your portfolio kind of broadly in terms of revenue and EBITDA? Are they stable? Are they declining? What are you seeing from the broader portfolio?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes. We're seeing kind of upper single digits, 8%, 9% growth of revenues and EBITDA across the portfolio. Again, that blended in there is our handful of underperformers. But by and large, we're seeing reasonable growth. Again, a lot of health care, a lot of government services, defense, a lot of stable business services, some home services that are doing well. Who would have thought that garage door repair would be the high-growth industry, but it is. We've had some nice -- as one example, garage door consolidation -- garage door repair consolidation has been a nice theme we've taken advantage of.

Arren Saul Cyganovich: And then on the PSSL II ramp, you're making good headway there, still a decent ways away from your around $1 billion targeted size. How much additional earnings accretion do you think you'll generate from that piece whenever we get fully invested there?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Well, we would hate to take away the modeling exercise from excellent research analysts at Truist and elsewhere. But I guess if you wanted to kind of model it out, it would probably be at least a couple of cents a share a quarter.

Operator: We'll go next to Christopher Nolan with Ladenburg Thalmann.

Christopher Nolan: Art, what are the target leverage levels you're looking to run these JVs at?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes. If you look at our other 2 JVs, they're roughly at 2x, obviously, higher than, let's say, the 1.5x we run PFLT. We think these -- the raw material we have, which are lower risk 4.5x levered covenanted core middle market loans are a good match for securitization technology. So we finance these JVs and in many cases, the BDC parent with securitization technology. We really think it's nice and safe. And we do have -- in our institutional side of our business, we do put these in for institutional investors.

There are institutional investors who like these assets, again, a different risk-adjusted return, 4 or 5x leverage, and they can get an upper teens to 20% return on their junior capital, again, with the securitization box, which can be -- we view as safer than, in some cases, a credit facility because you don't have to worry about a credit officer in a corner office having a bad hair day. If there's issues, it's orderly, it's not anyone yanking your chain. So we like for our lower-risk senior loans and securitization technology, and we use it in these JVs.

Christopher Nolan: And then on the JV, is there a mark-to-market risk where if interest rates go up and then the discount rate used in the fair value, the portfolio investments also go up? Does that result in you and your JV partner having to kick in more equity into the fund?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: That's a nice thing about securitization is not mark-to-market. So it's a box. It's a long-term box. It's a 10-year box. It's locked in. If you have credit underperformance, it's a very orderly wind down. It's not a fire sale or having to sell assets at exactly the worst time. And we've been operating these securitization boxes going back to 2019, which included... [Technical Difficulty]

Richard (Rick) Allorto: One second, Chris. I think Art just ran into a little bit of technical difficulty.

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Am I back on? Sorry, I had some technical difficulty. Crazy things are going on out there. So as I was saying, we've been using this technology since 2019 and dealt with it during COVID. So we kind of saw kind of the worst possible case and it's a very robust box.

Christopher Nolan: Great. And then I guess, I know that you guys -- on the dividend, I know you guys have committed to the current dividend payout through the end of the calendar year. Any comment you can give beyond that?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Look, we don't -- on the dividend, our base dividend is $0.24. We think we should be earning a reasonable amount above that, and we've committed to our supplemental being 50% of the excess. So if you model it out, if you grow the JV, you want to throw in a base rate increase or 2, we don't think of any -- there's any real risk to that base dividend of $0.24 or $0.08 a month, and we think there's some nice upside to it.

Operator: We'll go next to Paul Conrad Johnson with KBW.

Paul Conrad Johnson: There was another fairly meaningful write-down in PSSL I this quarter. And that JV has been, I think, a little bit of a headwind this year in terms of some write-downs in the equity. But I'm just curious, balance sheet credit quality remains fairly good. Nonaccruals are only 1.8%, PIK is relatively low. So I'm just curious, what has kind of been the driver of losses there? And why has PSSL I underperformed, I guess, relative kind of to the balance sheet, whether that's just been vintage or further seasoning that portfolio? Any sort of color you have there?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes. So it's a good question, Paul. And many of the same names and themes at PFLT, a car wash company a company that sells shoes on the Internet. So it's the same kind of names that you see. And so there's no difference other than to the early point, a little bit more leverage. So it's going to be a little bit more exacerbated. But that said, it also can swing to the other side. This particular quarter, we had those handful of names. We're hoping we're working through the challenges from that 2021, 2022 vintage, and we'll be out of the other side pretty soon here.

Paul Conrad Johnson: Got it. And I mean, in terms of like new deployments, I guess, what has been maybe the pickup from last year? You kind of mentioned spreads where they are but is structure materially better? Or is it just pricing in your opinion, kind of in terms of the deployment that's going into the JVs in the portfolio today, how -- what's, I guess, better about this vintage versus the prior vintage?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes. Look, I think it's kind of what I said earlier, Paul, which is in that upper portion of our space, the $25 million to $50 million of EBITDA because the big brands have receded, we're seeing a greater opportunity there where we can lend to $25 million to $50 million EBITDA companies at wider spreads than we could, let's say, a year ago. When the big brands were still raising a lot of money and every so often they come down and compress kind of in that $25 million to $50 million EBITDA range. So that's where some of the funds flows are helping us a bit as we execute on our model.

So again -- and we feel good about kind of our main industries that where we have real domain expertise, we're feeling good about the tailwinds behind those particular industries in this environment. So that's maybe where it's a little bit better than it was a year ago.

Paul Conrad Johnson: Got it. And I mean, in terms of relative to the seasoning that you're talking about in the stock, the credit seasoning I'm talking about, both in the JVs and the portfolio, the stock trades at now one of the lowest valuations in years. balance sheet is a little bit constrained from a leverage standpoint, clearly, there's growth left in the PSSL II JV. But why is -- I guess, there are no consideration of a buyback even if it's not something that's aggressively executed. But just to have something like this available when the stock is trading at such a big discount to NAV, why can't that be balanced, I guess, alongside just continued deployment?

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Yes. No, it's a great question. And I just want to say all options are always on the table, including a buyback, including other ways to add value. So we're not saying there's not a discussion of that. We agree with you. It's a really attractive valuation right now for investors with a steady income with floating rates going up here with a manageable nonaccrual rate with among the lowest PIK in the industry. So we agree.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer portion of today's call. I would like to turn the call back over to Art Penn for any closing remarks.

Arthur (Art) Howard Penn: Thank you, everybody, for being on the call today in this season of Thanksgiving. We certainly are grateful and have the attitude of gratitude for our investors in PFLT, and we're extraordinarily appreciative, and we wish everyone a terrific Thanksgiving.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.

#3127. Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You

Routine posting leaves a trail of breadcrumbs for recruiters to discover

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent.

You can read this as a polite way of saying, “I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored.

Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand.

Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market.

Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up?

You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn.

Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find.

You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs.

LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.”

Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.)

And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text.

Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.”

You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends.

Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know.

Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast.

The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions.

It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could.

The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you.

To help researchers search through the millions of peer-review publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library, IEEE has released a custom AI suite optimized for STEM literature. The suit allows users to search with natural-language queries and provides overviews with reference links.

AI has made it easier to access information in different domains, but specialist knowledge and human judgement still serve an essential role. Today, an engineer’s core value comes from knowing how to ask the right questions—not from knowing everything.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

#3126. OpenAI reportedly hires from the CIA as foreign spies target AI labs

A Russian charged with stalking Palantir staff, a bug in an OpenAI meeting room and the Nvidia affair have put state espionage on Silicon Valley’s agenda. Anthropic’s IPO filing warns of fake job applicants.

Sam Altman speaking at Semafor’s Silicon Valley conference, November 2026

OpenAI has hired from the CIA and walls off parts of its offices with “tented spaces” and turnstiles, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. Anthropic has recruited from the US intelligence community for “internal risk” roles that watch its own staff. Both are defences against state espionage, which the FT says now targets the biggest tech companies.

In a Big Read for the Financial Times, Patrick McGee and Rafe Rosner-Uddin describe how Big Tech is catching up with spying by hostile governments. The paper cites a person familiar with each company’s plans. At Meta, the Superintelligence Lab sits in a Menlo Park building that other staff cannot enter. Even senior vice-presidents need prior approval to visit, the FT reported.

OpenAI hired Aristedes Mahairas, an FBI veteran of nearly 24 years, as its global head of corporate security in August 2025. Its board includes Paul Nakasone, a retired general who once ran the National Security Agency. At OpenAI’s offices, private and public meeting rooms sit in separate areas with different access rules, according to the FT.

“We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement to the FT.

Last year, Anthropic set up a national security advisory council that includes former senator Roy Blunt and David Cohen, twice a CIA deputy director. The company told the FT it runs strict personnel vetting, access controls, and insider-risk monitoring.

Its filing with the SEC before last week’s listing names the threat directly. It also warns that state-backed actors and competitors could pressure staff after they join.

“We have been and expect that we will continue to be targeted by individuals seeking employment under false identities,” Anthropic wrote in the filing.

In October, OpenAI’s security team found a recording device behind a television in a meeting room used by executives. It came wrapped in toilet paper, according to the FT, and the company called the FBI. Federal agents arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer and Saudi national, on wiretapping charges. He has pleaded not guilty, and his trial starts in January. His lawyers call him an “overly curious tinkerer” with no harmful intent. Sam Altman also spoke about the bug when he told a Semafor audience that OpenAI’s security had not been perfect.

Last week, the US Justice Department indicted Igor D’iu, a Russian national, on four counts. Prosecutors say Russian handlers sent him to watch staff at a Silicon Valley technology and defence company because it supplied weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. The department did not name the company. The FT identifies it as Palantir.

According to the Justice Department, D’iu photographed employees’ laptop screens in a coffee shop near the company’s Palo Alto office. He also followed one employee for nearly 30 miles. FBI agents later found a notebook with profiles of at least three staff, including their family members’ names and assessments of their strengths and weaknesses.

Nvidia is the third case. On Monday, its board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, 11 days after he resigned. He had stepped down after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities consider a Chinese intelligence asset. China’s foreign ministry calls the allegations a smear. Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe anyone compromised national security or Nvidia’s secrets.

Greg Levesque runs Strider Technologies, a firm that tracks state-backed threats to companies. He told the FT that the Huang affair should wake up Silicon Valley.

“The biggest tech firms now operate on the scale of countries, and foreign intelligence services target them in the same way,” Levesque told the FT.

D’iu remains in federal custody. The Justice Department listed his next court appearance for 24 November.

Looking for something new to watch this weekend? Don't just sit around in a turkey haze when you can wake up your senses with the pulse-pounding thrillers newly available on Prime Video. Each week, I comb through the streaming service's latest additions to hunt down the suspenseful picks actually worth carving out time for.

November's new-arrivals shelf is still buried under holiday movies, so I dug through the tinsel to find three standout thrillers for your queue. I'll grant that one leans a little more action than pure suspense — an '80s hostage-rescue caper starring Chuck "Walker, Texas Ranger" Norris — but it packs more than enough tension to earn its spot alongside a razor-sharp Cold War mind-bender and a blood-soaked modern thriller about a rogue CIA assassin.

All three are well worth adding to your watchlist before the leftovers run out. Let's get into the three new-to-Prime Video thrillers I'd recommend streaming this week. You'll be glad you didn't just eat and sleep over Thanksgiving weekend.

If you only stream one of my picks this week, make it this one. More than sixty years later, John Frankenheimer's "The Manchurian Candidate" is still one of the best political thrillers, and it feels surprisingly fresh. Frank Sinatra gives one of his finest screen performances as Major Bennett Marco, but it's Angela Lansbury who makes one of cinema's most monstrous mothers years ahead of her turn in "Murder, She Wrote."

During the Korean War, a U.S. Army platoon is captured and brainwashed by Communists, and Sergeant Raymond Shaw (Laurence Harvey) comes home a decorated war hero. He has no memory that he's been reprogrammed as a sleeper assassin, triggered by the sight of a particular playing card. Marco (Sinatra), plagued by the same recurring nightmare as the other survivors, starts investigating, and the conspiracy leads straight to Shaw's domineering mother (Lansbury) and her senator husband (James Gregory) as the culprits.

Watch "The Manchurian Candidate" on Prime Video now

I'm not going to sugarcoat it: "Delta Force" is prime cheese, the kind of action thriller where Chuck Norris mows down terrorists from a rocket-launching motorcycle. It's got an absurd bench of old-school talent, led by Lee Marvin in his final film role as the gravel-voiced Colonel Nick Alexander, and it'll keep you on the edge of your seat.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Loosely inspired by the 1985 hijacking of TWA Flight 847, the film follows an elite U.S. commando unit sent in after Lebanese militants seize a passenger jet and reroute it to Beirut. Norris plays Major Scott McCoy, who's pulled back into service to rescue the hostages. If you want to check out a gem with plenty of explosions and unexpected twists, this is one of the best in Norris's early catalogue.

Not to be confused with the Vince Vaughn–Owen Wilson comedy, this 2026 "Internship" is an R-rated action thriller with a nasty streak. It follows a CIA-trained killer, raised from childhood in a secret program that recruited kids under the cover of an "internship," who sets out to burn the agency down.

Lizzy Greene takes the lead role as Renee, the assassin who rallies her fellow "interns" into a bloody uprising against the organization that stole their childhoods, forcing the CIA to answer with equally lethal force. Megan Boone ("The Blacklist") and Sullivan Stapleton ("Blindspot") round out the ensemble.

#3124. Apple announces Ted Lasso season 5 is coming

Apple TV (now $6.99/month for limited time) has just announced that Ted Lasso will return for season 5. Here are the details.

This summer Apple TV aired the highly anticipated return of Ted Lasso.

Season 4 debuted three full years after the last season ended, and brought a fresh start to one of the streamer’s all-time most beloved series.

But after the season 4 finale aired, Apple provided no indication whether the show would continue or not.

Now, uncertainty around the show’s fate is over.

Apple has announced that Ted Lasso season 5 is officially coming.

Following its hit fourth season, Apple’s global phenomenon “Ted Lasso” is officially returning back to the pitch for season five. Starring and executive produced by Emmy Award winner Jason Sudeikis, the fourth season of “Ted Lasso” introduced the Lady Greyhounds, with critics hailing it as “a perfect setup for a fresh return” and “one of the most beloved comedy shows of the decade.”

The announcement is light on further details. However, there should be a much shorter wait for season 5 than there was for season 4.

Before Ted Lasso returned this year, Jason Sudeikis shared that he had a new three-season arc in mind. Apple’s Eddy Cue also suggested the company would be happy to continue making more seasons for years to come.

But until today’s announcement, the lack of official news still put Lasso fans’ hopes on pause.

Whether it returns in 2027 or, perhaps more likely 2028, Ted Lasso isn’t going away again anytime soon.

Are you excited for Ted Lasso’s season 5 renewal? Let us know in the comments.

#3123. Kodak SlideTag is a $35 AirTag alternative with an E-Ink display for your photos

Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the new Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.

The Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same company, Reto, that launched a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. The tracker’s E-Ink display is designed mainly to showcase your photos, with storage built-in for up to 12 photos, but also the ability to show lists and QR codes.

The SlideTag’s extra features are controlled by the Kodak Memory Link app, while tracking is handled in the Find My app on iPhone just like an AirTag (and the Find Hub app on Android phones).

There are nine total styles for the SlideTag, all sold in a blind box format. You can order one tracker for $35 with the whole set also available for purchase.

Eight of the styles have a one-in-eight chance of finding, while the ninth style is only found in one out of every 64 boxes.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

#3122. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown University where he is also a founding faculty member of the Center for Digital Ethics. He's the author of multiple bestselling books about human flourishing in a technological world and is the host of The Cal Newport Show podcast.

The issue at hand as I see it is the human intelligence behind the AI. The AI does not say to itself, attack this server and extract this information, that is the human and the AI makes them powerful. Asking a computer to decide what it wants to do today without it accessing an LLM will be very difficult. For it then to decide to destroy mankind, again, without an LLM that specifically helps it do that. Also, there is no stopping what will come from peoplekinds AI adventure. Rogue nations will pursue it.

It's an interesting thought. I think we can draw parallels to the development of nuclear weapons. Notable scientists expressed fears about what they were creating, however proceeded due to fears about what would happen if the other side completed first. However, this time, it is OpenAI vs Anthropic, with elements of competition from China thrown in. And this time, the incentives are arguably stronger as they are immensely more profitable. Hubris will always manifest in the creator of such transformative devices so that they believe only they can control it.

Concerns about AI are legitimate. These systems can be used to intensify surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate cyberattacks, and concentrate economic and political power. More capable systems may introduce additional risks, particularly when deployed without adequate testing or oversight.

We should not dismiss these dangers. But neither should we treat catastrophe as inevitable simply because a technology is powerful.

The answer to risk is not blind faith. It is serious evaluation, independent testing, appropriate safeguards, accountability, and governance proportionate to the potential harm. High-risk applications warrant greater scrutiny than routine uses.

#3121. Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after its worst email outage, Reuters reports

Engineers traded 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats during the outage. Under the Microsoft Code Red, the company now wants to resolve any global incident within an hour.

The Microsoft logo on the side of one of its office buildings.

Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” to change how it prevents and handles major outages, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing internal memos. The Microsoft Code Red follows the global outage of 12 to 13 November. It knocked out Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot for about 24 hours.

Jaspreet Singh broke the story in a Reuters exclusive. Jason Henderson, president of M365 Core, called it the most customer-impacting incident in Exchange Online’s history. Never before had so many customers gone without email for so long, he told staff in a memo on Friday. The outage hit governments from Australia and Japan to the US, delayed trading firms, and disrupted airline communications.

“Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote, according to Reuters.

Amanda Silver oversees M365 Core and Work IQ as a corporate vice-president. She described the response in a separate memo on Monday. Engineers worked through a “fog of war”, she wrote. Responders sent more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats.

Diagnostic data sat in separate internal tracking systems. As a result, the team struggled to keep one shared picture of its theories and decisions, Silver wrote.

Charles Lamanna is Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platform. He told a Code Red review that the failed part had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures”, according to Silver’s memo.

Microsoft has blamed a dormant July defect in Windows for the outage, a scalability bug that went undetected for months. Chief executive Satya Nadella apologised publicly. Microsoft says cyber activity and AI agents played no part.

Silver set out five workstreams under the Code Red, covering load shedding, splitting traffic by region, and faster recovery. Microsoft wants to resolve future incidents worldwide within an hour. It also plans to use AI agents to help engineers read system health data faster.

Henderson will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, plus weekly reviews. Substrate runs the engineering behind Microsoft 365’s core services. A Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters that its teams keep working around the clock to apply the lessons learned.

Earlier this month, Henderson wrote that urgent patches to M365 Core services took too long to reach users worldwide. In one recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days. For the most urgent security issues, he wants an hour from detection to safe worldwide deployment. Microsoft is not there yet, he wrote.

Last week, Nadella said that AI-found bugs will make outages more likely. Henderson also wrote that he had reviewed the organisational and structural problems behind the failure.

“Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” Henderson wrote.

Early Black Friday deals on action, 360 and vlogging cameras

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Black Friday deals have arrived, and although it's only Tuesday, there are already plenty of great discounts on the best action cameras, 360 cameras and vlogging cameras.

I'm Pete, reviews editor here at Tom's Guide and the man in charge of our camera coverage. I test all action and 360 cameras, so I have to keep an eye on pricing throughout the year. This is usually the best time of the year to pick up a deal on action cameras and other gear. After all, it's never too early to start planning out your content for next year!

My favorite deal so far is on, well, my favorite action camera. The DJI Osmo Action 6 is the best action camera around, and is now $70 off at Amazon. This is the latest DJI flagship, so it's the first time I've seen this camera discounted in the U.S., and $70 is nothing to sniff at.

The biggest discount, and arguably best deal around right now, is on the GoPro MAX2 360 camera, which is down 45% from its $499 MSRP to just $274 at Amazon. Crazy value, in all honesty. But there's plenty more where that came from, including vlogging cameras like the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 at its lowest ever U.S. price of $373 at Amazon.

I'm only including deals that are actually good. I'm discounting any products (ahem, Insta360 X3, ahem) whose prices have been deliberately hiked before the sales events to make it look like a good deal. Read on for genuinely good savings!

Don't be fooled by the $299 MSRP — this camera usually sits around the $220. However, at $179, the DJI Osmo Action 4 still just hit its lowest price in the U.S., so there's never been a better time to pick up this little camera. It might be a couple of years old, but if you need professional-looking 4K video for YouTube, it's still plenty capable enough.

I'm shocked at this one. The GoPro MAX2 is the latest 360 camera from GoPro and a serious contender against the Insta360 X5 and X6, and Osmo 360 II. The fact it's second place in price order on this list is therefore pretty wild. If you want the flexibility of 8K 360 footage, I'm pretty sure this deal right here is the cheapest way there's ever been to get that.

The X4 Air is the revamped X4 — the first 8K 360 camera. The X4 Air packs some choice updates, namely to its audio (featuring the X5's wind guard) and stripped down weight. It's dropped to $299 before, but never lower, and tends to sit at the $399 MSRP outside of sales events. This is already a good deal, but I'd maybe wait to see if it drops a little further as Black Friday itself approaches.

DJI has faced an uphill struggle in the U.S. recently, thanks to its ongoing feud with the government and trade tariffs affecting its pricing. As such, the newer Pocket 4 models are borderline outrageously priced in the U.S. The DJI Osmo Pocket 3 is still a brilliant choice for content creators though, offering 4K gimbal-stabilized video. This is actually the lowest we've seen it drop (the previous low being $378).

The DJI Osmo Action 6 is the latest and greatest flagship action camera. It's my top pick for action cameras generally, and it's the camera I use personally. It offers the best blend of high-res capture, stabilization, battery life and waterproofing. As this camera is still relatively new, this is the first time we've seen a serious discount in the U.S., and $70 is a decent saving for the best-of-the-best, if you ask me.

I gave the Insta360 X5 our full five stars when I reviewed it in 2025. And it was well deserved. At the time, it was pushing the boundaries of what a 360 camera could do, with 8K/30fps 360 footage, strong internal audio and effective wind reduction. Insta360 gear always has a premium, but this is the lowest price we've seen the X5 drop yet.

Not satisfied with DJI constantly wearing the 'content creator gimbal camera' crown, Insta360 has had a pop. The Luna Pro offers 8K HDR gimbal-stabilized footage, giving you effortlessly smooth, professional output and plenty of space to crop while maintaining 4K resolution. It's pricey, but since when has cutting edge camera gear been cheap? Again, this is a pretty new camera, so this is the first time we're seeing real sizeable discounts.

The GoPro Mission 1 Pro is still fairly new, so typically sits around $699, but it's spent a couple of months at $599 recently. So while this is a good deal, it could well drop further as we approach the weekend. Keep an eye out. The Mission 1 Pro is an awesome camera for pros, offering 8K open gate and custom firmware via GoPro Labs.

The Insta360 X6 is the latest flagship 360 camera from Insta360. It offers improved imaging over the X5, excellent battery life, an OLED display, and is the first Insta360 camera to feature internal storage. This isn't a huge discount, which is to be expected given how new this camera is, but it's still the lowest price we've yet seen the X6 drop.
