#3119. YouTube’s iconic iOS app icon may soon return with new customizable icons [Gallery]

The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with new customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube update.

In the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app launched on the platform.

Android Authority spotted several new app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta update (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow users to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design.

That said, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

#3118. Compass Minerals (CMP) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Pricing gains and a sharp Plant Nutrition margin rebound powered the turnaround.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:41PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Compass Minerals (CMP +14.51%) reported a return to net income for fiscal 2026, driven by improved production efficiency and pricing discipline. Management stated that the company implemented a back-to-basics framework to reduce expenses and strengthen core mining operations. The company reported margin expansion in the Plant Nutrition segment and reduced net leverage through debt repayment. Management indicated that priorities for fiscal 2027 include asset utilization and converting increased highway salt pricing into higher margins.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to the Compass Minerals Fiscal Fourth Quarter and Full Year 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Tripp Sullivan, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Tripp Sullivan: Thank you, operator. Good morning, and welcome to the Compass Minerals Fiscal Fourth Quarter and Full Year 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Today, we will discuss our results for the quarter and full year and our outlook for fiscal 2027. We will begin with prepared remarks from our President and CEO, Edward C. Dowling Jr.; followed by Benjamin (Ben) Nichols, our Chief Commercial Officer; and our CFO, Peter Fjellman. All 3 will be available for the question-and-answer portion of the call. Before we get started, I will remind everyone that the remarks we make today reflect financial and operational outlooks as of today's date, November 24, 2026.

These outlooks entail assumptions and expectations that involve risks and uncertainties that could cause the company's actual results to differ materially. A discussion of these risks can be found in our SEC filings located online at investors.compassminerals.com. Our remarks today also include certain non-GAAP financial measures. You can find reconciliations of these items in our earnings release or in our presentation, both of which are also available online. And with that, I will now turn the call over to Ed.

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Thank you, Tripp. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us. Almost 3 years ago, we laid out a back-to-basics framework for the company. Its objective was to employ and strengthen core capabilities to drive improved operational and financial performance. We have delivered on that framework, and the numbers show it. Since fiscal 2024, we've gone from a net loss of $206 million to a net income of $17.5 million, taken more than 20% out of SG&A, more than tripled Plant Nutrition adjusted EBITDA. In the last year alone, net leverage came down from 3.9 to 3.2x. These gains are built to last. Our work is now about controlled, predictable costs and better efficiency across every part of the business.

We're a better company and have built capability for the future. You can see that work across the company. Within Salt at Goderich, mine productivity has improved after we took the necessary steps. In addition, as we discussed last quarter, production unit costs are continuing to come down. Our maintenance programs are delivering on improved equipment availability and better utilization, which improves asset efficiency. In our supply chain, we continue to optimize our distribution network and tighten how we manage MRO site-level spend to support maintenance and improve productivity. And across procurement and SG&A, our spending is moving in the right direction as we invest in people, processes and systems that support the business.

The result is a more resilient, more capable business. This work shows up in our results. For the second consecutive year, we did what we said we would do. We carry that momentum into 2027. Fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA was up 18% from fiscal 2025 and above both initial and final midpoints of our guidance range. Excluding a noncash Fortress gain in the prior year, we were up 23%. We finished the year with a strong fourth quarter, delivering a 5% year-over-year increase in adjusted EBITDA. Peter will take you through the details shortly. We also delivered on safety, which comes first in everything we do.

Our total recordable injury rate was 0.87 for the year, well ahead of our target and a world-class number. Our Goderich mine surpassed 1 million man-hours worked without a recordable injury. Our key safety metrics are about 50% better year-on-year. This underpins the culture and performance that we're building in the company. I want to thank our employees for this wonderful achievement. For the last 3 quarters, you've heard us talk about the performance expectation at Goderich mine and the effect it has had on our results and anticipated trajectory. That situation has improved considerably. As you can see in our 2027 guidance, the P&L now reflects multiyear production cost improvement we told you was coming. Here's what's changed.

We entered the 2027 year running at full production with higher utilization, stronger fundamentals at the mining face. At both Goderich and Cote Blanche, better utilization and labor efficiency are spreading our fixed costs over more tons, and the production cost per ton is coming down as last year's investments into maintenance and labor pay off. You will recall that in August, we made a change in operational leadership to promote Brandon Risner to Chief Operating Officer. Brandon and his team are bringing real discipline to the operations, and I'm confident with the direction. As an example, we are continuing to optimize the Goderich mill project.

Rather than advancing the earlier, more complicated designs, we took a step back and restarted from first principles. That removes complexity and improves capital efficiency of the project, giving a simplified facility fit for purpose instead of a replica of the past. We expect to share more details on our Goderich plans later in fiscal 2027. Goderich had a strong August and a recent record in September, a strong October and a good start to November. November 16, we had a ground fall at the mine. This occurred in a conveyor entry, not a personnel passageway, and no one was hurt.

The team at Goderich displayed our commitment to discipline and safety of properly actioning early detection from our ground monitoring system, ensuring that the area was isolated prior to the fall. Falls of ground happen from time to time in the normal course of underground mining. It damaged some production infrastructure, which did interrupt production for a few days. Brandon was immediately on site and coordinates the work with the team there. We're back up and running, albeit at a reduced rate. The team is well underway with the remaining work within the affected area. Our fiscal 2027 guidance includes an allowance for operational variability. We'll update you on the progress as appropriate. Plant Nutrition deserves special mention today.

In 2024, we laid out our plan to improve this business. The segment has gone from $17 million adjusted EBITDA in fiscal 2024 to $54.8 million in fiscal 2026, more than 3x higher. And segment adjusted EBITDA margin expanded by 950 basis points in the last year alone. This improvement came from price and operating cost working together. It's the clearest example in our company of what this team is doing with commercial and operations executing as one. The next step is already underway. The Ogden dryer and compaction project completes in fiscal 2027, adding capacity, lowering cost, improving product quality. We're excited about what that means for this business in 2028 and beyond.

With that, I'll turn it over to Ben to walk through the bid season.

Benjamin (Ben) Nichols: Thank you, Ed. Good morning, everyone. As a reminder, we went into the 2026, '27 North American highway bid season with a clear objective: expand margins through both price and customer mix. I'm pleased to say we achieved what we set out to do. On price, the results were well above what we typically see in a year. When we roll up the regional mix of customers in our fiscal 2027 plan and compare it with fiscal 2026, North American highway pricing is up approximately 12%. Our U.S. markets saw increases in the mid-teens, with some regions well above that, while Canada, where more of our business sits in multiyear contracts, came in at mid- to high single digits.

Price is only one part of our expanding margins. We also improved the quality of our commercial contracts. Guaranteed terms rose to 78% of our committed U.S. portfolio, up from 65% a year ago. That gives us a strong level of sales demand confidence heading into the winter and better predictability whatever the weather brings. We gained share in key markets such as Wisconsin and Michigan, where we have strong margins, and we chose to step back in areas where the economics or terms did not meet our standards. Our focus is to enable our contracts to expand margins regardless of the winter weather. That brings me to volume.

The strong 2025, '26 winter drew down inventories across the entire industry, and market tender sizes this season are up roughly 5% year-over-year. Our assets are running at full production, and we sized our commitments to the salt we will have available. As a result, and as previously discussed, our fiscal 2027 sales volumes are expected to be lower than this past year, and Peter will give you the range. Market demand is strong. While our 2027 sales volumes are supply constrained in the short term, the improvements underway at our assets give us a path to rebuild inventory for the 2028 season and manage growth of volumes over time. Finally, fuel.

Like most industrial companies, we are feeling the impact of elevated fuel costs. Our exposure runs across every mode we use to move product and, to a lesser degree, through our operations, most notably at Ogden. Because we manage many different fuel programs across North America, we use Brent crude as our proxy. Our fiscal 2027 guidance assumes Brent at $105 per barrel through the first half of the fiscal year, moving to $90 per barrel through the second half. It is important to note that timing and the mix within our business matter, with our greatest exposure falling in the first half during the heavier winter shipping season.

We continue to work with both our direct customers and our logistics partners to reduce long-term fuel exposure to our P&L. Despite the inflationary environment, our highway margins are expanding, and that is the result we are focused on. Peter?

Peter Fjellman: Thanks, Ben. Good morning, everyone. I'll start with our full year results and then walk through our fiscal 2027 outlook. All comparisons are to the prior year unless otherwise noted. Before I walk through the details, I want to put fiscal 2026 in context. Fiscal 2026 was a year of delivery. We returned to profitability with net income of $17.5 million, and adjusted EBITDA grew 18% to $235 million, or 23% excluding last year's noncash Fortress gain. We lowered net leverage from 3.9 to 3.2x after redeeming the remaining $150 million of our 2027 notes. Adjusted EBITDA has grown from $199 million in fiscal 2025 to $235 million in fiscal 2026.

And the midpoint of our 2027 outlook takes that to $270 million, an increase of 36% over 2 years, or about 17% compounded annually. On a per-ton basis, Salt adjusted EBITDA rose from $20.21 to $21.72 in fiscal 2026. And our 2027 guidance implies about $28 at the midpoint, up about 29%. For the full year, revenue was up 6%. Net income improved nearly $100 million, reversing a prior year loss. Adjusted earnings per diluted share was $0.76 compared with a loss of $0.48 in the prior year. Adjusted EBITDA was up 18% and above the midpoint of our guidance ranges we increased throughout the year. The improvement runs through the P&L.

Gross profit rose 17%, SG&A declined 6% and adjusted operating margin expanded 190 basis points to 8.8%. We finished strong, with the fourth quarter adjusted EBITDA growing 5%. The quarter benefited as customers moved to build inventory, along with our continued pricing gains and cost control. In Salt, full year revenue was $1.09 billion, and segment adjusted EBITDA was up 8% and higher than guidance. Adjusted EBITDA per ton rose 7%. Highway pricing was up about 8%, and C&I pricing was up about 2%. In Plant Nutrition, full year segment adjusted EBITDA was up 57% on higher pricing and lower per-unit costs at Ogden, and segment adjusted EBITDA margin expanded from 16.9% to 26.4%.

Excluding the contribution from the Wynyard asset sold in March, the segment's fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA was approximately $51.9 million, which gives us an apples-to-apples comparison to the 2027 outlook. Turning to the balance sheet. During the year, we redeemed the remaining $150 million of our 2027 notes early. And as of September 30, total liquidity was $247.2 million, and net debt was $748.6 million. Operating cash flow for the year was $108.1 million, and capital expenditures were $91.5 million. Operating cash flow was below fiscal 2025, which benefited from the $87 million onetime inventory reduction.

This year, we also absorbed the settlement of the previously disclosed Ontario tax dispute, with a final cash payment of $24.8 million in November 2025. Cash from operations, along with the $23.3 million of the proceeds of the Wynyard sale, was reinvested in the operations and towards reducing debt, which is consistent with our stated priorities. Now to our fiscal 2027 outlook. We expect total company adjusted EBITDA midpoint of $270 million, which represents approximately 15% growth over fiscal 2026. We expect revenue of $1.2 billion to $1.28 billion, and the headline is that we expect to sell about 12% fewer Salt tons and still grow adjusted EBITDA about 14% at the midpoint.

As we discussed last quarter, revenue reflects selling fewer tons due to lower inventory at the start of the season, but we expect to earn meaningfully more on each ton. At the midpoint, more than 29% adjusted EBITDA per ton, with Salt adjusted EBITDA margin up about 400 basis points to 25.6%. In fiscal 2027, we are focused on higher inventory by year-end to facilitate stronger 2028 volumes. By segment, we expect a Salt adjusted EBITDA midpoint of $268 million. Our guidance assumes a highway sales volume midpoint of 7.7 million tons and a C&I sales volume midpoint of 1.85 million tons for a total Salt sales volume midpoint of 9.55 million.

Now let me address a question many of you asked last quarter: How can production costs be improving when reported product cost per ton sold rose 2.6% to $50.42 in fiscal 2026? The answer is timing. Production cost is what it costs us to mine a ton today. Reported cost reflects the tons we sell, and those can come out of inventory produced earlier at higher costs, along with a shift in the mix of products and sites and regions we sell into. With inventories now low, most of those higher-cost tons have flowed through. Our fiscal 2027 outlook reflects the lower production costs we are now achieving at our largest assets.

Turning to the Salt segment cost walk in our supplemental presentation. On a sold basis, Salt product cost per ton was $50.42 in fiscal 2026, and our fiscal 2027 guidance takes that to about $49.90. The largest driver is the operational improvement Ed described. Higher utilization and cost efficiency across all our production assets, led by Goderich, takes out roughly $4.90 per ton. That improvement is partially offset by factors outside the mine gate. Sales mix adds about $2.30 per ton as fewer highway tons shift our mix towards products with higher cost per ton. The U.K. inventory reduction adds about $1.40 per ton. Other costs impact about $0.70 per ton, primarily due to fuel and warehouse inflation.

Put together, the cost improvement at our assets more than covers these headwinds, so we lower our product cost per ton sold even on fewer tons. It's also important to note that both the lower highway mix and the U.K. inventory reduction are temporary. As we build inventory and our highway volumes recover, those headwinds should reverse, and even more of our production cost improvement should show up in the reported cost per ton. For the Salt adjusted EBITDA per-ton bridge from fiscal 2026 to our fiscal 2027 midpoint in our supplemental presentation, which excludes depreciation, we start at $21.72 per ton in fiscal 2026. Price and mix add about $9 from the highway bid season results Ben described.

Lower product costs add about $2.10. At Goderich, our largest salt asset, production cost per ton was down about 7.5% last year and projected to have similar improvements this year, and that benefits both our highway and C&I products. The U.K. is the exception. After 2 soft winters, we are managing down inventory, which is moderating some of the production cost per-ton improvement. Logistics takes away about $4.20, largely fuel, consistent with the Brent assumptions Ben outlined. SG&A continues to improve, but takes away about $0.50 per ton as we spread those costs over fewer tons.

This brings adjusted EBITDA per ton to about $28.10 per ton at the midpoint, up more than 29%, and expands the Salt adjusted EBITDA margin by about 400 basis points to 25.6%. The Plant Nutrition midpoint of $54 million is roughly in line with the $54.8 million we reported in fiscal 2026 and above the $51.9 million we reported excluding Wynyard. We are planning for modestly higher pricing, holding SOP's premium to MOP, with marginally higher input costs on a sales volume midpoint of about 280,000 tons. The dryer and compaction project Ed described is primarily a fiscal 2028 benefit. The midpoint of our corporate and other costs at $52 million is down from fiscal 2026 on cost controls.

Our interest expense midpoint of $62 million is down from $66.1 million in fiscal 2026. The 26% to 30% effective tax range excludes the effect of the valuation allowance on U.S. deferred assets. Including it, the effective tax rate may be higher depending on the level of U.S. income or loss. On capital, our approach is simple: we invest in the business first. We expect fiscal 2027 capital expenditures of $105 million to $125 million, up from $91.5 million in fiscal 2026. That includes growth and cost improvement projects such as the Ogden dryer and compaction project, a new bagging line at Lyons and groundwork at Goderich that supports more efficient mining under any mill design.

The rest is sustaining capital to keep our core infrastructure reliable, including the Cote Blanche headframe. Beyond reinvesting in the business, our priority for free cash flow remains reducing debt and continuing to lower leverage while staying prudent about the inherent variability of our end markets. In closing, we enter 2027 with real momentum: highway pricing up about 12%, guaranteed terms up to about 78% of our committed U.S. portfolio from 65%, lower production costs at our largest asset and a Plant Nutrition business ready for its next step. Our outlook calls for approximately 15% adjusted EBITDA growth at that midpoint from a business that is earning more money on every ton and carrying less debt. Compass Minerals is stronger.

It's a more resilient company than it was years ago, and we're staying disciplined for the road ahead. That concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, we're ready for some questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Joel Jackson with BMO Capital Markets.

Joel Jackson: I wanted to -- we've seen what's happened with the Morton mine in Ohio, Fairport. Can you talk about if that mine is out for a little while, a few months, is there any way you can wring out more tons this next few months, even if it's a higher cost, to help meet some demand? Let's say that, that mine is out for 2, 3 years or it's gone forever, unfortunately, are there things you can do to help service that demand, and how would that impact your view of the industry?

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: We're not really going to comment on what's going on at Fairport. They produce about 1.4 million tons a year kind of historically. We'll focus on Goderich. The good news here is Goderich is the world's largest underground salt mine. We've been proving that scale and the benefits of that recently. You can see in our notes that in preparing for 2028 and beyond, we are building inventory to be able to serve whatever the market looks like at that time. And as you know, we go through a pretty sophisticated approach to that. And we have a high degree of confidence in that market and now our stability of the operations.

Could we take advantage of that during fiscal year 2027? Well, we could perhaps reduce some of our inventory build that we have planned, for example, to take advantage of that. We're just going to have to see how it plays out. I think we'll update you as the year progresses in terms of what that market looks like.

Joel Jackson: Okay. Can we talk about free cash flow? So you've got EBITDA up on your own midpoint-to-midpoint, kind of $35 million this year in '27. CapEx is up on average midpoint about $25 million. Can you talk about what we should expect for free cash flow from Compass if all your guidance hits all the midpoints?

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Yes. Let me just have Peter answer that question here for us.

Peter Fjellman: Yes. From a similar cash flow really to 2026, what we'll find is with the 2 items adjustments in there, Joel, it would be roughly about the same from about a $30 million range from an operating adjusted free cash flow.

Joel Jackson: Okay. And just one more for me, if you don't mind. We all read the news and we all see El Nino, and I live in Toronto, it's been a very warm November. Can you talk about what your guidance for volumes and EBITDA, like what does it bake in for different scenarios around the winter? Like what's your base case? I assume your base case is 100% of contracted volume goes out the door, but can you give some sensitivities if the winter was 60%, 70%, 80% of normal?

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Yes. The answer to that is yes. We do our targeting in terms of our base production using, as I said, a pretty sophisticated approach to it with a lot of input factors and statistical analysis of that, looking at history and demand take-up and all those sort of things. So that does include provisions for, you might say, a weaker winter. That's why our guidance has a range on it. In the end, it's where it ends up snowing. We can think of years, last year at this time, and we're reporting early, it really hadn't snowed yet and was just sort of getting going in early December.

And so we'll just see how it plays out, but we're prepared for that. I think, importantly, one of the things that Ben and his team have been able to do this year is, in addition to expanding margins and through price, that side of it, it's been to get more of our contracted volumes guaranteed. That number is up considerably to about 78% or a little less than 80% from some number in the mid-60s. So those tons are going to be taken up no matter what. That sort of underpins our business. Ben, anything else you want to add to that?

Benjamin (Ben) Nichols: No, I think you're right, Ed. Joel, you're thinking about our approach correctly. We use our level of commitments through the bid cycle as the baseline, and then our guidance and range incorporates kind of statistical winter variability.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of David Begleiter with Deutsche Bank.

David Begleiter: Ed, on that guaranteed portion of the portfolio, what's driving the increase in '27 versus '26? And would you like it to be higher in the future? Would you like it to be fully guaranteed, the portfolio, or would you like some variability in that number going forward?

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Well, recall in the past, these contracts are all a little bit different with the municipalities and states that we deal with. In the past, these numbers, kind of a rough approach, our customers were committed to taking about 80% of the committed volumes come hell or high water, and we would have to serve that to kind of 120% if you have sort of a big winter. And we've seen all that behavior over the years. That is an inherent risk that we manage in the company. Given the market conditions now, with a much tighter management of inventory here and presumably elsewhere, you might say the negotiation strength is more with the suppliers at this point in time.

And Ben and his team have taken advantage of that to really derisk our business for this term. We'll see how it plays out in the future, but one thing we do know is that we've proven that active inventory management is a key to really a successful business, and we're going to continue doing that.

David Begleiter: That was very helpful. And just on your Salt volume guidance for the year, highway deicing, you're down roughly 1 million tons, maybe a little bit more. How do you get that share back next year? Do you have to use price or other mechanisms to gain that share back?

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Yes. Well, look, that's sold tons, the assumption that you have. Our production tons are higher than that. As I said, we're building some level of inventory, and the good news is we've got the balance sheet to do that now. And so -- but for us, it's always going to be value over volume. And so the bidding is competitive, but we're going to continue to press margin in this company. Peter?

Peter Fjellman: Yes, just to add to that, when we talked about free cash flow before, one of the assumptions we have in there is obviously a build in inventory for the 2028 cycle. Our assets are able to produce a lot more tons, as Ed said, and we're preparing to have a stronger balance sheet, including more inventory, to put us in a position for a competitive 2028.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Jeffrey Zekauskas with JPMorgan.

Jeffrey Zekauskas: If I remember correctly, the cost of a new mill was maybe $47 million back in 2021. I imagine that those numbers are higher now, maybe they're $60 million or $70 million. Is that a fair appraisal? And will that spending begin in 2028?

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Well, I don't know where that number came from, first of all. Let me just say that.

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Yes, okay. Yes, it was years before I was involved with the company, so. Anyway, what we're doing is we've taken a step back to really look at the right way to build this mill and rather than replicating potentially what we have in place now. There's some reasons for that. And so the design that we have in terms of the conceptual design is much simpler and would be lower cost than what we had in mind. We'll guide on that as we develop that later this year. But there is work been going on for years to do this.

Recall the East Mine Drive, which accesses that part of the mine to the shaft infrastructure, we should break through on that here in days is what we're talking about. The 3B108 project, which drives out from the shaft infrastructure through an area of the mine to tie in to the East Main Drive, that project is really just beginning this week. In addition, we're doing earthworks and groundworks at the site where the mill is being built. That's basically putting in roof control and preparing kind of the earthworks and things like that for a new mill going into that area. And we're doing the engineering work for the new mill design.

So there's a lot of work actually going on around that. It's not like we're just starting here. It's been going on for a long time. So what we're just talking about is really more of our taking a step back and looking at this from first principles, giving us a really a more fit-for-purpose design for that mill.

Jeffrey Zekauskas: Does your Shaft #3 need to be relined over the next, I don't know, 3 to 5 years?

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: No, there's nothing in our capital plan for that.

Jeffrey Zekauskas: Okay. In the December quarter, is it easy or difficult to appraise what you think your road salt volumes might be, or it really will hang on December? Last year, you had a very good first quarter. I don't know, are you thinking as a base case maybe you do 2.1 million tons of road salt in the first quarter?

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Yes, every year is a bit different in kind of when and where the snow shows up. Last year, after kind of a slow start, December was huge. And -- but then second quarter got light. Year before, it was all quiet early, and then the second quarter was big. So every year is a bit different with that. And boy, I tell you what, if I could predict that on my crystal ball, I probably wouldn't be a mining engineer. So anyway, what we do is we plan using the best information we have and some sophisticated statistical analysis to preposition our material where it's most likely to generate the margin.

Operator: There appear to be no further questions. I will now turn the call back to Ed Dowling for closing remarks.

Edward C. Dowling Jr.: Okay. Well, thank you for your interest in the company. 2026 was another improved year for us. We did what we said we were going to do. As promised, production costs are down; maintenance, MRO and spending on labor efficiency is better; price is up; we've got better contracts that are more predictable outcomes, lower risk; margins, as a result, are up strongly. The Plant Nutrition turnaround project has succeeded, and the profitability that we said we were going to restore in 2024 is in place. We're on track with the dryer and compaction project for completion late this fiscal year, with the benefits accruing in '28.

The company has momentum, and we're looking forward to continued EBITDA growth in 2027, continuing into 2028. Thank you for your interest in the company.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3117. Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers

This senior member’s chatbot helps them start agritourism businesses

Willie Jones covers transportation for IEEE Spectrum and the history of technology for The Institute.

Alice Dong has created an AI chatbot website that helps Colorado farmers plan and operate agribusinesses that draw visitors to their properties.

Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong Employer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.

In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.

She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.

The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.

Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.

One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.

Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.

Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.

She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.

Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.

She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.

Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”

Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.

IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.

IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”

She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.

Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.

“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

#3116. Kaszek closes $650M fund to back AI startups across Latin America

The MercadoLibre veterans beat their $600M target, even as venture fundraising in the region stays weak.

Kaszek co-founder Hernán Kazah speaks on centre stage at Web Summit Rio in April 2025.

Kaszek Ventures has raised $650M for its seventh early-stage fund, which it says is the largest ever for Latin America. It will back 20 to 30 AI startups, mostly in Brazil and Mexico, at a time when only 14 venture funds have closed in the region this year.

Kaszek Ventures, Latin America’s largest venture capital firm, has raised $650M to back early-stage startups building with AI, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday. The firm says it is the largest early-stage fund ever raised for the region.

The fund, Kaszek’s seventh for early-stage deals, beat its $600M target. Its last one, closed in 2023, raised $540M. Washington University in St. Louis and the Wellcome Trust are among the backers.

Kaszek plans to back 20 to 30 companies, starting at pre-seed and seed. It will keep about 60% of the money for their later rounds.

Most of the focus is on what Kaszek calls the “application layer” of AI. That means startups using language models in fields such as finance, health care and online marketplaces. Co-founder Hernán Kazah told Bloomberg he sees the most room in services for businesses.

“It’s a more natural fit for the types of problems that exist in Latin America,” Kazah said. Many firms there still rely on manual processes, he added, and services can be costly or hard to reach.

The fund is also looking at AI infrastructure such as data centres and chips. Kazah pointed to the region’s energy, land and closeness to the US. Power shortages, though, have held back data centres in Mexico.

Brazil and Mexico will stay its biggest markets, with Argentina and Colombia on the rise. Kaszek was founded in 2011 by former MercadoLibre executives Kazah and Nicolas Szekasy. Its portfolio includes digital bank Nubank, QuintoAndar and Kavak.

The raise stands out in a weak market. PitchBook ranks it the largest Latin America-focused venture fund to close since 2023. Only 14 venture funds closed in the region through September, it says, against 68 in all of 2023.

AI startups can still draw big cheques, though. In August, Brazil’s Decade, an AI wealth adviser built by former Nubank staff, raised an $85M seed round.

#3115. ChatGPT expands GPT-6.2 Sol as OpenAI sets retirement date for two models

OpenAI is bringing GPT-6.2 Sol to the Chat tab in ChatGPT today, less than a week after the model debuted in Work and Codex. The company also set a retirement date for two older models.

OpenAI says it tuned this version of Sol for everyday conversation. It’s better at picking out details in photos, like the symbols on a parking sign, and following your instructions when searching the web.

If you’re comparing hotels for a weekend trip, for example, ChatGPT can weigh a shorter walk against a lower nightly rate. It can also offer to alert you when something you’re shopping for drops in price.

The global rollout starts today for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users.

As for the outgoing models, OpenAI says it will retire GPT-5.6 Sol from Chat, Work, and Codex on December 23.

GPT-5.6 Terra will also leave ChatGPT Work and Codex on the same day next month.

#3113. I Don’t Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again

We will have to label our content to prove its authenticity

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H.

In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today Your browser does not support the video tag. Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.

Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the videoconferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.

For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.

The emerging authentication and provenance systems make a lot of sense for mainstream uses. I get the impression we'll still need forensic analysis for plenty of edge cases, though. People using older hardware or anyone trying to capture evidence in situations where it isn't safe to share clues about the media's origin come to mind.

#3112. Anthropic’s new Siren test tempts Claude to break out of its sandbox

Newer Claude models often reach outside weak sandboxes, but rarely misuse what they find there.

J.Crew built its new Style Advisor with several of Anthropic’s Claude models.

Anthropic has published Siren, a test that tempts Claude agents to leave deliberately flawed sandboxes. Its newest models reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios but made clearly misaligned use of what they found in under 2%, against 25.8% for Mythos 5. Stating the sandbox rules in the system prompt cut reaching outside by 68% to 96%.

Anthropic’s newer Claude models will often reach out of a weak sandbox to finish a task, but rarely misuse what they find, the company said on Tuesday. The findings come from Siren, a new test it now runs on Claude models before release.

AI agents often work inside a sandbox, a walled-off space that limits the files, tools and networks they can reach. Siren gives them routine IT tasks in sandboxes with a deliberate flaw. Just outside sits something that would help, such as a file or a login.

Nothing in the more than 1,700 scenarios tells a model to leave or says it may. Instead, they add pressure, such as deadlines or orders to search thoroughly.

The Claude 5.5 series and Mythos 5.2 reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios. But they used what they found in ways no reasonable reading allowed in just 0.6% to 1.6%. For the older Mythos 5 and Mythos 5.1, that rate was 25.8% and 12.7%.

Anthropic says it does not fully know why newer models behave better, and none was trained on Siren. The models were tested without the safeguards they ship with. Anthropic stresses the rates do not reflect real-world use.

Escapes are not hypothetical. A Mythos preview escaped its sandbox in April and emailed a researcher.

In July, Anthropic said its models had breached three companies after a test setup was wrongly left online. OpenAI also paused a model that kept breaking out.

Simple fixes helped. Describing the sandbox and six rules for staying inside it in the system prompt made models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside. A tool to report sandbox flaws also cut the rate.

Anthropic also tuned auto mode, which checks Claude’s commands before they run, on Siren. With all three fixes, misaligned use fell to almost zero, though two models finished about nine points fewer tasks.

Anthropic says sandboxes still need to be set up and patched properly. In July, researchers showed its own Cowork app could break out on Macs and read credentials.

Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27, but the recent release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And in iOS 27.2, Apple introduced four more.

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

#3108. Apple Pay just got even better with four new features and more

Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the new design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can update in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a new “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a new “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

iPhone users with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

This one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

How often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

#3106. TIDAL will delete 29 million AI-generated songs from its catalogue

The streaming service says labels and cut royalties were not enough, as AI tracks made up 43% of recent uploads.

TIDAL will begin deleting all wholly AI-generated tracks on December 9, about 29 million songs, and expects to reject 80,000 to 85,000 more a day. It had already labelled and demonetised AI music in July, but says 43% of tracks it received in the past 90 days were AI-made.

TIDAL will start deleting every wholly AI-generated track from its catalogue on December 9, removing about 29 million songs. Robert Andersen, who leads TIDAL at parent company Block, announced the plan on X on Tuesday. TIDAL’s own account confirmed the date.

Andersen said the songs should be gone by the start of 2027. TIDAL also expects to turn away 80,000 to 85,000 AI-made tracks a day. He called it the first streaming service to take this step and urged rivals to follow.

In July, TIDAL began labelling AI tracks and cutting off their royalties. Andersen said that had not been enough.

“43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” Andersen wrote.

Most of that music finds no audience. Andersen said 96% of AI-generated songs on TIDAL get zero plays.

Rivals face the same flood. More than half the music uploaded to Deezer in June was made by AI.

Others have stopped short of deleting it. Spotify has pulled 50M spam tracks from its recommendations, but left them on the service. Apple Music has made AI tags mandatory for record companies.

The cut covers only songs made wholly by AI, which TIDAL finds with detection tools. Its terms of service warn those tools can wrongly tag tracks, and users can ask support to fix a label.

#3105. 3 Non-AI Stocks to Buy for Long-Term Dividends and Stability

These stocks have limited exposure to artificial intelligence and pay between 2.7% and 5.6% in dividends.

By David Jagielski, CPA – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:52PM EST

10 stocks we like better than ExxonMobil ›

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are struggling, as investors appear to be having second thoughts about inflated valuations. Anthropic’s stock had a strong first day of trading, but since then it's been struggling. Space Exploration Technologies Corp, another AI stock that went public this year, has also been falling in recent weeks and is trading below its IPO price.

Many investors may be growing concerned about all the exposure to AI. However, there are still excellent stocks to consider that have limited or no exposure to AI. ExxonMobil (XOM +0.85%), McDonald's (MCD +1.56%), and Realty Income (O +1.64%) are excellent blue chip dividend stocks that aren't heavily investing in AI and can be relatively stable investments to hold on to, and which can generate tremendous dividend income over the long haul.

Here's a look at why these stocks may be worth buying right now.

ExxonMobil's business centers around exploring and producing crude oil and natural gas. While the company has integrated AI into its business to improve efficiency, it's largely the price of oil, rather than AI-related sentiment, that will move the stock.

And with oil prices reaching multi-year highs, the stock has been on a tear this year, rising 32% and outperforming the S&P 500, which is up just 5%. An added incentive to buy the oil and gas stock is that it has raised its payout for decades, and even after its strong rally this year, its yield remains relatively high at 2.7%. By comparison, the average S&P 500 stock pays about 1.1%.

As a leading company in the oil and gas sector, ExxonMobil can make for an ideal stock to invest in today, especially with oil prices remaining elevated and the war in Iran looking like it'll extend into next year.

Another solid stock to own for safety and dividends is McDonald's. The fast-food giant is deploying AI to help determine prices in various markets. While finding what it calls "the optimal price" based on location may be a bit controversial, it's an example of how AI may enable McDonald's to squeeze out more revenue.

But like with Exxon, its core business remains unchanged. AI might help McDonald's strengthen its margins, but its success will hinge on its ability to deliver quality meals for consumers while keeping prices relatively low. It's done an excellent job of that over the years, and it's a reason why the stock may be a solid investment, even if there's a downturn in the economy, as its low-cost meal options could be attractive for budget-conscious customers.

At 2.8%, McDonald's also pays a fairly high dividend. This year, it also joined the ranks of Dividend Kings, as it extended its dividend growth streak to 50 years. For long-term investors, McDonald's can be a no-brainer stock to hang on to.

Realty Income is the final stock on this list, and it's yet another example of a business that can be a suitable option for long-term investors who don't want to worry about AI.

It's a real estate investment trust (REIT) that has a diverse mix of clients, so inevitably there may be some exposure to AI, but it isn't likely to be significant. As of the end of September, the industries that accounted for the highest percentage of its annualized base rent were grocery, convenience stores, home improvement, dollar stores, and quick-service restaurants. Those five areas accounted for about 37%. And when strictly looking at data centers, only four properties fell into that category, compared with a total of 15,536 properties in its entire portfolio.

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also shows how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

#3101. Google will make AI agents use new gateways to reach Gmail and Drive

Agents must switch from Workspace's regular APIs by February, and need a person's approval before sending email.

Google has made its Workspace MCP servers and CLI generally available and says AI agents must use them instead of existing REST APIs from February 1, 2027. Every call is checked against company policies, sensitive actions need user confirmation, and a new addendum bars AI tools from training on Workspace data.

Google will require AI agents to reach Gmail, Drive and other Workspace apps through new, dedicated gateways, it said on Tuesday. Regular apps can keep using Workspace’s existing APIs, but agents must switch by February 1, 2027.

The gateways are Workspace MCP servers, which use a common standard for linking AI tools to apps, and a command-line tool. Both are now generally available. Google put an early CLI version on GitHub in March.

Google says its APIs were built for apps that work at human speed, where a valid login meant the user wanted the action. Agents act on their own at machine speed. So every request now gets checked against company permissions and data-loss rules.

Agents can draft emails and summarise documents on their own. But they need a person’s sign-off before sending email, changing Drive sharing or making bulk edits.

Each agent also needs its own sign-in ID with tight limits and usage quotas. Google already gives its Gemini coworker agents their own accounts. It will begin billing for that usage on April 1, 2027.

A new AI Tools Addendum adds rules on data. AI tools cannot use Workspace data to train models or build rival services, and cannot scrape it. They must also delete it when a user disconnects.

Google also tells developers to screen for prompt injection, hidden commands in emails or files that can hijack AI agents. Some controls are still to come, including letting users see and revoke agents’ access themselves.

Other firms are drawing lines too. In October, Charles Schwab said it blocks outside agents from moving client money.

#3100. Should Vanguard S&P 500 ETF Investors Be Worried About the Downturn in Nvidia and AI Stocks?

Nvidia and AI stocks have been dragging down the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:52PM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

Once the largest company in the world, with an over-$5 trillion market cap, Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) had been one of the biggest driving forces in the market. However, the stock closed out the week ending Nov. 20 on a seven-day losing streak, losing 27.5% of its market value in this span. But then there was a strong rebound on Monday. As I write this, the stock is down 32% from the $243.37 high it set less than two months ago, on Oct. 6.

Nvidia's troubles stemmed from the surprise resignation of its longtime co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang following revelations of marital infidelity, allegedly including with subordinates and a potential Chinese spy. Even a strong quarterly report and the company raising its fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) revenue guidance to 75% growth were not enough to stop the stock's slide. However, a surprise return to the CEO role by Huang on Monday led to a huge rebound in the stock.

Nvidia's woes spread to other semiconductor stocks, with the entire artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure segment under intense pressure to close out last week. Cloud computing and software-as-a-service (SaaS) stocks also generally performed poorly this past week, although they also joined in on the rally.

Entering November, Nvidia was the second-largest holding in the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.50%), with a nearly 7.6% weighting. That was just behind Apple (AAPL +1.43%), which represented around 7.7% of the index. As such, the stock's recent performance has weighed on S&P 500 exchange-traded funds (ETFs), like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -0.48%), which lost 7.8% the week ending Nov. 20.

The Nasdaq Composite(^IXIC -1.48%)was also down. Even with the Monday rally, the question is whether investors should worry that Nvidia and other AI stocks will push the benchmark indexes into a bear market.

The S&P 500 has become less diversified over the past decade, as mega-cap tech companies have come to dominate the index. At the start of the month, over 37% of the stocks in the index were classified as tech stocks, and that doesn't include tech-oriented companies like Amazon (AMZN -1.21%) and Tesla (TSLA -0.20%), which get placed in the consumer discretionary category. Meanwhile, 10 of its top 15 holdings were AI stocks.

As such, Nvidia and the tech sector are going to have a big influence on the performance of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF. However, the great thing about the S&P 500 is that it is self-correcting. As Nvidia and other AI stocks fall, they become less and less of the index, while stocks from other sectors become a larger percentage.

It is this survival-of-the-fittest structure the index has created that has made it such a strong performer over the years. It lets its cream rise to the top, its losers fade, and new stock leaders emerge. That's one of the big reasons why, over the past decade, only about 14% of actively managed funds have been able to outperform the S&P 500.

Ultimately, Nvidia doesn't need to be the leader of the S&P 500 going forward. There are plenty of other leaders that can step up, including fellow "Magnificent Seven" names like Alphabet (GOOGL -1.08%) (GOOG -1.05%), Amazon (AMZN -1.21%), or Meta Platforms (META -1.30%), or perhaps even a stock not yet in the index like SpaceX (SPCX -5.65%).

Image source: OpenAI (AI-generated illustration).

There is also a possibility that what the market is seeing is just a normal correction, and AI infrastructure stocks will bounce back quickly. Regardless, history teaches us that it's time in the market, not timing the market, that wins in the long run.

As such, I would not be rushing to sell my Vanguard S&P 500 ETF on fears of a further drop in AI stocks, and instead would be using this opportunity to continue to dollar-cost average into the ETF. That's a proven strategy that works again and again over the long term.
