#3085. Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite

Anthony Vetro’s journey from multimedia pioneer to executive

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

At the 2025 IEEE Vision, Innovation, and Challenges Summit, IEEE Fellow Anthony Vetro discusses the need for open innovation models to keep pace with rapid technological change taking place at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories.

The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

Anthony Vetro Employer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.Title President and CEO Member grade FellowAlma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.

Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.

Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.

His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.

He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.

Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.

“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.

Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.

Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.

“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.

“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”

Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.

“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.

He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.

“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”

It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.

“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”

“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”

After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.

He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.

Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.

“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.

After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.

“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”

He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.

To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.

The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.

The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”

The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.

Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.

“Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.”

The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems.

The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says.

“The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard, MIT, and many other universities a stone’s throw away.”

Vetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says.

“In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences.

“In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.”

Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society. He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals.

He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program, launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences.

Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards: the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing.

“Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3084. Anthropic Stock Just Broke Below Its $83 IPO Price. Is It a Bargain Buy?

Anthropic fell below its $83 IPO price on its fourth trading day.

By Johnny Rice – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:55PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

On Thursday, the frontier AI lab Anthropic (ANT -6.54%) made its public debut, with the offering bringing in an incredible $93.5 billion at closing. That makes it the biggest in history -- bigger even than the record set by SpaceX (SPCX -5.65%) in June. With investors scrambling to get shares on day one, the stock opened at $111.50, well above the offer price of $83.

But today, on its fourth trading day as a public company, Anthropic stock is trading below that initial offer, hovering below $80.

So, is this a golden buying opportunity? Here's what you should consider before jumping in.

Before we look at Anthropic itself, it's useful to look at what the historical record says about how stocks perform after an IPO.

University of Florida professor emeritus Jay Ritter -- known as "Mr. IPO" for his research -- looked at more than 9,000 U.S. listings from 1980 through 2024. He found that the average stock gained about 19% on its first day. Investors who got in at the offer price trailed the broader market by 3.3 percentage points over the study's three-year window, while those who bought at the first-day close trailed it by 20.5 points.

OK, but that's a pretty wide data set. A narrower one with companies that are at least somewhat comparable -- admittedly hard when dealing with a company as unique as Anthropic -- will tell us more.

Companies already doing at least $1 billion in annual sales fared better, though they still finished 2.1 points behind the market when measured from the first-day close.

At about $80 a share, Anthropic is worth roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis that includes shares reserved for future issuance. The company's trailing 12-month revenue comes in at $35.3 billion, meaning the stock is trading at about 41 times sales. That is expensive.

Bulls argue that the company is at the very forefront of a technological revolution and its product is so valuable that it will grow into this valuation. It's a fair argument, especially given the pace of that growth -- revenue jumped from $1.4 billion to $17 billion year over year in Q3. That's basically unheard of at this scale.

If we assume last quarter's sales pace holds, you're paying about 21.5 times annualized sales at today's price, or about 16 times based on shares outstanding. That's still expensive -- Nvidia (NVDA -5.86%) trades at about 8 times annualized sales on that same outstanding-share basis -- but more in the realm of reason.

My concern is twofold -- one, spending, and two, moat (or lack thereof).

Anthropic's compute and infrastructure spending ate up 58% of sales in Q3, up from 48% in Q2, and Q2's $974 million operating profit turned back into a loss of $567 million. I'm still not convinced that this business can reliably turn a profit over time.

That's especially true if the company is forced to compete on price with other model providers in order to defend its market share. That's the problem with having, in my view, very little moat. The company's current advantage comes from having the best models.

That makes for a fairly shallow moat. Not only will it need to innovate relentlessly and spend incredible amounts training new models, but it may find itself with fewer and fewer customers willing to pay premium prices for those latest models when cheaper open-weight models can do the job.

Image source: OpenAI (AI-generated illustration).

So, while the company's dizzying growth makes today's price look like it could end up a bargain given a few years of expanding its top line at lightning speed, I would question whether the growth of the last two years is at all indicative of the growth in the next two. And if it is, what will earnings look like down the line?

#3082. Three xAI co-founders launch Epochal to teach AI to predict the future

Their first product lets AI agents browse a trillion-page archive of the web, frozen at any moment since the 1990s.

Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, three of xAI’s co-founders, have launched Epochal, a startup building AI that forecasts events. Zhang has put in $100M of his own money, Bloomberg reported. Its first product, Time Portal, lets agents browse the web as it was at past dates, so they can practise forecasting without seeing the outcome.

Three of xAI’s co-founders have launched Epochal, a startup that wants to teach AI to forecast events. Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss announced the company and its first product on Tuesday.

Zhang has put in $100M of his own money, Bloomberg reported. No other investors have been named.

All of xAI’s co-founders have since left the company, as Elon Musk rebuilds it after its merger with SpaceX. Another co-founder, Igor Babuschkin, raised $1.1bn for his own startup, River AI, in August.

Today’s AI models learn from an internet where they can already see how things turned out, Epochal says. People, by contrast, have to make choices before they know the result.

Its first product, Time Portal, lets AI agents browse the web as it looked at any moment over the past 30 years. Epochal says it covers more than 1 trillion pages, down to the minute on busy sites. A matching Linux sandbox sets its clock, software and downloads to the same date, so agents cannot spot the trick.

To test it, Epochal ran forecasting agents on 347 live questions from prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket. Weeks later, it replayed the same questions through Time Portal. In its own test, the replayed forecasts closely matched the originals, with a correlation of 0.98.

Developers can try a limited version for free. Epochal has not said how it gathered the archive or whether the pages are licensed.

#3081. Amentum (AMTM) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management outlines fiscal 2027 targets and a new $500 million buyback plan.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 24, 2026 at 2:56PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Amentum (AMTM +20.10%) completed its primary integration objectives and reached its net leverage targets during fiscal 2026. Management stated that the company is now entering a new phase of value creation focused on accelerating organic growth and driving operational excellence through technology-enabled solutions. The company reported expansion in its adjusted EBITDA margins and growth in free cash flow, supported by a mix shift toward higher-margin work in digital and nuclear markets. Management indicated that the business remains aligned with durable national security priorities and is positioned to return capital to shareholders through a newly authorized repurchase program while maintaining flexibility for strategic investments.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by, and good morning. Welcome to Amentum's Fiscal 2026 Fourth Quarter Earnings Conference Call. Today's call is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the call over to Joe DeNardi, Senior Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead, sir.

Joseph (Joe) William DeNardi: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. We hope you've had an opportunity to read our earnings release, which we issued yesterday afternoon and is posted on our Investor Relations website. We have also provided presentation slides to facilitate today's call. So let's move to Slide 2. Please note that this morning's discussion will contain forward-looking statements that are subject to important factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from anticipated. I refer you to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors including the Risk Factors section of our annual report on Form 10-K. The statements represent our views as of today, and subsequent events may cause our views to change.

We may elect to update the forward-looking statements at some point in the future, but specifically disclaim any obligation to do so, except as required by applicable law. In addition, we will discuss non-GAAP financial measures, which we believe provide useful information for investors. Both our earnings release and supplemental presentation slides include reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP measures. We do not provide reconciliations of forward-looking non-GAAP financial measures due to the inherent difficulty in forecasting and quantifying certain significant items. These non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for financial measures prepared in accordance with GAAP.

Our safe harbor statement included on this slide should be incorporated as part of any transcript of this call. With me today to discuss our business and financial results are John E. Heller, Chief Executive Officer; and Travis Barton Johnson, Chief Financial Officer. We are also joined by other members of management, including Steve Arnette, Chief Operating Officer. With that, moving to Slide 3, I'll turn the call over to John.

John E. Heller: Thank you, Joe, and good morning to everyone joining our call. Fiscal 2026 was a year of strong operational performance with continued business development momentum, expanding margins and substantial cash generation. Financial performance highlights, which Travis will cover in more detail shortly, include normalized revenue growth of 1% to $13.8 billion, adjusted EBITDA of $1.13 billion, benefiting from robust margin expansion of 50 basis points and growth in both adjusted diluted earnings per share and free cash flow of 13%. In addition, we successfully completed our primary integration objectives and reduced net leverage to 2.7x. Achieving these results has expanded our ability to invest in the business, return capital to shareholders and advance to the next phase of our strategy.

Accordingly, as we announced yesterday evening, the Board has authorized our first-ever $500 million share repurchase program, underscoring its confidence in the business and our ability to create long-term value. Looking to fiscal 2027, we expect underlying revenue growth of approximately 4%, excluding the impact from NASA insourcing, continued margin expansion and earnings growth, and to generate at least $600 million of free cash flow. Overall, we remain confident that the strategy we are executing is delivering tangible results with clear evidence of progress this year and momentum building for the future. Let's now turn to Slide 4 to review our fiscal 2026 business development highlights.

For the year, we exceeded our $35 billion submits target and delivered book-to-bill of 1.4 and 1.2x for the fourth quarter and full year, respectively, excluding the debooking related to contract changes at NASA. These results reflect the strength of our addressable markets and sustained demand for our differentiated solutions. Just as importantly, our team successfully supported this high level of activity through disciplined execution, scalable processes and a relentless commitment to customer outcomes. Looking ahead, we remain focused on leveraging technology, including AI, to drive greater efficiency, enhance our capabilities and further differentiate our solutions in the marketplace.

Our awards this year demonstrate continued expansion into attractive higher-margin growth markets, including data analytics, space and missile defense and global nuclear energy, while also validating our differentiated capabilities in technology-enabled infrastructure, advanced training and complex mission support solutions. Let me highlight 3 examples from the fourth quarter. First, we secured an $800 million 10-year award with the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency to deliver technology-enabled facilities and system solutions for its Washington D.C. campus. This award underscores our expertise in supporting complex mission-critical infrastructure for the intelligence community. Second, we received a new $700 million 5-year award supporting the Navy's live, virtual and constructive integrated training solutions environment.

The program highlights our differentiated capabilities in advancing training solutions and simulation and will help enhance mission readiness through increasingly sophisticated integrated training solutions. Third, an Amentum-led joint venture in the United Kingdom was selected as preferred supplier for a $2.8 billion program to provide full life cycle capabilities at Sellafield, one of the world's largest and most complex nuclear decommissioning and waste management sites. Our selection demonstrates Amentum's reputation for excellent program delivery performance and a commitment to innovation, including the deployment of technologies such as digital visualization and advanced robotics.

These 3 awards, together with our other notable wins and strong bid activity across the portfolio, contributed to year-end backlog of $48 billion, including an 8% year-over-year increase in funded backlog to $6 billion and pending awards of $25 billion, providing a strong foundation for growth moving forward. Turning to Slide 5 for an update on our areas of strategic focus. Fiscal 2026 marked an important milestone as we completed all major integration objectives and delivered on the key commitments we established following the merger, including achieving our cost synergy targets, maintaining a book-to-bill above 1x and reducing net leverage below 3x.

With those objectives achieved, we are entering the next phase of value creation by intensifying our focus on 3 priorities that have been central to our strategy: accelerating organic growth; driving operational excellence; and allocating our capital in a disciplined manner. First, we will accelerate organic growth by bringing differentiated technology-enabled solutions to our customers' most complex mission challenges. We are shaping opportunities earlier, concentrating resources on our highest value pursuits and moving more quickly from award to revenue. In fiscal 2027, this translates to mid-single-digit growth, excluding NASA, driven by defense, space, global nuclear energy and homeland security.

Together with our backlog, pending awards and pipeline this momentum gives us confidence that we can deliver and sustain profitable growth going forward. Second, we will continue to expand margins by focusing on accretive end markets, driving operational excellence and moving innovative solutions into the field faster. We see increasing opportunities to win based on our solutions and are investing selectively in technologies that can be demonstrated for our customers in their operating environments as a result. This approach is allowing us to meet changing customer priorities, which are increasingly focused on speed and solutions, including the use of flexible acquisition pathways to accelerate the transition from prototype to production.

For example, Amentum has been awarded 16 OTAs, including 9 over the past year, with combined potential contract values over $1 billion. Across the contracts we have won, we engineer and develop prototypes to enable a number of high-priority Department of War capabilities from thermal management for hypersonics to ground-based testing of national security space systems. Internally, we are increasingly looking to apply AI and process performance tools in areas like program management, cash generation and back-office operations. Combined with continued process improvements, disciplined contracting and a growing mix of higher-margin work, these actions will help us execute more effectively, drive margin expansion and create additional capacity to invest in the next phase of our growth strategy.

Third, we will make investments, deploy capital and manage our portfolio to drive long-term shareholder value. This includes continuing to take a strategic approach in directing investment, talent and business development resources toward markets where customer demand is durable, our capabilities are differentiated and we have the strongest right to win. It also means continuously evaluating our portfolio to ensure it remains aligned with our long-term strategy and financial objectives. Lastly, we will focus capital deployment on areas that produce the highest risk-adjusted rate of return. In the near term, we expect to prioritize share repurchases while assessing selective acquisitions that add differentiated capabilities and meet rigorous strategic and financial criteria.

Together, these priorities are designed to improve execution and margins in the near term while positioning the portfolio to drive faster growth and long-term shareholder value. Turning to Slide 6. As we have discussed previously, one of the clearest opportunities for growth is in our nuclear business, where Amentum combines deep technical expertise, differentiated customer relationships, global reach and full life cycle capabilities in a market seeing substantial investment. These strengths and the actions we are taking to expand them provide a natural example of how we intend to focus resources in markets where we believe we have compelling competitive advantages and significant growth potential.

The nuclear market continues to gain momentum, driven by growing demand for reliable, secure energy and advancements in next-generation nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors. Customers are pursuing fleet scale reactor deployment, accelerating licensing and regulatory execution, and exploring innovative power solutions to support expanding digital infrastructure needs and national security priorities. As investment accelerates, demand for experienced engineering, licensing and program management solutions continues to grow. Our global technical workforce and continued investment in talent position us well to support increasingly complex nuclear programs at scale. We are seeing encouraging signs of progress across technical, regulatory and financial fronts.

Recent strategic investment commitments from Japan and South Korea provides substantial funding for U.S. nuclear development, including small modular reactors and large-scale generation while strengthening the domestic supply chain and supporting deployment at scale. This momentum is particularly evident at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, where next-generation nuclear OEMs are advancing technologies and moving toward deployment. We recently opened Amentum's global nuclear headquarters in Oak Ridge to enhance collaboration, accelerate innovation and expand our capacity to serve customers. We are also developing the industry's long-term talent pipeline through initiatives such as the Amentum Nuclear Scholars Program, in partnership with leading institutions, including the University of Tennessee.

Together, these investments strengthen our competitive positioning and support our strategy of concentrating resources in markets with attractive long-term growth opportunities. In closing, we enter fiscal 2027 with a strong backlog and pipeline of pending awards, expanding margins, strong free cash flow and greater capacity to return capital to shareholders. Our priority is to deliver on our fiscal 2027 commitments while investing in the markets and capabilities that can accelerate growth and compound value for shareholders over time. With that, I'll now turn the call over to Travis.

Travis Barton Johnson: Thank you, John, and good morning, everyone. I'm excited to discuss with you today another solid quarter and successful finish to fiscal year 2026, highlighted by continued strong operational performance, improved margins and profitability and robust cash generation. I'll also provide an update on our capital deployment priorities, including our first-ever $500 million share repurchase program John mentioned earlier and review our outlook for fiscal year 2027, and which is consistent with our remarks on the third quarter call and reflects growth across all key metrics. Turning to Slide 7. I'll review our financial performance on a normalized basis excluding the impact of the prior year extra week, joint venture transitions and divestitures.

Revenue totaled $3.6 billion for the quarter and $13.8 billion for the year, both reflecting 1% normalized growth as the ramp-up of new contract awards and on-contract growth more than offset the expected completion of certain legacy programs. Adjusted EBITDA of $304 million in the quarter resulted in $1.13 billion for the full year, reflecting adjusted EBITDA margin expansion of 50 basis points to 8.2%. The strong margin performance is well ahead of our original expectations and was enabled by accelerated progress in our margin expansion strategy, including a favorable mix shift and strong operational performance.

Adjusted net income was $173 million for the quarter and $615 million for the year, which generated adjusted diluted earnings per share of $0.71 and $2.51, respectively. Adjusted EPS grew 13% year-over-year, driven by the strong operational performance as well as lower interest expense following our successful debt reduction and refinancing actions. Moving to our reportable segment results on Slide 8. Digital Solutions generated revenue of $1.5 billion for the quarter and $5.7 billion for the year, representing 8% and 7% normalized growth, respectively. Year-over-year increases were driven by the continued ramp-up of previously discussed new contract awards in our digital infrastructure and space markets.

Adjusted EBITDA increased to $117 million for the quarter and $441 million for the year, resulting in full year adjusted EBITDA margins of 7.7%. Turning to Slide 9. Global Engineering Solutions revenue was $2.1 billion for the quarter and $8.1 billion for the year, both reflecting the expected ramp down of certain historical programs, partially offset by contributions from new contract awards and on-contract growth. Adjusted EBITDA increased to $187 million for the quarter and $691 million for the year, resulting in full year growth of 4% and adjusted EBITDA margins of 8.5%. Now turning to Slide 10 to cover our cash flow and capital structure highlights.

Fourth quarter free cash flow was robust at $370 million, ahead of our expectations driven by strong cash earnings, disciplined working capital management and lower cash taxes and resulted in a 13% increase for the full year to $583 million. The strong performance enabled additional debt repayments of $300 million during the quarter, bringing full year repayments to $434 million and reducing our net leverage to 2.7x, completing a key post-merger objective and giving us greater flexibility in deploying capital. As we have said previously, we will allocate capital to opportunities that offer the strongest long-term returns while maintaining net leverage within our target range of 2 to 3x.

In the near term, share repurchases will be a primary use of excess capital, which we will execute under our recently authorized $500 million share repurchase program. Given conviction shared by our leadership team and the Board in Amentum's ability to grow earnings and generate substantial free cash flow, we are confident that share repurchases will be accretive to long-term shareholder value. We intend to opportunistically repurchase shares under this authorization while targeting net leverage at fiscal year 2027 year-end below 2.5x. Given the current interest rate environment, we believe this approach properly balances returning capital to shareholders, while further strengthening our balance sheet for strategic optionality to drive durable growth and free cash flow per share over time.

Looking ahead, let's turn to Slides 11 and 12 to discuss our fiscal year 2027 guidance. We entered the year with improved visibility, including approximately 94% of revenue coming from backlog or recompetes, 3 points higher than at this time last year. We expect revenue in the range of $13.8 billion to $14.05 billion, reflecting reported growth of 1% at the midpoint and 4%, excluding the impact from NASA insourcing. With the insourcing actions now substantially complete, our head count supporting NASA has stabilized, and we believe the business has reached a level from which it can grow as mission requirements expand.

Mid-single-digit growth across the rest of the portfolio is expected to be driven by a lower headwind from program completions than in recent years, the new business wins John mentioned earlier and growth on existing programs. From a timing perspective, we expect revenue of approximately $3.15 billion in Q1 as NASA insourcing and program completions offset the benefit from last year's government shutdown. Following Q1, we expect quarterly sequential increases as the program completion headwinds moderate and newly awarded programs ramp up throughout the year.

We expect adjusted EBITDA in the range of $1.135 billion to $1.175 billion, reflecting adjusted EBITDA margins of 8.3% at the midpoint, balancing investments for long-term growth with continued execution of our margin expansion strategy and benefits from operational performance. We expect adjusted diluted earnings per share of $2.50 to $2.70, which assumes a flat share count year-over-year and tax rate of approximately 24.5%. And finally, we expect free cash flow to be greater than $600 million, driven by higher cash earnings, lower integration-related payments and reduced cash interest from our debt reduction initiatives, all of which will be partially offset by higher cash taxes given one-time benefits in fiscal year 2026.

In closing, fiscal year 2026 marked an important milestone for Amentum as we successfully completed our integration commitments while continuing to strengthen the business and enhance our financial profile. With growing momentum across our markets, a strong backlog, robust pipeline and disciplined capital allocation strategy, we believe we are well positioned to accelerate growth, expand profitability and deliver long-term value for shareholders. With that, operator, we are ready for questions.

John E. Heller: Yes. Thanks, Seth, and good morning to you and everyone. This is John. Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Gavin Parsons with UBS.

Gavin Parsons: Guys, I just wanted to ask about the phasing of revenue throughout the year, if we're starting down 3% and ramping sequentially. Travis Barton Johnson: Yes, sure. A couple of different things to point out as we look at the progression of revenue throughout the year. I guess the first thing that I would say is that it follows kind of typical seasonality trends that the business has historically experienced, Q1 typically the lowest due to a variety of different reasons, including working days and Q4 being the strongest. So from that perspective, it's fairly consistent with historical trends. There are a few other dynamics that I'll call out for FY '27 specifically to give additional color. First, relative to the prior year in Q1, you can think about the NASA insourcing that we've talked about, largely offsetting the benefit from last year's government shutdown.

And in Q1 and in Q2, there's going to be a larger impact from program completions that moderate in the second half. And then finally, the second half will benefit from the ramp-up of newly awarded programs, many of which John mentioned in his prepared remarks, including the U.S. Army program in Germany, NITE and some of the classified intel work we mentioned. So you can think about the progression of growth throughout the year being a combination of lesser headwinds from program completions as well as incremental growth from new business.

But maybe more importantly, a few things that, obviously, we look at to make sure we have confidence in our outlook and the guidance that we're providing are the leading indicators. And I'll highlight just a few that underpin our guidance this year. First is that we have 94% of revenue coming from firm or recompete work. That's up 3 points relative to where it was last year at the same time. We have an 8% increase in funded backlog. So good visibility there.

And then finally, as it relates to kind of pending awards and business development, we have $25 billion of pending awards, which is up 25% from this time last year with good line of sight for a good majority of that to be awarded in the first half of '27. So taking all that together, we will see kind of the typical progression that we see throughout the year, but have good visibility into where the revenue needs to come from.

Gavin Parsons: Okay. I appreciate all that detail. And then any update you can share on Savannah River?

John E. Heller: Yes. But at this time, we're not reporting anything specific. The work progresses, and we do expect to see progress throughout the fiscal year that we can discuss in greater detail. But this is an exciting opportunity to not just be involved in bringing additional power capacity to the Southeast and to help develop power that will enable development of one of the largest data center projects in the country. But again, we're in the middle of those discussions right now.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Ken Herbert with RBC Capital Markets.

Travis Barton Johnson: Yes. So in firm, we have 90% of our revenue coming from firm, which anticipates all revenue from backlog, which includes a typical amount of on-contract growth, low single digits that we typically experience. And that's up 3 percentage points from where we were at this time last year, Recompetes is 4% of that, which is consistent with the prior year and then new business, which is 6% of revenue. So in a really good place relative to where we were at last year at this time on the visibility we have on where the revenue is going to come from in FY '27.

Kenneth (Ken) Herbert: Okay. And as we look at the new wins and obviously the backlog growth, can you talk about what you're seeing in terms of implied margins of that business? I mean, obviously, we've got the '27 guide here. But what kind of longer-term margin expansion could we see? Or would the more recent wins and backlog growth support as we think about margins over time?

Travis Barton Johnson: Yes, certainly. The first thing I would start with is just the excitement and how proud we are of the team for what they were able to accomplish in FY '26. Growing the business margins 50 basis points in 1 year is certainly above our expectations. And I think it speaks to the focus of our teams that despite some of the challenges we saw on revenue, we were able to deliver EBITDA through disciplined program execution, indirect cost control, acceleration of synergies, continued focus on higher-margin work, a higher composition of fixed price work. So FY '26, that was really a highlight for us.

As we look to FY '27, you'll see that we're balancing margin expansion with investments for growth. So we do have some targeted investments that we're going to make in the business where we see accelerated growth opportunities. You can think areas like nuclear. So that will obviously require some investment. But offsetting that, we still have 20 basis margin expansion baked in for operational performance, continued mix shift that we're excited about. And we think that can continue into the future beyond FY '27 as we continue to refine and focus on the higher-margin markets that we serve.

And also from an operational efficiency perspective, we have a lot of initiatives that we're beginning to ramp up that you'll hear us talk more about as we move through FY '27 on just running the business more efficiently from a back-office perspective, et cetera, and using AI and technology to deliver for customers in a more efficient way, which obviously benefit our fixed price and T&M programs.

John E. Heller: And we've really highlighted this the last few quarters, and we're seeing it come to fruition with the performance this year with the 50 basis point margin improvement. It's really driven by the company strategy. It's focusing on areas like digital systems, nuclear, space, RDT&E, and the core of our strategy to focus on enduring long-term projects focused on well-funded national security priorities, utilizing technology to deliver enhanced value for our customers that can allow us to compete in higher-margin end markets and then operating extremely efficiently, as Travis mentioned, to drive free cash flow, which is what's happening.

Our team is doing an exceptional job on all those fronts, and it's coming out in the performance that you're seeing in this report.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Tobey Sommer with Truist Securities.

Tobey Sommer: I wanted to get a little bit of color on potential M&A and tuck-ins in your growth areas. Are there any constraints that you'll try to solve for from a multiple perspective or a margin perspective or sort of accretive to EPS? Any guidelines you could give us for your philosophy on M&A would be helpful.

Travis Barton Johnson: Yes, sure. I'll start, and then maybe John can also provide some commentary. I think the first thing I'd say is we're really proud of the cash generation we've been able to deliver on since the merger that it ultimately is resulting in our -- in a position that we're in to have more flexibility as it relates to capital deployment. And with net leverage now at 2.7x and obviously, the share repurchase authorization that we announced yesterday evening, we're in a position to have greater flexibility in how we allocate excess capital.

Obviously, we've signaled that our current valuation provides an attractive opportunity to invest in our own business while maintaining flexibility to fund organic growth, pursue strategic acquisitions, which is at the heart of your question, and also preserve a prudent balance sheet. We've also signaled that we expect net leverage below 2.5x. So I think that just shows our commitment to make sure we're maintaining that optionality and flexibility moving forward. And as it relates to M&A, obviously, we've said that we're going to focus on the capital deployment opportunities that provide the highest risk-adjusted rate of return.

So you'll think about our M&A as being capability focused and it's going to have to meet very high strategic and financial criteria to ensure that we adhere to that commitment.

John E. Heller: And I think trust is really important. And when we set out over 2 years ago, we said our focus was on getting leverage below 3x and we focused on that as a leadership team, focusing on integration, organic growth and cash flow. And we're now excited about being at 2.7 leverage and continuing to focus on delevering and now with the opportunity to have a share repurchase program. But at the same time, we'll look to invest in our business. But we're going to focus on investments in those higher-margin accretive end markets that we've discussed around Digital Solutions, cyber, space and nuclear that we think have great tailwinds, generational tailwinds that can help drive our business forward.

But as Travis said, we're going to be very judicious in how we deploy cash in a way that can drive the best shareholder value.

Tobey Sommer: If I may ask a follow-up in your guidance for '27, do you -- is there any difference in the rate of growth between your domestic business and your international exposure? And if so, kind of which one is leading the way?

Travis Barton Johnson: There's no material difference between the domestic and international growth in the '27 guide.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Andre Madrid with U.S. Bancorp BTIG.

Andre Madrid: I wanted to start first on maybe FY '27 outlook at a segment level. How should we be thinking about growth and EBITDA expectations through the year looking at the 2 segments?

Travis Barton Johnson: So it's interesting as you look at it at a segment level. Obviously, this year, Digital Solutions had a remarkable year from an organic growth perspective, delivering 8% growth in the fourth quarter, 7% for the year. Obviously, the NASA insourcing will impact the growth trajectory of that segment next year. So you can think about it being down low to mid-single digits as a result of that NASA headwind.

At the same time, we saw margins stabilize in that segment in the back half of the year, and that's going to provide a good launch point for them as we head into FY '27, and I think they'll be the predominant driver of the margin expansion that we expect in the year. And then on Global Engineering Solutions, obviously, a little bit of an opposite story there. Growth was a little bit more pressured in FY '26, but we've had some really nice wins in that segment that are going to drive the growth in FY '27 with NITE, the U.S. Army work we're doing in Germany, just to name a few things. And then we'll expect their margins.

They had 100 basis points margin expansion in FY '26. So we'll expect that to be consistent as we head into FY '27.

Andre Madrid: Got it. That's really helpful. And then maybe just looking ahead of '27, I'm not trying to piece out what your what you guys are anticipating. But you have provided the 4% to 6% long-term growth outlook previously even excluding the NASA impact this year, you're kind of at the low end of the range. I'm really just trying to understand what gets you -- what would need to happen to see the midpoint or even the high end of your long-term growth outlook? And maybe even beyond that, like what's the bull case here that you guys foresee that would get you to, I guess, at the midpoint or the higher end of your range?

Travis Barton Johnson: Yes, I'll offer a few thoughts, and John might add as well. I think you're exactly right in thinking about exactly how we're thinking about it. First, the underlying business is going to grow 4% this year, excluding the impact of NASA. So that's a good launch point as we head into FY '28 and beyond. Second, I think you got to look at the leading indicators in our business development performance that we've seen since the merger, 1.2x in FY '25, 1.2x in FY '26, excluding the NASA debooking that we saw. So the business development engine is working. We continue to see strong demand for our solutions that we offer to our customers.

We continue to see a high volume. We exceeded our $35 billion submits target this year, as John noted in his prepared remarks, and as I said earlier, we're ending the year in $25 billion of pending awards. So we think that the foundation for that mid-single-digit growth continues to be there, and kind of the history there, excluding the headwinds, which we don't expect things like NASA to continue into the future, give us a good confidence in how growth will look '28 and beyond.

John E. Heller: I also think it's our end market focus. We've talked a lot about space that we are in a very solid position in terms of the work we do across NASA, Missile Defense Agency, Space Force and the growing demand for services and technology that's going to drive that market forward and where we sit right in the epicenter of all that. Our work in cyber, which we continue to see the challenge and the opportunity that exists in the cyber area across every end market that we support, every customer. And then of course, nuclear in general, that this is a market that is starting to expand with many different projects in the works.

As these projects come online, our revenue profile increases and it's going to take time for some of these projects to matriculate and you think of the SMR areas, we are working with a large number of OEMs in helping bring SMR technology to certification level so that they can begin construction. Once these designs get approved and these projects move into production, that will mean a significant uptick. And we put out a profile, and it's in today's presentation that shows '26 to '30, '30 to '35, the growth we expect in the nuclear market.

And we're still confident we had showed this to everyone in the past, and we wanted to reiterate that based on the confidence we're seeing in the nuclear market in general. And we expect to see that be a key driver of growth '28 and beyond.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Greg Parrish with Morgan Stanley.

Gregory (Greg) Parrish: Congrats on the quarter. Maybe just starting with the 4% normalized top line guidance. I mean, how would you characterize the level of conservatism built in? Is there room to outperform some of the newly awarded contracts that are built in? Is there risk from any protest there? Just maybe help us with the line of sight.

Travis Barton Johnson: Sure. I would say, just like any year, we provide a range that provides a variety of different potential outcomes. That said, I think it's a reasonable guide. And I also say, just repeat what I said earlier in the fact that we've got better visibility this year at this time than we had last year, right? So we still have 6% of new business to achieve, but we've got a good line of sight into that. Nice start to the year here in the first quarter, but still have work to do. But coming from a position of strength with 94% in firm or recompete is certainly a good place to start the year.

And then also having a few contracts which are already in transition. We're not dependent on protest resolution on them. They were already protested once, and now they're out of protest, and we've actually begun work on them in the first quarter here. NITE is a good example of that. U.S. Army work we're doing in Germany, another good example of that.

John E. Heller: Yes. And I think if you look at the market environment, too, I think it's important to understand that we're seeing pretty good stable bid volume. We're -- of course, protests are normal and occur in just about every instance. So we factor that in, but we're pretty satisfied with the bid volume. Awards are slower. It just take -- still take some time. I think there are -- what you would say, our customers are faced with a number of priorities like war in the Middle East and that -- and the administration changes in policy and other things. But we've seen these in the past.

And although we haven't seen necessarily an opportunity to see some of these factors disappear. We have tried to reflect that in our guidance going forward.

Gregory (Greg) Parrish: Yes, fair enough. That's all very helpful. And then maybe just one on the defense budget. How do you view the Senate version? I'm not sure if there's anything to call out there. And then what are your big items that you're watching for in the final bill?

John E. Heller: Well, we fully expect that there will be bipartisan support for defense spending. So I think everyone is kind of expecting that somewhere between $1 trillion and $1.1 trillion. But frankly, we're not counting on anything specific in the budget itself, as long as we're in that range, I mean, let's face it, this is still significantly higher than we have seen in prior years. So from our perspective, it remains -- the outlook still remains positive. Also keep in mind that 20% of our revenue is derived from other than U.S. government sources and those end markets, international, AUKUS in Australia, where we have seen recent success and very excited about the future there.

The U.K. both on the defense and nuclear infrastructure side and then overall nuclear energy itself driving demand for our business. So we feel pretty comfortable about the U.S. budget expectations, along with the non-U.S. sources of revenue remaining strong and supportive of our plan for '27.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Trevor Walsh with Citizens JMP.

Trevor Walsh: Travis, you touched on it a little bit in one of the prior answers to a couple of questions ago. But you mentioned the $35 billion in submit bid volume kind of target made for '26. Are you able to provide or maybe even just at a high level, give us a sense of what the magnitude of that is going to be in '27 as far as expected bids and how that's factoring or not into guidance?

John E. Heller: Yes. And we talked about a very strong year in '26, probably above our expectations in some respects, and that was great. Some of those might have been a little bit earlier than we expected, which drove the number up. But we're still expecting for '27 around $35 billion, and hopefully, we set that kind of expectation with our team. Our team does a great job of identifying work and trying to exceed expectations. So at a minimum, we're confident in our pipeline that we can hit that $35 billion submit target again.

Travis Barton Johnson: The other thing that I'd add is we're focused on quality, not just quantity, and making sure that we're pursuing the opportunities where we have the highest right to win, and our capabilities are best aligned with what the requirements of the customer are. So it's -- volume can ebb and flow depending on what's out there, but we're just as much focused on the quality of the opportunity. And the second thing I would say as it relates to '27, we're not counting on a significant volume of submit award translate to revenue in the fiscal year '27. So really, what we're going to be submitting in '27 will have an impact in '28 and beyond.

Trevor Walsh: Got it. Super helpful. Appreciate it both. Maybe just a quick follow-up, more on just some cash flow dynamics. Anything to call out as far as seasonality in '27? I appreciate the build you provided for cash flow for the full year, over $600 million. Anything quarterly we should think about that's maybe different this year? And then just generally speaking, I know you're not going beyond '27, but as we think about maybe those tax payments that seem to be kind of coming in a little bit, is that about what we should expect, Travis, kind of in the year-to-year just range or I guess, just size of that going forward now?

Or just trying to get a little bit more how we don't want to get over our skis as far as free cash flow in and out years.

Travis Barton Johnson: Yes, sure. We're really happy with how we ended the year from a free cash flow perspective, came in a little bit above our expectations due to some working capital timing as well as lower cash tax payments we were able to realize from some tax planning initiatives. So really nice place to end the year coming in above the high end of our guidance range there. Obviously, like I said, there could be some timing associated with that. But looking to FY '27, we're confident in our ability to deliver greater than $600 million. And from a time phasing perspective, you may recall in '26, there was a bit of a difference in the number of pay periods.

That will be consistent from '26 to '27. So you can expect the cadence to be relatively consistent with what you saw in FY '26. The only thing I would call out that might be a little different is we did have the impact of the government shutdown in Q1 of last year, which was roughly $100 million and then that recovered in the second quarter of '26. So we'll expect that to be a little bit more normalized in '27. But other than that, the cadence will remain pretty consistent with Q1 being an outflow quarter, call it, $75 million to $100 million and Q4 being the strongest quarter.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Ronald Epstein with Bank of America.

Andrew Steinhardt: This is Andrew Steinhardt on for Ron. I guess, just first here, how are you guys thinking about the potential impacts of an extended CR into calendar 2027? Is that scenario a threat to any existing work in the portfolio or more so an impact to potential awards on new programs?

John E. Heller: Yes. I mean we've been through this, I don't know, just about every year. And we have seen minimal impact in the past, and we expect the same thing. Our work is very tied to critical mission support. And of course, 20% of our work is not U.S. government as well. So of the U.S. government work, we have traditionally seen minimal impact from CR given the work we're doing is funded long-term contracts, average contract length, 7 to 8 years and tied to basic critical missions that have to get done for the government to operate. So just we're expecting minimal to no impact.

Andrew Steinhardt: Got it. Got it. Makes sense. And just a quick follow-up. I guess, just in terms of the capital allocation strategy with the $500 million authorized for buybacks. Where do your guys' priorities stand beyond share buybacks?

Travis Barton Johnson: Yes. So a few thoughts there. First, I think we wanted to be transparent on where we were focused in the near term, given the opportunity that we think the current valuation presents -- the opportunity that the current valuation presents. So we provided that we're targeting to deploy 50% in FY '27 of the $500 million share repurchase authorization. At the same time, we're focused on maintaining a prudent balance sheet and signaled that we intend to end the year with net leverage less than 2.5x.

And then looking at M&A still from a capability, strategic focus is still going to be on the road map, but as we talked about earlier, it's going to have to be aligned with clear strategic and financial criteria to move that forward. So that's how we're thinking about it here in the near term.

John E. Heller: I think we've outlined our strategy this past year, our focus on key national security end markets and nuclear. I outlined some of those again on this call. We think we're having great progress in areas like space and cyber and nuclear and digital. And frankly, we think the market undervalues Amentum. And we're confident of the strength of this company and the value of this company. And as the market undervalues it, we see it as an opportunity given our strong free cash flow. And so that, I think we have great conviction on. And as long as the market undervalues it's an opportunity from our perspective. But at the same time, our focus is on investing organically.

And if necessary, making other investments in the business to drive our growth in those core end markets that we're confident in.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Matt Akers with BNP Paribas.

Matthew (Matt) Akers: Most of mine have been answered. I just wanted to follow up on NASA. And just curious how much of your business remain that's with NASA? And just how are your discussions going with that customer in terms of do they want to start to grow the remaining portion of your business, or just kind of the general outlook for that customer?

Stephen Arnette: Yes. As we actually covered in the prepared remarks, NASA has moved to speed on executing the plan. And so they're really essentially complete with all of their insourcing actions, so that happened pretty quickly. Our remaining NASA business today know that our head count has stabilized, still is at a run rate of about $1 billion annually. So all that is good. And then to the second part of your question, we do and are already positioning for future opportunities with the agency. The fact remains we've established a many-decade partnership and based on the basis of successful engineering and scientific support to their missions. We are excited about specific growth opportunities that are in the future for us.

And so this year will be a reset to the lower revenue level. But beyond that, we think we'll begin to regrow from that baseline.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. This concludes today's call. You may now disconnect.

#3080. iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using

iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.

Since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of users have encountered—including Justin Bieber—it’s very easy to hit by accident.

Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

Will you disable the audio button in Messages? Let us know in the comments.
